project_abstract_text: Peptide sequence periodicity is a simple design tool that can be used to generate functional peptide-based surface coatings. De novo designed peptide N3-PEG-VK16 is characterized by a hydrophobic periodicity of two that avidly binds to native polystyrene priming its surface for subsequent targeted functionalization via chemical ligation. The peptidic portion of N3-PEG-VK16 is responsible for surface binding, converting polystyrene's hydrophobic surface into a wettable and electrostatically charged environment that facilitates cell attachment. Native polystyrene surfaces are coated by simple peptide adsorption from an aqueous buffered solution and the resulting primed surface easily functionalized by cycloaddition chemistry. Herein, we show that ligating a vitronectin-derive peptide to primed polystyrene surfaces enable adhesion, expansion, long-term culture and phenotype maintenance of human induced pluripotent stem cells.

project_title: Identification and characterization of FGF target genes
project_abstract_text: Fibroblast Growth Factor (FGF) signaling is one of the major mechanisms through which cells communicate to each other. We are nearing completion of a publication draft wherein we describe the defects that occur when we inactivate the FGF receptors (Fgfr1 and Fgfr2) in the presomitic mesoderm of the early mouse embryo. An attractive approach to charactizing these embryos and identifying FGF target genes that are regulated by FGFR1 or FGFR2 or both, would be to sequence the RNA in the relevant single cells of these embryo. However, this is a challenge given that a large number of embryos at the precise embryonic stage must be collected and genotyped for this effort. Heretofore, we could not freeze embryos, making such an effort extremely arduous. However, we have now used a new technology from !0X Genomics (Chromium Single Cell Gene Expression Flex) that has allowed us to generate RNA from single cells in embryos that we have frozen. This innovation allows us to access the transciptome of mutant embryos with unprecedented precision.

project_title: Retrovirus Biology
project_abstract_text: We have continued our collaboration with Dr. Yun-Xing Wang of the Protein-Nucleic Acid Interaction Section, Center for Structural Biology, CCR, NCI-FCRF. In the past, this collaboration has analyzed the 3-dimensional structure of the Rev Response Element (RRE), a functional element in HIV-1 RNA that is required for the export of unspliced and singly spliced viral RNAs from the nucleus. Using small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), we reported several years ago that the 351-base RRE forms an 'A' shape in solution (Fang et al., Cell, 2013). This structure was completely unanticipated and was of great interest, particularly since the distance between the 'legs' of the A seemed to correspond well with the dimensions of the viral Rev protein dimer that is known to interact with the RRE. We highlighted the significance of this distance in further detailed studies of RRE structure and function (O'Carroll et al., J. Virol., 2017). More recently, Dr. Wang has developed the use of Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) as a tool for the determination of 3-dimensional RNA structures. The special virtue of AFM for these studies is that information can be obtained from images of single RNA molecules; this is unlike the great majority of structure-determination techniques in which information from numerous molecules is pooled or averaged before analysis. This feature is especially important for RNA as RNA is so flexible that a population of identical RNA molecules will inevitably contain a mixture of different conformations. Dr. Wang has devised computational methods for the sorting of images into groups of related structures and the refinement of structural models from these images (Ding et al., Nature Comm. 2023; Degenhardt et al., submitted). Preliminary results using these new methodologies provide striking confirmation of the 'A' shape of the RRE. It is hoped that the high-resolution information expected with these techniques could enable the design of new antiviral reagents targeting the RRE.

project_title: Characterization of the Osteosarcoma Genome
project_abstract_text: Osteosarcoma (OSA) is a rare bone tumor of children, adolescents, and adults. There is considerable variability in the clinical presentation and tumor histology of OSA. Some forms such as parosteal osteosarcoma can be managed by surgery alone. In contrast, high grade OSA's remain vexing to clinicians and the cause of morbidity and mortality in patients. Multidisciplinary management with neoadjuvant chemotherapy and surgery benefit many patients. However, the propensity of these tumors to metastasize and the relative dearth of new therapeutics leaves many patients without curative options. Our goal is to characterize the OSA genome and identify options for new therapeutic approaches and to define aspects of the genome that can be used as biomarkers. From our collaboration with the Children's Oncology Group we have developed a significant multi-omics dataset for previously untreated patients under the age of 40. Our study also includes array based RNA and DNA methylation data as well as q-PCR miRNA expression data generated in collaborating laboratories. These data have been deposited in public databases. Currently, we are continuing to investigate candidate clinically relevant genomic biomarkers and continue to identify genes and pathways which may have therapeutic implications. Significant results include the recognition that nearly all osteosarcomas contain mutations in TP53 and/or other cell cycle regulators. Gain of function is almost exclusively the consequence of gene copy number amplification with only rare activating mutations of signal transduction genes. We noted a robust pattern of co-occurence and mutual exclusion of molecular properties in the dataset. As a result, we are now able to classify osteosarcoma tumors into groups based on these molecular features. We have also gained insights into the mechanisms and specific events that shape the exceptionally complex genomes of these tumors. Remarkably, multiple mechanisms leading to genome rearrangements can coexist in one tumor (e.g. kataegis, chromothripsis, extrachromosomal DNA, and complex linear rearrangements. Although osteosarcoma is not responsive to current immunotherapies, we have identified a protective inflammatory signature that strongly suggests that the immune microenvironment is related to clinical outcomes. These data provide a resource for future analyses and point to numerous opportunities for preclinical research. Tumor clonality and divergence is extremely important in the context of precision therapies for osteosarcoma. Diverse clones are likely to have diverse response to targeted therapies with selective pressure from such therapies being likely to promote expansion of pre-existing resistant clones. It is particularly difficult to study clonal evolution in human primary tumors as samples collected at diagnosis are typically too small for these analyses. Efforts to use single cell analysis of human primary tumors are promising, but due to the rarity of OSA, it is difficult to collect a large sample set. Currently, canine osteosarcoma presents an excellent opportunity to attack some of the more difficult aspects of OSA biology in the context of a naturally occurring OSA model. As we and others have reported, canine osteosarcoma is similar to the human disease in many respects. The high frequency of OSA in large breed dogs, the use of chemotherapy post-operatively, and the rapid recurrence of disease provide excellent opportunities for clinical and translational research. Our overarching hypothesis is that comparative genomics studies in human and canine OSA will help to deconvolute the complexities found in both species. In collaboration with the CCR veterinary oncology program collaborative studies with Dr. Amy LeBlanc are ongoing in the canine model with the intent of integrating canine and human genomic data to help define the critical oncogenic pathways and mechanisms of genome instability shared between these two species. The recent availability of mature canine genome assemblies greatly facilitates these studies. We are particularly interested in using the canine model to study tumor clonality in primary tumors, a topic that can more easily be addressed in the canine system which does not incorporate neo-adjuvant chemotherapy prior to definitive surgery. Although some differences in mutation frequency distinguish canine tumors from their human counterpart, shared pathways identify the core functional modules in both species and are likely to uncover important aspects that are relevant to both canine and human osteosarcoma. Additionally, a concurrent goal is to gain understanding tumor clonality in untreated canine primary tumors. As in humans, canine OSAs are often quite large at the time of the diagnosis. By collecting multiple geographically mapped regions of primary tumors obtained at the time of limb amputation, it will be possible distinguish regionally localized mutations. The results are critically important to the implementation of novel precision therapies and the development of multiagent therapies. This information will be of interest to veterinary and human oncologists.

project_title: Tumor Microenvironment in Cancer Progression
project_abstract_text: Our research program for this project is to determine the microenvironmental regulation of cancer progression. By outlining the stepwise events in the microenvironmental changes that contribute to metastasis we propose an approach to effectively treat cancer and limit or reverse metastatic progression. Targeting unique mutations for individual cancer cells hold challenges given the adaptability of the tumor cells. Our recent investigations in murine studies of the earliest changes in the microenvironment has delineated the key components of the pre-metastatic niche and the functional role of myeloid cells in establishing an immune suppressive microenvironment. These cells are immune suppressive myeloid cells derived from mobilized bone marrow-derived hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells which play an integral role in regulating T cell responses (Giles et al Cancer Research 2016; Kaczanowska et al Cell 2021). We are able to manipulate metastatic progression by altering these unique bone marrow-derived cell enriched areas. We have new data demonstrating that the pre-metastatic niche has similar features to physiological stem cell niches in order to promote distant tumor cell survival. We have found that the localized tumor prior to established metastasis is activating the hematopoietic stem cell niche within the bone marrow and inducing proliferation of hematopoietic stem cells and mobilization of these cells into the circulation. We have found that there are changes that occur in the bone marrow microenvironment in response to tumor secreted factors that induce the myeloid skewing and expansion of hematopoietic progenitor cells that we have seen during tumor progression (Giles et al Cancer Research 2016, Jackett et al Nature Cancer). Targeting the skewing to prevent the expansion in hematopoietic progenitor cells and myeloid cells may be a way to reset this maladaptive response to a growing tumor and prevent metastatic progression. We have on-going investigations examining the small molecular inhibitor PLX3397 that targets CSF1R found on myeloid cells, cKit and FLT3-ITD which we have determined that when the drug is given in the adjuvant setting can limit metastatic progression in tumor bearing hosts. We have initiated and completed the Phase I dose escalation of PLX3397 in pediatric and adolescent patients with recurrent or refractory tumors (Boal et al Clinical Cancer Research). We are now focused on Turalio (PLX3397) for pediatric tenosynovial giant cell tumors. We are assessing efficacy and biomarkers in these patients. We have also developed a new cell therapy approach platform to reprogram these recruited immune suppressive myeloid cells by introducing genetically engineered myeloid cells (GEMys) that express IL12. These IL12 GEMys can reverse the immune suppression program in the pre-metastatic niche and lead to inhibition of metastatic progression and significantly prolong overall survival in highly metastatic murine models (Kaczanowska et al Cell 2021). IL12 GEMys when given following fludarabine and cyclophosphamide tumor bearing hosts lead to long term cures in these metastatic pre-clinical models (Kaczanowska et al Cell 2021). We have developed a clinical protocol for human IL12 GEMys and have generated a functional manufacturing pipeline for human IL12 GEMys for the first in human phase I trial planned. We are performing IND enabling studies and are performing process quality runs for the CMC package for FDA. In addition we have performed deep tumor and metastatic microenvironment analyses of a syngeneic orthotopic model of osteosarcoma and found parallels with our rhabdomyosarcoma and breast carcinoma models. These consistent microenvironmental changes in pre-, early and late metastatic sites suggest that the metastatic microenvironment is not only a viable therapeutic target but may hold more consistent and applicable modifications that can limit the metastatic process in many different genomically diverse cancers. We have recently found that IL12 GEMys have efficacy in alleviating myeloid mediated immune suppression in osteosarcoma which we determined is a heavily myeloid dense cancer. The lack of efficacy of checkpoint blockade therapy and other T cell based therapies in Osteosarcoma may be due to this dense immunosuppressive myeloid cell infiltration. More recently we have translated the findings in murine studies to study metastatic microenvironment in patients with osteosarcoma and adrenocortical carcinoma and find similar changes in the microenvironmental components including abundant and diverse myeloid populations including recruited monocyte populations that have gene expression associated with myeloid derived suppressor cells. A compartment wise approach shows not only consistent and targetable findings but a deeper insight into microenvironmental compartment wise changes that induce metastatic progression and can be effectively targeted. Our more recent studies in human metastatic tissue from patients with adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) has revealed many commonalities with the key findings delineated in our syngeneic orthotopic metastatic models including abundant myeloid cell infiltration and recruitment, stromal cell plasticity and activation and extracellular matrix remodeling. ACC can frequently be metastatic and both lung and liver can be common sites. We have analyzed by single cell analyses human lung and liver metastases and their associated microenvironment as well as metastasis free tissue from lung and liver in these ACC patients. The changes we have observed in metastasis free tissue from lung and liver when compared to publicly available analyses of lung and liver tissue highlight a coordinated program across multiple compartments that orchestrate the metastatic process. In addition to activated hematopoietic stem/progenitor cell niche, we also continue to investigate the essential changes in stromal cells including pericytes, vascular cells and fibroblasts as well as the extracellular matrix in the pre-metastatic and metastatic niche. We have established several lineage tracing models to better track and characterize these stromal cell populations as well as genetically manipulate key genes within specific cell populations. Using these models, we can interrogate the function of specific proteins to these cells and their role in the metastatic process. These studies support our preclinical work with specific cell populations including engineering mesenchymal cells to modulate the extracellular matrix and myeloid cells to deliver cytokine to reverse immune suppression and promote effective anti-tumor immunity. Components of immune suppression and stromal cell activation and enhanced extracellular matrix deposition and remodeling are key factors in these dysregulated microenvironments that are targetable for clinical translation. More dense matrix is associated with malignant tissue. We continue to explore the impact of matrix remodeling on metastatic progression. We have developed robust cell engineering strategies, culture conditions and reproducible assays for cell therapy development. We continue to develop functional studies that help demonstrate human genetically engineered mesenchymal cells (GEMesys) that modulate extracellular matrix remodeling. These studies have shown preclinical efficacy in murine orthotopic, syngeneic osteosarcoma. Studies investigating microenvironmental changes that mediate the metastatic process provide deeper insights into cancer progression but also provide avenues for using cell therapy to effectively reprogram these dysregulated microenvironments for therapeutic gain. Our ongoing preclinical studies and planned clinical study will yield promising insights into the utility of this approach.

project_title: Neuropsychological outcome measures in patients receiving whole brain radiation
project_abstract_text: Accural of NIH protocol 08-C-0214 human subjects and their followup has been completed. Currently, we are doing the final analysis of the banked biomarker specimen data, performing radiomics algorithms to analyze the archived imaging data from our patient cohorts, and performing correlative analysis to neuropsychological performance metrics. One aspect of the analysis will be to compare gender differences in outcome and neuropsychological parameters captured, should there be any statistically significant differences observed.

project_title: Biomarkers and Therapeutic Targets in Tumor Microenvironment and Metastasis
project_abstract_text: Cancer is a complex multicellular process that involves genetic alterations leading to unique clonal populations and requires interaction with its local microenvironment to allow for growth and survival. Metastasis the process of cancer cell dissemination and progression at sites distant from the primary tumor is particularly dependent on microenvironmental changes. We have focused on delineating the key changes in the microenvironment during metastatic progression. The changes we identified are recruitment of bone marrow derived myeloid cells that suppress anti-tumor immunity and the preceding vascular changes, stromal cell activation and extracellular matrix remodeling. The myeloid cell recruitment is localized to specific sites based on changes in vascular permeability and extracellular matrix that create angiocrine signals and a repair response that provide growth and survival signals that elicit the myeloid cell recruitment. Our lab has identified key microenvironmental events in metastatic murine models. We have used this timeline and mapping of key microenvironmental changes essential for metastatic progression to use these models to test cell therapy based on microenvironmental modulation. More recently we have begun investigations in human metastatic microenvironment. We have performed single cell sequencing on metastatic lung and liver and adjacent lung and liver in patients with metastatic cancers. These studies have provided new insights into pivotal microenvironmental changes that are a result of systematic changes coordinated across multiple cell types to promote cancer progression. This coordinated process with changes across cell compartments was conserved across multiple cancer types and across metastatic sites. We are measuring circulating microvesicles released by tumor cells and tumor associated myeloid and stromal cells that may impact important cell behavior and are known to be critical to cell-cell communication and determine the potential biomarker of this coordinated metastatic process. Current investigations in our laboratory are focused on examining the mechanisms of inducing this coordinated program and developing cell therapy based microenvironmental modulation that can be effectively reverse these changes for clinical translation. Myeloid cells are abundant in cancers but their functional role has not been well elucidated. Our research program has been focused on delineating the behavior and function of myeloid cells in cancer. Utilizing both quantification and functional assays, including flow cytometry and immune suppression and phagocytosis/trogocytosis assays, we are assessing the circulating bone marrow-derived myeloid cell populations in pediatric and adult patients with malignancies. We are currently performing genetic screen of myeloid functional assays to determine the key drivers of these processes. We have recently leveraged the data we have generated from our first clinical trial of chimeric antigen receptor T cells targeting GD2 in patients with osteosarcoma and neuroblastoma. This collaboration with Dr. Lynn Hedrick and team now at University of Georgia and Dr. Mackall and team at Stanford has allowed deep transcriptomic, mass cytometry and epigenetic investigations into immune response in patients on CART trial. We found that myeloid cells are key regulators of the CART cells. We have found that myeloid cells depending on the subpopulations and their receptors can be helpful in promoting effective anti-tumor immunity and conversely myeloid subpopulations can also limit CART expansion. These studies speak to the diversity of myeloid populations and their functions and importance of studying these aspects. These investigations are shaping a new understanding of myeloid mediators of CART expansion and may ultimately impact efficacy and serve as a path to combine myeloid and T cell based therapies. Furthermore, myeloid markers of CAR efficacy will be further explored in our current GD2 CART PERSIST trial. Capitalizing on the findings of CXCR3 on myeloid cells and epigenetic markers of T cell and myeloid cells will be investigated in our current correlative studies in solid tumor CART cell trials. We have on-going investigations to explore circulating monocytes and monocyte function and the impact on metastatic risk. Our recent studies have determined host cell plasticity and cell state determine the microvesicles released from these cells and this plasticity in perivascular cells play key roles in regulating metastasis. We are currently investigating markers of this perivascular stromal cell plasticity as a predictor of metastasis and response to conventional therapies and immune based therapies. We also now have a marker of tumor associated fibroblast activation and stromal cell lineage tracing mice in order to monitor activation of these cells in this process. We have performed serial in vivo mouse experiments examining modulation of myeloid cells and stromal cells to determine their impact on metastatic progression. We are using different investigational agents to determine their specific impact on each microenvironmental cell. We have preclinical studies that harness mesenchymal cell plasticity and function to modulate metastatic microenvironment. We have developed using genetic engineering to modify extracellular matrix remodeling in mesenchymal cells that have matrix remodeling as main functionality. We use our established syngeneic murine models of metastasis. These studies have shown efficacy alone and in combination with chemotherapy highlighting strategies to rebalance the altered cancer microenvironment hold promise as an adjunct therapeutic approach. We have recently developed a new trial to modulate the myeloid mediated immune suppressive environment. We have developed a new cell therapy based on genetically engineering myeloid cells (GEMys) that can be novel delivery vehicles given their propensity to accumulate in tumor and metastatic sites. These cells can be engineered to deliver Il12 into the tumor milieu and reprogram multiple cell types, change gene transcriptional signatures and reverse immune suppression and enhance anti-tumor immunity. We have developed humanized murine systems to examine human cell therapy with advanced human tumors. On going work to bring this to clinical setting is on-going and harnessing myeloid cells for introduction of signaling in tumor microenvironment. Recently we have developed human IL12 GEMys and are planning to open a clinical trial by end of next year.

project_title: Generation of T-cell receptors recognizing antigens on non-melanoma tumors
project_abstract_text: This project has included a long standing effort to understand the basis of the immunotherapy responsiveness of renal cancer using state of the art tools. Many of the paradigms that define and explain the immunoresponsiveness of other cancers do not appear to apply to renal cancer. We have so far not consistently found neoantigen reactive T-cells in RCCs and RCCs do not appear marked by high mutational loads. Although we continue to collect renal cancer specimens and data, this project was greatly impacted by the hiring freeze imposed by CCR.

project_title: Clinical protocols for the treatment of gastrointestinal cancer
project_abstract_text: We are conducting clinical trials in patients with primary and secondary liver cancer. We use different drugs to enhance T cell function. By doing in depth correlative studies we hope to better understand how certain treatments work or do not work in patients and how e can improve treatment efficacy. Small proof of principal studies conducted at the NIH Clinical Center together with our in house collaborators provide a cornerstone for this type of research and allow us to collect patient specimen we cannot collect anywhere else.

project_title: Analysis of cancer-related immune suppressor mechanisms in mice
project_abstract_text: We have placed a particular focus on immune cells not widely studied such as mucosa associated invariant T cells and innate like T cells as well T regulatory T cells. All these cells provide a specific immunological environment in the liver and can be potentially targeted to enhance anti-tumor immunity in the liver. We have conducted studies to describe the frequency, phenotype and function of these cells and how these cells can be potentially manipulated. Findings can be used to develop novel research questions with the aim to develop better and more effective treatment options.

project_title: Bladder Cancer Program
project_abstract_text: Immunotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors, particularly agents targeting the axis of programmed cell death protein 1 and its ligand (PD-1/PD-L1), has improved treatment outcomes in many tumor types. The rationale for assessing immune checkpoint inhibitors in advanced urothelial cancer is supported by a high prevalence of tumor somatic mutations and the presence of PD-L1 expression on tumors and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in the tumor microenvironment. Avelumab is a fully human anti-PD-L1 IgG1 antibody that inhibits PD-1/PD-L1 interactions but leaves the PD-1/PD-L2 pathway intact. The first-in-human trial of avelumab was led at the intramural NCI and I led the clinical effort for avelumab in advanced/metastatic urothelial carcinoma which showed clinical benefit, leading to approval by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for this indication. Given the activity of several immune checkpoint inhibitors in this setting, I was eager to test these agents in an earlier disease setting in patients with high-risk muscle-invasive disease. I initiated a phase 3 clinical trial of adjuvant pembrolizumab post-cystectomy in patients with high-risk muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma of the bladder and upper tract. I am the principal investigator on this Alliance/NCI-sponsored study. The trial is accrued with 702 patients randomized. If positive, would provide a treatment choice for patients with urothelial carcinoma in this setting.

project_title: Targeted treatment of B-cell Lymphoma
project_abstract_text: We have been evaluating 1) synergistic combinations of targeted agents in DLBCL cell lines; 2) the safety of combination targeted therapy with ViPOR; and 3) the efficacy of ViPOR in relapsed/refractory DLBCL, follicular lymphoma (FL) and mantle cell lymphomas (MCL). Accomplishments: In collaboration with Craig Thomas from our Branch, we assessed combinations of targeted agents that are directed against survival pathways in DLBCL. We have planned a randomized phase II study of ViPOR +/- polatuzumab in relapsed/refractory DLBCL with stratification by CD10 expression.

project_title: Microenvironmental regulation of glioblastoma radiosensitivity
project_abstract_text: Towards generating novel insights into the radiobiology of GBM, future studies using GSC-initiated xenografts will focus on this radioresistant subpopulation. Along these lines, an aim of this research is to identify the mechanisms and processes responsible for the radioresistance of tumor cells in the OB. Studies will address both intrinsic (e.g., DNA damage response) as well as extrinsic processes (microenvironmental cues). These studies should not only provide fundamental information regarding the mechanisms of GBM radioresistance, but also suggest both tumor cell and microenvironmental targets for radiosensitization. In a study performed in last funding period, radiation was shown to drive the evolution of GSC orthotopic xenografts. However, this initial analysis was conducted before the identification of the OB as a radioprotective niche. Future studies will investigate the role of this radioresistant subpopulation in the radiation-driven evolution of GSC orthotopic xenografts. These studies should generate insight into the fundamental biology and treatment response of recurrent GBMs. Finally, we will continue to use GSC-initiated xenografts as a preclinical model for testing strategies aimed at improving GBM response to radiotherapy. Agents to be evaluated will be those targeting the molecular determinants of radiosensitivity identified above and in project 1. Moreover, to further understand the impact of the OB radioresistant niche, the effects of targeted agents on the radiosensitivity of glioma cells in the OB will be determined. Consistent with the goals of the ROB, this project, in addition to fundamental information, should provide a source of targets for primary and recurrent GBM radiosensitization.

project_title: Radiation-induced translational control of gene expression
project_abstract_text: The overall goals of this project are to define the processes and molecules participating in the radiation-induced translational control of gene expression and their role in determining radiosensitivity. Towards this end, an aim of the ongoing research is to determine the contribution of microRNA (miRNA) to radiation-induced post transcriptional control. These studies will focus on defining the effects of radiation on the miRNAs bound to AGO2, which corresponds of active miRNA, a measure not discernable from analyses of the total miRNA pool. In addition, studies will be aimed at defining the role of alternative splicing (AS) of precursor mRNA in cellular radioresponse. These studies will focus on serine/arginine-rich splicing factors (SRSFs), a major class of pre-mRNA splicing factors regulating both constitutive splicing and AS, as well as the kinases that regulate their activity. The final aim is to test the hypotheses that ribosome biogenesis is a target for tumor radiosensitization and a determinant of the radiation-induced translatome. These studies will focus on rDNA transcription and will include analyses of metarrestin, an RNA polymerase I inhibitor currently in clinical trials. Since the last review we have shown that eIF4A, the RNA helicase component of eIF4F and subject to inhibition by small molecules, is a tumor selective determinant of radiosensitivity. In addition, an inhibitor of rDNA transcription CX-5461, currently in clinical trials, was shown to enhance tumor cell radiosensitivity, although through an alternative mechanism. Thus, investigations into the radiation-induced translational control of gene expression contribute to the fundamental understanding of radioresponse as well as the identification of clinically relevant radiosensitizing agents, both goals of the ROB.

project_title: Studies of amplification in rhabdomyosarcoma
project_abstract_text: In our early studies of gene amplification in fusion-positive (FP) rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS), we identified MIR17HG as a key target of the 13q31 amplicon. MIR17HG is a 'host gene' in which six microRNAs (miRNAs) (including miR-17, miR-18a, miR-19a, miR-20a, miR-19b-1 and miR-92a-1) are processed from the RNA transcribed from an intronic region. We determined that there is elevated expression of these miRNAs in FP RMS tumors with 13q31 amplification as well as in a subset of FP tumors without this amplification. In our studies of FP RMS cell lines, we found variable expression of these miRNAs consistent with the premise that a subset of our FP RMS lines express high levels of these miRNAs and are similar to FP RMS tumors with 13q31 amplicons. In more recent work, we identified a synergistic effect between P3F and MYCN in the upregulation of these miRNAs. During the last year, we have explored the phenotypic contributions of these miRNAs in FP RMS. In particular, we designed lentiviral-based sponge constructs in which multiple copies of the binding sites for one or more of these miRNA's are contained within the 3' untranslated region of a doxycycline-inducible eGFP reporter gene (such as GFP). After transduction into cells followed by doxycycline induction, high-level expression of these reporter genes will result in binding of the corresponding miRNA's to these binding sites in the 3' UTR and thereby inhibit the effects of these miRNA's in the cells. In our recent studies, we designed one sponge construct (SET1) with binding sites for miR-17, miR-20a and miR-92a-1 and a second sponge construct (SET2) with binding sites for miR-20a, miR-19a and miR-19b. Finally, we designed three individual sponge constructs for miR-17, miR-20a and miR-92a-1. These sponge constructs (as well as control constructs without the miRNA binding sites) were then transduced into Rh5 and Rh30 human FP RMS cells as well as a subclone of immortalized human myoblasts with a doxycycline-inducible P3F cDNA and a constitutively expressed MYCN cDNA. To assess the phenotypic effects of inhibition of one of more of these miRNA's, we monitored population growth on the Incucyte platform and assessed colony growth of sparsely plated transduced test cells and focus formation of sparsely plated transduced test cells mixed with an excess number of non-transformed NIH 3T3 cells. Based on the first set of results from these experiments, our findings indicate that one or more of these miRNA's are needed for growth and transformation of the Rh5 and Rh30 FP RMS cells and the P3F/MYCN-expressing myoblasts. Although there appears to be some differences among the cell lines in terms of the specific miRNAs that are required for growth and transformation, a consistent finding in all three cell lines is a loss of growth and transformation following the inhibition of miR-20a action. In addition to experiments that confirm and extend these findings, we are also isolating protein extracts from these various cells to analyze the changes in expression of cellular proteins in the presence of these various sponge constructs. Our findings thus highlight the critical role of these miRNAs from the MIR17HG gene in growth and transformation of FP RMS.

project_title: Brd4 is an atypical kinase that regulates transcription
project_abstract_text: Understanding how the bromodomain 4 (BRD4) exerts its pleiotropic functions requires a detailed understanding of its structure, both in terms of functional domains and 3D organization. The N-terminal half of BRD4 contains the highly ordered bromodomains and ET domain, whose X-ray structures have been resolved. We recently characterized the N-terminal B motif as responsible for BRD4 dimerization and the kinase domain within the BD2-B-BID domain. Additional N-terminal elements - A motif and SEED domains - are largely uncharacterized, both structurally and functionally. The C-terminal half of BRD4 is predicted to be intrinsically disordered; it is responsible for forming phase separated condensates, both in vitro and in vivo. Our studies on BRD4 structure led to the finding that the full-length molecule exists as a dimer, both in vitro and in vivo, which is nucleated by the central B motif. The structure and biophysical properties of the full-length intact molecule remain to be fully established. In an effort to establish the 3D structure of the full-length BRD4 molecule, we entered into a collaboration with the laboratory of Sriram Subramaniam in which purified full length BRD4 was subjected to cryoEM analysis, either alone or in the presence of its various substrates. Due to the highly disordered C-terminal domain of BRD4, we encountered challenges that precluded our being able to generate a set of data that converged on a single structure, despite repeated attempts to generate a homogeneous array on a variety of cryoEM grids. We hypothesize that the flexibility of the BRD4 structure enables it to interact with multiple substrates which bind to different motifs within the molecule and that the C-terminal domain of BRD4 adopts discrete conformations as a function of binding its substrates or post-translational modifications. Unfortunately, none of its known substrates - MYC, Pol II CTD, AcCoA - were able to stabilize the molecule into a single conformation, likely due to insufficient affinity. To further pursue the structural characterization of BRD4, we have undertaken a screen of a natural products library, in collaboration with Barry O'Keefe (NCI), for molecular binders that either stabilize or destabilize BRD4 structure, as assessed by differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF). To date, we have identified approximately two dozen small molecules that stably interact with BRD4. In preliminary experiments, we find that BRD4 stabilizers enhance its kinase activity. We have also identified de-stabilizers and are examining their ability to inhibit BRD4 kinase or HAT activities. Thus, these compounds will be highly useful in studies of both BRD4's structure and enzymatic activities and may have clinical utility in the long run.

project_title: Transcription and Splicing Dynamics in Single Cells
project_abstract_text: The spliceosome is a megadalton protein-RNA complex which removes introns from pre-mRNA, yet the dynamic early assembly steps have not been structurally resolved. Specifically, how the spliceosome selects the correct 3' splice site (3'SS) amongst highly similar non-functional sites is not known. Here, we develop a kinetic model of splice site selection based on single-molecule U2AF heterodimer imaging in vitro and in vivo. The model successfully predicts alternative splicing patterns and indicates that 3'SS selection occurs while U2AF is in complex with the spliceosome, not during initial binding. This finding indicates the spliceosome operates in a 'partial' kinetic proofreading regime, catalyzed in part by the helicase DDX42, which increases selectivity to the underlying U2AF binding site while still allowing for efficient forward progression. Molecular targeting to mitochondria is poorly characterized, yet it is crucial for understanding normal cellular processes. The RNA binding proteins U2AF1/2 form a heterodimer (U2AF) that shuttles between the nucleus and cytoplasm, regulating splicing in the nucleus and translation in the cytoplasm. Our research identifies an unexpected role for U2AF in mitochondrial function. We demonstrate that U2AF, localized to the outer mitochondrial membrane, interacts with nuclear-transcribed mitochondrial mRNAs and proteins, inhibits translation, and regulates mRNA localization to mitochondria. Moreover, an oncogenic point-mutation in U2AF1 disrupts this regulation, leading to altered mitochondrial structure, increased translation, and OXPHOS-dependent metabolic rewiring, recapitulating changes observed in bone marrow progenitors from patients with myelodysplastic syndromes. Thus, we identify a non-canonical role for U2AF in signaling between nuclear and mitochondrial genomes.

project_title: Studies of gene fusions in rhabdomyosarcoma
project_abstract_text: As part of our studies of P3F-induced oncogenic activity in RMS, we are investigating the role of Myc family proteins as important collaborating events. In our past studies with the human myoblast system, the combination of high-level exogenous P3F and MYCN expression (P3F/MYCN) induces high-level transformation and rapid tumorigenesis (~3-4 weeks). In contrast, in the setting of P3F expression without exogenous expression of a Myc family protein (P3F-only), there is no detectable transformation and delayed tumorigenesis (~8-9 weeks). Of note, when cells from the P3F-only tumors are cultured and retested in oncogenic assays, these tumor-derived cells display high level of transformation and rapid tumorigenesis (3-4 weeks), similar to the activity found in cultured cells derived from P3F/MYCN tumors. We next investigated expression levels of MYCN and the related MYC protein in these cells. In both parental and tumor-derived P3F/MYCN cells, we detected comparably high levels of MYCN and very low levels of MYC. In contrast, parental P3F-only cells express very low levels of MYCN and low levels of MYC whereas the corresponding tumor-derived P3F-only cells show increases in MYCN and MYC expression to a final low level of MYCN and moderate level of MYC. This finding suggests that cells with higher MYCN and MYC expression were selected in the P3F-only population during tumorigenesis . To determine how Myc family proteins contribute to oncogenic activity in these tumors, we used CRISPR/Cas9 methodology to knock out expression in these tumor cells. These findings indicate that in P3F/MYCN tumor cells, oncogenic activity is primarily dependent on MYCN expression whereas in P3F-only tumor cells, oncogenic activity is primarily dependent on MYC (or MYC and MYCN) expression. In more recent studies, we analyzed expression and function of Myc family proteins in human FP RMS cell lines. In our analysis of MYC and MYCN protein expression in eight such cell lines, we found a range of expression of these two proteins. In five of these cell lines, there was both high MYC and high MYCN protein expression. In one line, we found low MYC and high MYCN protein expression whereas in two of the lines, we found high MYC and low MYCN expression. We used gene targeting experiments to assess the function of Myc family proteins in these three subsets of human FP RMS lines, and specifically expanded our CRISPR/Cas9 methodology to knock out expression of either P3F (or P7F), MYC, MYCN or both MYC and MYCN. In FP RMS lines with high MYCN and MYC expression, our growth and transformation assays demonstrated near complete loss of oncogenic activity with P3F knockdown. In line with the comparably high expression of both MYC and MYCN, there was only partial loss of oncogenic activity with knockdown of either MYC or MYCN, but there was near complete loss of oncogenic activity with combined knockdown of MYC and MYCN. We next studied a FP RMS line (Rh5) in which there is low MYC and high MYCN expression. In this line, we again found near complete loss of oncogenic activity with P3F knockdown. However, in line with the dominant MYCN expression in this line, we now found no loss of oncogenic activity with MYC knockdown, near complete loss with MYCN knockdown and a similar near complete loss with the combined MYC/MYCN knockdown. Finally, we studied a FP RMS line (CW9019) in which there is high MYC and low MYCN expression. In this line, which contains the P7F fusion gene, there was substantial loss of oncogenic activity with P7F knockdown. In line with the dominant MYC expression in this line, there was also substantial loss of oncogenic activity with MYC knockdown, much less change with MYCN knockdown, and even greater loss of oncogenic activity with combined MYC/MYCN knockdown. In conclusion, these recent studies revealed variation in MYC and MYCN protein expression in FP RMS cell lines and an oncogenic dependence on whichever Myc proteins is dominantly expressed in a specific line. These findings thus highlight the molecular heterogeneity within the FP RMS subset and variation in the events collaborating with P3F/P7F fusion oncoprotein. Furthermore, these findings corroborate that our human myoblast cell culture system provides a useful and accurate model for studying aspects of this molecular heterogeneity.

project_title: Role of IKK alpha in lung cancer development
project_abstract_text: Most cancer patients do not respond well to anti-PD-1 immunotherapies. Here, we detected a tight correlation between CD4 and CSF1R expression in human lung squamous cell carcinomas (LSCCs) and poor survival in these patients expressing high levels of CSF1R with lipid-metabolic genes, STAT6, or IL4R. In a macrophage-dependent LSCC mouse model, although PD-1 levels were associated with LSCC development, an anti-PD-1 antibody treatment failed to improve lung conditions. Alternatively, the interaction between macrophages and Il4-expressing CD4 T cells promoted the macrophage lipid metabolism. Excluding Il5, Il33r, Blimp1, and amphiregulin, only IL-4/IL-4R/STAT6 signaling sustained IL-4 production in CD4 T cells, which activated IL-4R/STAT6, leading to lipid-rich foamy macrophage differentiation and motility, serving as energy/nutrition/inflammatory reservoirs. Depleting Il4, Il4r, or Stat6 in CD4 T cells and macrophages blocked foamy macrophage differentiation/migration and carcinogenesis. Treatment with an inhibitor of acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferases dampened macrophage-STAT6 activity and carcinogenesis. Thus, the combined adoptive and innate immunocyte-mediated aberrant lipid metabolism drives carcinogenesis. Lipid regulators can be targeted for anti-LSCC therapies.

project_title: Regulation of Ciliogenesis and Ciliary-related signaling
project_abstract_text: The Westlake laboratory is focused on understanding the molecular mechanism of primary and motile ciliogenesis important in normal development and homeostasis. Cilia are critical for proper cellular signaling including Hedgehog, Notch, and PDGF pathways, and impairment in these and other ciliary signaling processes are associated with genetic disease and cancer. Key approaches being used to study primary and motile ciliogenesis include advanced microscopy approaches (super resolution fluorescence [SRM] and volume electron microscopy), biochemistry/proteomics and animal models. Our previously published work (Westlake et al., 2011, PNAS; Lu et al., Nat Cell Biol. 2015; Insinna et al., Nature Communication. 2019; Walia et a., Dev Cell, 2019; Cuenca et al., JBC, 2019, Accogli et al., Nature Communication 2024) has helped establish the requirements for membrane trafficking in the initiation and progression of primary ciliogenesis. We have shown that factors associated with the small GTPase Rab11-Rab8 cascade are important for ciliogenesis regulation. Moreover, our work has demonstrated that the docking of small preciliary vesicles to the mother centriole is required to initiate ciliogenesis processes at the mother centriole and to assemble a larger ciliary vesicle (CV), upstream of ciliary axoneme growth. We first reported membrane trafficking regulation of ciliogenesis is controlled by the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway (Walia et al., Dev Cell 2019). Through this work we showed that Akt directly regulates Rab11 binding to its effector WDR44 which suppresses ciliogenesis initiation (Walia et al., Dev Cell 2019). Notably, we have reported that this and other ciliogenesis initiation membrane trafficking related processes are associated with ciliopathy (Shimada et al., Cell Rep. 2017; Accogli et al., Nature Communication 2024). In FY24, we have continued to investigate mechanisms important for ciliogenesis and published two papers and have another manuscript under revision. Primary ciliogenesis FY24 progress: In a paper published in Nature Communication (Accogli et al., 2024 PMID: 38191484) we described families with variants in WDR44 which display an overlapping pleiotropic disease, many associated with ciliopathy. This work was undertaken in collaboration with Dr. Accogli (McGill University) and Dr. Park (Seoul National University) and I am the senior corresponding author of this manuscript and a former postdoc Dr. Saurabh Shakya is a co-first author. In this work we demonstrated WDR44 variants in the WD40 repeat domain have a gain-of-function in ciliogenesis repression through binding more tightly to Rab11 and thus preventing ciliogenesis initiation. We are further interrogating the structure of WDR44-RAB11 complex in collaboration with Dr. Susan Lea (CCR, NCI) and examining other disease causing variants in WDR44. In this work we are using cell line and animal models (fish and mouse) to understand WDR44 associated with disease. A study aimed at understanding the molecular mechanism of the Rab11-Rab8 cascade was completed in FY24 and a revised manuscript is being prepared for resubmission before the end of this year. The Rab11-Rab8 cascade is important for ciliogenesis, neurite outgrowth, apical lumen formation, however the molecular mechanism of this membrane trafficking pathway is poorly understood. In this work we examined the Rab11-Rab8 cascade using biophysical and advanced fluorescence imaging approaches. We discovered that Rab11 and the Rab8 GEF Rabin8 recruit Rab8 to membranes, including the ciliary membrane and membrane tubules. Using super resolution fluorescence microscopy for the first time we could demonstrate the dynamics of Rab11, Rab8 and Rabin8 association with cellular membranes. We are continuing investigation of this pathway with a goal of identifying regulators (GAPs and effectors) of this pathway using proteomic approaches. We are also examining this pathways involvement in membrane tubulation which is a poorly understood trafficking process at both the molecular and physiological level. Our previously published work demonstrated a striking association of membrane tubulation in ciliogenesis, and for connecting the intracellular cilia membrane to the plasma membrane (Insinna et al., Nature Communication 2019). We continued to investigate the architecture of membranes involved in ciliogenesis which has led us to discover previously uncharacterized membrane structures associated with reorganization of the mother centriole in preparation for cilia growth. We used FIB-SEM volume electron microscopy (vEM) approaches to investigate membrane structure during ciliogenesis in collaboration with Dr. Kedar Narayan at the Center for Molecular Microscopy (CCR). Wild-type cells and cells with CRISPR-Cas9 knockout of ciliogenesis regulators were used to systematically identify new intermediate membrane structures important for cilium assembly. A manuscript is prepared for submission this summer. We have also continued to develop approaches and analysis tools (Python and MATLAB based) to investigate membrane trafficking in the centriole microenvironment to understand this mechanism which pointed to connections between asymmetric vesicle trafficking and different subcellular structures. Finally, my laboratory continues to investigate ciliogenesis initiation dysfunction in cancer associated with WDR44-RAB11 binding and regulated by PI3K/Akt signaling. A postdoctoral fellow was hired mid-FY24 to work on this project and the goal is to complete studies aimed at investigating this pathway involvement in ciliogenesis dysfunction in cancer cells using cell culture models and xenograft studies in FY25. Motile Multiciliogenesis: How cells develop hundreds of cilia in multiciliated cells (MCC) important for brain, lung and female reproductive function is poorly understood. We are using similar fluorescence and vEM imaging approaches used in our primary cilium studies to investigate MCC ciliogenesis. We have established expertise and collaborations in MCC studies. I published a senior author paper on MCC ciliogenesis in EMBO Reports in FY22 (Zhao et al. 2022) and I was a contributing author on a paper published by the Reiter lab in FY24 (Choksi et al., 2024. Nature). Mechanistically we are investigating the roles of membrane trafficking regulators in MCC ciliogenesis to test a model that MCC assembly cilia using a similar mechanism as the primary cilium. Currently, we are collaborating with the Aquatics Core and Dr. Ira Daar (CDBL) to use fish and frog embryos as a model for investigating MCC formation, and a postdoctoral fellow was hired in FY24 to work on this project.

project_title: microRNA Profiling in the Spectrum of Kidney Tumors
project_abstract_text: We are studying the microRNA (miRNA) expression analysis for the most common histological subtypes of human renal neoplasms appearing in either sporadic or hereditary forms. We also aimed to test the hypothesis that microRNAs can act as an alternative mechanism of VHL gene inactivation and therefore might be correlated with tumorigenesis in ccRCC. Finally, we wanted to explore whether we can detect specific miRNA expression in liquid biopsies, specifically in urine, and to correlate with the miRNA that are present in the tumors of the same patients.

project_title: miRNA profiling of prostate cancer in young and older male patients
project_abstract_text: Our goal is to investigate the miRNA profiles of prostate tumors occurring in young patients and compare with the miRNA expression of prostate cancers occurring in the elderly patients. We will evaluate if there are differences in specific miRNA expression patterns of tumors with different grades of differentiation and different biological behavior. Prostate cancers will be manually microdissected to obtain pure populations of tumor cells as well as available normal epithelium distant to the tumor area. Histological features such as Gleason score, presence of perineural, lymphatic invasion, extracapsular or seminal vesicle invasion were also evaluated and recorded for each case. Differentially expressed miRNAs will be defined as those with a two-fold change (up or down) and a p value 0.05. Different miRNAs expression profiles will include comparison between the low grade tumors (Gleason score 6 and 7) vs. high grade (Gleason score 8 and 9) lesions. Then, each tumor group will be compared with their respective group of normal epithelium. Patients of younger 40-50 years and older will be selected for the study.

project_title: Allogeneic T cells Transduced with an Anti-CD19 Chimeric Antigen Receptor
project_abstract_text: This project has been aimed at learning about T stem memory cells (Tscm) in recent years. A clinical trial testing these T cells in the setting of infusions of HLA-matched T cells has been completed. We infused donor-derived T cells from the human leukocyte antigen-matched donors of patients with persistent B-cell malignancies after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. These T cells were transduced with an anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) prior to infusion. We are now continuing a variety of cellular and molecular experiments on patient T cells to better understand the in vivo biology of human Tscm cells. This work is a collaboration with Professor Luca Gattinoni, an extramural collaborator This work should lead to a publication in the next year.

project_title: Improved Chimeric Antigen Receptor Therapies B-cell Malignancies
project_abstract_text: In the past year we have completed the following objectives in this project: 1) We are conducting a clinical trial of T cells expressing a bicistronic CAR construct targeting CD19 and CD20; 2) We have developed methods and published a paper on producing anti-CD19 CAR T cells for treatment of chronic lymphocytic leukemia. We published a paper entitled 'Optimization of anti-CD19 CAR T cell production for treatment of patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia; 3) Within the next 2 weeks, we will begin enrollment on a trial testing our new optimized CAR T-cell methods in a clinical trial.

project_title: Modulating Cancer Stem Cell Signaling in Thoracic Malignancies
project_abstract_text: We have continued our efforts to explore the potential utility of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC) models for characterizing epigenetic mediating sternness, treatment resistance and metastatic potential of thoracic malignancies, and identifying novel therapeutic targets in these neoplasms. Our lab was the first to demonstrate that Additional Sex Combs Like-3 (ASXL3), which encodes a component of the polycomb deubiquitinase complex not previously reported to be up-regulated in reprogrammed cells is an essential mediator of pluripotency in human respiratory epithelia and a novel epigenetic target for SCLC therapy. During the past year we have extended these findings to examine potential mechanisms by which ASXL3 contributes to reprograming of normal cells to pluripotency and stemness in human lung cancers. We observed that ASXL3 upregulation coincides with transition from G1 to early S phase, and functions to enhance firing at origins of DNA replication while decreasing the speed of DNA strand synthesis resulting in reversal of the order of early vs late gene synthesis. We have also developed novel inducible in-vitro models as well as GEMM to characterize the timing and functional relevance of ASXL3 upregulation during reprogramming of normal cells to iPSC and implications of ASXL3 upregulation in SCLC. ASXL3 upregulation occurs during a relatively tight time window during reprogramming in normal human epithelial cells. Preliminary experiments indicates that inducible knockout of ASXL3 significantly retards the development of SCLC in RPM mice; once validated, these newly established GEMM will be submitted for patent. Upregulation of ASXL3 in ASCL1 type SCLC appears to be associated with translocation of ASXL3 and nearby genes from chromosome 18 to as yet unidentified loci on other chromosomes. A comprehensive manuscript describing these findings will be submitted for peer review once we have gathered more data regarding the frequency and specificity of the translocations in SCLC specimens. These studies have been hampered by the lack of high-specificity antibodies and the inability to overexpress full length ASXL3 in any cell regardless of endogenous ASXL3 expression. Nevertheless, we continue this line of research because such efforts could provide novel insights into the role of ASXL3 during the development of highly lethal SCLC and identify potential strategies to target stemness in these malignancies. In related studies we performed comprehensive analysis of transcriptomes and DNA methylomes in a panel of SCLC and NSCLC lines relative to small airway epithelial cells (SAEC) and iPSC (Lu iPSC) derived from these normal airway cells. Significant commonality of transcriptomes and DNA methylomes was observed between Lu-iPSC and SCLC; however, this analysis was uninformative regarding pathways unique to lung cancer. We next performed DNase I hypersensitivity followed by deep sequencing (DNase-seq) to identify regulatory elements defined by the state of chromatin configuration among SCLC relative to LuiPSC and SAEC. The majority of DNase hypersensitive sites (DHS) were within enhancers in Lu-iPSC and SCLC. Integration of DHS and transcriptome data demonstrated that less than 5% of non-promoter differentially open regions (DOR) mapped to the nearest neighbor gene, indicating gene regulation by distant regulatory elements. A subset of DOR was unique to SCLC. Analysis of peak-to gene links and gene-to-peak links across all samples showed that 95% of genes mapped to at least one open chromatin region, whereas each peak mapped to a mean number of 9 genes. Many of the predicted DOR-to-gene links occurred in clusters in which multiple nearby peaks were predicted to be linked to the same gene, suggesting that these clusters function as part of regulatory units or enhancers. Bivariate analysis of Genomic Footprint (BaGFoot) identified NFIC as having the highest increase in digital footprinting and occupancy within open chromatin sites specifically in SCLC. Knockdown of NFIC impaired glucose metabolism, decreased stemness, and inhibited growth of SCLC cells in-vitro and in-vivo. ChIP-seq analysis identified numerous sites occupied by Bromodomain-containing protein 4 (BRD4) in the NFIC promoter region. Knock-down of BRD4 or treatment with Bromodomain and extra-terminal domain (BET) inhibitors (BET1) markedly reduced NFIC expression in SCLC cells and SCLC PDX models. Approximately 8% of genes downregulated by BETi treatment were repressed by NFIC knockdown in SCLC, whereas 34% of genes repressed following NFIC knockdown were downregulated in SCLC cells following BETi treatment. Collectively these findings constitute the first demonstration that NFIC is a key TF and possible mediator of transcriptional regulation by BET family proteins in SCLC and highlight the potential of genome-wide chromatin accessibility analyses for elucidating mechanisms of pulmonary carcinogenesis and identifying novel targets for lung cancer therapy. A manuscript summarizing our studies was published recently in the Journal of Thoracic Oncology. Based on our encouraging results pertaining to modeling of lung cancers, we have extended our reprogramming efforts to characterize and target epigenomic perturbations in esophageal cancer cells using a combination of established esophageal cancer lines, primary esophageal cancer specimens, esophageal cancer PDXs established in our lab from treatment naive patients, and esophageal-iPSC (Eso-iPSC) established in our lab from normal esophageal squamous epithelial cells. Notably, ASXL3 was highly upregulated in the Eso-iPSC. Integration of transcriptome and DNA methylome signatures enabled identification of a novel gene signature that is highly associated with decreased survival of esophageal adenocarcinoma patients. This signature is not prognostic in patients with esophageal squamous cell cancers, reflecting the specificity of the signature. An abstract pertaining to initial findings of these studies was presented in oral format at the recent AATS Thoracic Surgical Oncology Symposium, and a second abstract has been selected for oral presentation at the Annual Meeting of the Southern Thoracic Surgical Association in November 2024. A full manuscript describing these findings is being finalized for peer review. In related efforts, we isolated 24 stem-like clones from Lewis lung cancer cells which exhibit distinct stem cell and cancer-testis gene expression profiles in-vitro, and unique, highly reproducible organ-specific metastases. Predilections for organ specific metastases are associated with distinct transcriptome and DNA methylome signatures. Bioinformatics analysis of ATAC-seq data from these clones identified a novel gene signature that was highly associated with PFS and OS of lung cancer patients- particularly those with early-stage disease. Knockdown of one of the two genes with the highest occupancy scores abolished liver metastases in vivo. A comprehensive manuscript pertaining to these studies will be submitted for peer review in the next 6 months.

project_title: Structural Biology of GTPase Activating Proteins
project_abstract_text: This project develops and applies a multi-disciplinary biophysical and molecular biology approach to understanding the mechanism of signaling by the small GTPase Arf1. The unique insights provided by this project enable in situ examination of membrane surface protein complexes. The results suggest new avenues for modulating function of this class of proteins. It is intended that this knowledge will spawn new therapeutic approaches to cancer. Results published (Nat. Comm. 2023, J. Biol. Chem. 2023) have attracted significant attention from both clinical and basic science researchers, thus validating the impact and significance of the research.

project_title: Role of IKK alpha in lymphoid organ development
project_abstract_text: Currently we are investigating the crosstalk between CD4 T cells and macrophages and how these different cells regulate each other in the tumor microenvironment. In lung adenocarcinoma (ADC) development, we found that macrophages promote CD4 T cell transfer to T reg cells. Increased Treg cell numbers promote lung ADC development. We also identified that ROS derived from macrophages play a central role for this Treg cell development. We showed that increased Treg cell numbers promoted lung ADC development and that depleting Treg cells inhibited lung ADC progression. These finding are relevant to human tumorigenesis.

project_title: Epigenetic studies in rhabdomyosarcoma
project_abstract_text: To investigate the biological and clinical significance of global DNA methylation patterns in pediatric RMS, we established a cohort of frozen samples derived from 223 RMS tumors. This cohort includes 86 tumors previously hybridized on the Illumina Infinium HM450K methylation platform and 137 tumors newly hybridized on the Illumina Infinium EPIC methylation platform. In addition to DNA methylation data, we collected information concerning gene fusion status, small mutations, and copy number along with pathologic and clinical parameters. Unsupervised analysis of the genome-wide DNA methylation patterns in this large cohort confirmed that these RMS cases can be divided into two major clusters, one cluster consisting of fusion-positive (FP) cases (usually PAX3-FOXO1 [P3F] or PAX7-FOXO1 [P7F]) and a second cluster consisting of fusion-negative (FN) cases. In accord with our previous studies, we found that the FP cluster can be divided into P3F-enriched and P7F-enriched subsets, and the FN cluster can be divided into two subsets (designated as FN1 and FN2). The large FN2 category is composed of tumors with classical embryonal histology and frequent mutations of the RAS signaling pathway, including the three RAS family genes as well as NF1 and FGFR4. In our expanded cohort of cases, we now can use the DNA methylation data to divide the FN1 subset into at least 5 groups: two groups (FN1A, FN1B) with classical embryonal histology and either TP53 or RAS pathway mutations, a group of embryonal RMS tumors with recurrent MYOD1 mutations (MYOD1), a group of fusion-negative tumors with alveolar histology (AFN), and a heterogeneous group of other tumors (Outlier). Application of a published sarcoma methylation classifier confirmed that the FP, FN2 and MYOD1 groups have methylation patterns classified as RMS (ALV), RMS (EMB) and RMS (MYOD1), respectively. Furthermore, the FN1A and FN1B groups also have methylation patterns classified as RMS (EMB) whereas the AFN group has a methylation pattern classified as RMS (ALV). Finally, the Outlier group tumors have methylation patterns suggesting a variety of possible classification categories including some tumor types that are not included in the current classifier. Within the Outlier category, there is a small subset of cases classified as SARC (RMS-like) that have DICER1 mutations. Copy number analysis of the methylation array data revealed that the AFN cases are enriched in cases with amplification of the 1q34 chromosomal region (including MYCL) whereas FN2 cases are enriched for cases with gain of chromosome 8 or the 13q chromosomal region. Finally, analysis of clinical outcome in the FN tumors revealed the MYOD1 cases and AFN cases have a significantly worse overall survival compared to the FN2 category whereas there is no significant difference in outcome in the FN1A or FN1B categories compared to the FN2 category. These findings highlight the extensive heterogeneity within the RMS family of tumors and the utility of DNA methylation profiling to elucidate distinct biological subsets within the RMS family.

project_title: Immunohistochemical and genomic analysis of tumors
project_abstract_text: Large studies were completed on CD171 and PD-L1. The latter study supported development as PD-L1 as a clinical marker in the Laboratory of Pathology. PD-L1 is normally expressed only in placental trophoblasts and weakly in nerves, probably by Schwann cells. PD-L1 is consistently expressed in trophoblastic neoplasms, including choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumor, and trophoblastic elements of mixed germ cell tumors. Frequent expression was also confirmed in Hodgkin lymphoma, anaplastic large cell lymphoma, and squamous cell carcinomas. In gastrointestinal carcinomas, expression was more prevalent in tumors with mismatch repair-deficiency and EBER-positivity. Study of CD171 demonstrated affinity for schwannian tumors and rare expression in GIST, which differed from a previous study. Due to its very rare expression in GIST, CD171 was not found to be useful prognostic marker for GIST, which differed from the results of a previous study. Large studies of Sox10 and brachyury were also completed. These markers support clinical diagnosis and a number of protocols by offering more precise tumor classification. We also established that nuclear beta-catenin expression is a typical and potentially diagnostic feature for intranodal palisaded myofibroblastoma and sinonasal hemangiopericytoma/glomangiopericytoma, both of which also have corresponding CTNNB1 mutations. We also analyzed pediatric and retroperitoneal GISTs and currently study mutations and fusion as tumor progression factors in GIST. We collaborate with NIH investigator Karel Pacak on biology, pathology, and immunotherapy of paragangliomas. We recently collaborated with members of the Pediatric Oncology Branch, Genetics Branch, and others to complete a genomic analysis of neurofibromatosis 1 patients with atypical neurofibromas. Neurofibromatosis 1 is a genetic disease that increases the likelihood of childhood cancer, specifically peripheral nerve sheath tumors. We have continued study of fusion sarcomas. A recent genomic study on nasal melanoma revealed SPREAD1 mutation. Application of methylation classifier in tumor classification and clinical diagnosis of soft tissue tumors is a new and growing activity.

project_title: Role of T-bet in the pathogenesis of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis
project_abstract_text: Organ-specific autoimmunity arises from dysregulated activity of autoreactive CD4+ TH cells, with CD4+ TH17 cells being implicated in causing and sustaining tissue damage across various autoimmunity models. Despite its initial identification as the principal transcriptional regulator of CD4+ TH1 differentiation, we and other have shown that T-BET is a crucial driver of TH17-mediated pathologies. T-BET-deficient mice have increased numbers of IL-17A-producing TH17 cells, yet these TH17 cells are unable to initiate autoimmunity, demonstrating T-BET's essential role in TH17 cell pathogenicity. Additionally, T-BET expression in pathogenic TH17 cells is required but not sufficient for the development of CNS autoimmune disease. A key research objective in our laboratory is to investigate how T-BET, the TH1 lineage-defining transcription factor, governs autoimmune neuroinflammation.

project_title: The Role of Coherent Rotation in Adult Tissue Remodeling
project_abstract_text: Tumor cells have distinct mechanical phenotypes in 3D hydrogels of differing physico-chemical compositions and prompted us to treat organ-specific metastasis as three distinct stages regulated by different physical properties: a) Organ targeting- topography of vessel architecture and shear forces due to blood flow b) Extravasation- Force generation by cancer cells to penetrate the endothelial barrier c) Dormant vs Tumor outgrowth- Insertion into intact tissues to disrupt tissue integrity. Each of these conditions is regulated by the mechanical phenotype of the cancer cell, i.e. how soft, rigid, liquid-like to maintain cell shape, adhesion, and adaptation in response to environmental pressures. We posit that cancer cells can alternate between a multiplicity of mechanical states and that this dynamic range permits survival in response to a vast range of environmental perturbations. If we can restrict the number of states that cancer cells can adopt, we can then impair their survival in transit and in distant sites. However, we do not yet understand how cancer cells acquire this cunning mutability. Is it due to environmental pressures during tumor progression at the primary tumor, genetic diversity at the onset of malignancy, or due to perturbations at the latter stages of the cascade? In turn, tumor cells may modulate gene expression akin to 'organo-tropic' signatures as they transition from the confined environments of the circulatory system to the distinct viscoelastic properties of the organ parenchyma. In this cycle, we have determined that we can reconcile different mechanical mapping techniques to probe tissue viscoelasticity directly in a living animal. These approaches allow us to directly and mechanically map tumors at different stages of metastasis.

project_title: Viral Replication and Interactions with Host Factors
project_abstract_text: HIV-1 must travel through the cytoplasm to reach the nuclear envelope (NE) of an infected cell, transport through a nuclear pore complex (NPC) to enter the nucleus, and integrate its genome into the chromosomal DNA of the host cell. During this process, HIV-1 must reverse transcribe its RNA genome into double-strand DNA, protect its genome and proteins from host degradative enzymes, and avoid triggering host defenses that would inhibit its replication. We previously observed that HIV-1 viral complexes that enter the nucleus remain at the nuclear periphery and are not randomly distributed throughout the nucleus. We sought to determine whether viral complexes integrate at sites near the nuclear periphery similar to the location of the viral complexes. We developed in situ RNA and DNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) to identify transcriptionally active proviruses. We found that the viral DNA integrates at sites near the nuclear periphery. However, 5 days after infection, the transcriptionally active proviruses were randomly distributed, indicating that the locations of the integration sites become random after a few cell divisions. These results imply that different genes are present at the nuclear periphery in a population of target cells such that essentially the entire genome is available to HIV-1. In addition, the results imply that locations of genes in cells are not fixed and differ from cell to cell. After fusion, the complex of HIV-1 capsid core, reverse transcriptase, and RNA carry out reverse transcription. The viral core must disassemble (uncoat) before integration of the viral DNA into the host genome, but where and when viral core uncoating occurs are not well understood. We have developed a new method to directly label CA with green fluorescent protein (GFP) in infectious viral capsids with minimal loss of infectivity. We have used the direct GFP-CA-labeling method to gain insights into viral core uncoating in infected cells by live-cell microscopy. We observed that, contrary to current models of cytoplasmic or NE-associated viral core uncoating, intact viral cores enter the nucleus through NPCs and undergo uncoating in the nucleus just prior to integration. These groundbreaking studies have transformed our view of the early stage of viral replication and viral core uncoating. Our publication describing this work in the Proceedings of the National Academy of the United States of America (Burdick et al., PNAS 117: 5486-5493, 2020) was selected by Editors of PNAS to receive the Cozzarelli Prize as the most important publication from >300 papers published in the category of Biomedical Sciences. In 2024, we determined that synthesis of long double-stranded reverse transcription product is a critical molecular trigger for viral capsid disassembly. We also found that a minimum genome size >3.5 kb is required to induce efficient uncoating. Furthermore, atomic force microscopy studies indicated that HIV-1 nucleocapsid protein facilitates condensation of the viral DNA, which regulates the timing and efficiency of uncoating. Our previous studies showed that viral complexes exhibit long NE residence times, indicating that translocation of the viral complexes through the nuclear pore is a difficult and time-consuming step during viral replication. However, very little is known about the molecular interactions between viral complexes and host proteins that are essential for nuclear import. To gain insights into this essential yet poorly understood step in viral replication, we have performed a high-throughput imaging-based screen to identify host factors that facilitate HIV-1 viral core nuclear import. We found that NUP98 plays a critical role in facilitating nuclear import of HIV-1 cores. We are currently determining the mechanism by which NUP98 facilitates HIV-1 nuclear import.

project_title: Development of Chimeric Antigen Receptors Targeting Multiple Myeloma
project_abstract_text: In the past year, we have had the following progress: 1) We have made progress in determining why anti-SLAMF7 CAR T cells do not give the expected anti-myeloma results in the clinical trial that we performed. 2) We have continued follow-up on patients enrolled on our clinical trial of an anti-BCMA CAR designated FHVH33-CD8BBZ. This trial enrolled patients with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma. The progression-free survival of patients on this trial was 78 weeks with several patients currently continuing in ongoing responses. We published a paper in Molecular Therapy entitled 'Rapid anti-myeloma activity by T cells expressin an anti-BCMA CAR with a human heavy-chain-only antigen-binding domain. 3) We have established a collaboration with Dr. Lekha Mikkilineni at Stanford University to test teh FHVH33-CD8BBZ CAR at Stanford. 4) We published a paper in Nature Medicine on a previously completed clinical trial entitled 'Idecabtagene vicleucel for relapsed and refractory multiple myeloma: post hoc 18-month follow-up of a phase 1 trial.

project_title: Control of centrosome biogenesis
project_abstract_text: Centrosomes are minute multifaceted membrane-less organelles present in only two copies in a typical cycling animal cell. A centrosome's core is a nine-fold symmetrical cylindrical microtubule-based structure called a centriole. The centriole organizes the second major part of the centrosome, called pericentriolar material, which is a large and dynamic multiprotein complex and the site of most centrosomal functions. Centrosomes perform vital cellular functions such as microtubule nucleation, organization of the bipolar mitotic spindle pole during cell division, and cellular signaling, and they influence tissue architecture and cell motility. Centrioles also organize sensory and motile cilia, critically important for development and tissue homeostasis. Supernumerary and structurally aberrant centrioles and centrosomes can initiate tumorigenesis, promote tumor invasiveness, and are present in almost all types of tumors. Centriolar or ciliary defects are, in addition, an underlying cause of genetic disorders known as ciliopathies.
