Transcriptionally similar stem/progenitor (St/Pr) cells were identified for all lineage populations. Lineage tracing in amphicrine CRPC showed that heterogeneity originated from distinct subclones of infrequent St/Pr cells that produced mainly quiescent differentiated amphicrine progeny. By contrast, adenocarcinoma CRPC progeny originated from St/Pr cells and self-renewing differentiated luminal cells. Neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC) was composed almost exclusively of self-renewing St/Pr cells. Amphicrine subpopulations were enriched for secretory luminal, mesenchymal, and enzalutamide treatment persistent signatures that characterize clinical progression. Finally, the amphicrine St/Pr subpopulation was specifically depleted with an AURKA inhibitor, which blocked tumor growth. These data illuminate distinct stem cell (SC) characteristics for subtype-specific CRPC in addition to demonstrating a context for targeting differentiation-competent prostate SCs.

project_title: Bioinformatics: Characterizing Brain Tumor Data
project_abstract_text: As a hybrid science that links biological data with techniques for information storage, distribution, and analysis to support multiple areas of scientific research, including biomedicine, Bioinformatics has been driven by the great acceleration in data generation processes in biology. The NOB for the past years has enrolled over 1000 patients on the Natural History study which mandates the collection of tumor tissue as well as peripheral blood samples for germline DNA. This includes an unprecedented number of patients with rare CNS cancers. Moreover, the sample collection is accompanied by careful and prospective clinical data acquisition, allowing an unprecedented wealth of matched molecular and clinical data permitting a wide variety of analyses. Advances in the molecular analysis of genes, proteins and metabolite shave greatly improved our understanding of biological processes and disease and have increased our ability to monitor treatment response and stratify patients to improve treatment efficacy. Precision medicine facilitated by companion diagnostics is one of the driving forces accelerating the drug development process and improving therapeutic management. Launched in 2016, the NCI Genomic Data Commons(GDC) provides a single source for data from NCI initiatives and cancer research projects, including TCGA and TARGET, and the analytical tools needed to mine them. The new initiated NOB Bioinformatics has extended our bioinformatics and computational analyses efforts to utilize the GDC databases. For example, using the TCGA data effectively doubles the number of GBMs we have to work with and affords us the advantage of formulating computationally derived hypothesis based on one database with the ability to validate those hypotheses on a totally different database. For example, a significant amount of time has been spent by NOB Bioinformatics on the databases to try and understand the biologically basis for the more aggressive phenotype and thus shorter survival of GBMs from older patients compared to those of younger GBMs. To date we have found a very interesting set of differentially expressed genes and miRNAs as well as specific genome wide methylation patterns and specific chromosomal number variants that differentiate older versus younger patients with GBM. We are in the process of using some of these findings to perform wet lab experiments to better annotate the significance of these findings. Furthermore, in collaborated with NCI ClinOmics (now COMPASS) program we analyzed and created genomic profiling data from the rare CNS tumors, such as chordomas, and dissected signal transduction pathways, and aided in the design of novel therapeutics. In addition to characterizing the samples from patients enrolled, the NOB Bioinformatics has generated genomic-scale analyses of the many human glioma initiating cells/glioma stem cells (GIC/GSC) lines produced in laboratory. This characterization is both at the primary cell level (including evolution through passages) as well as evaluation of the impact of different treatments (differentiation, animal passages, drug treatment, etc) on the biological behavior of the cells.

project_title: Better Understanding and Handling of Tautomerism
project_abstract_text: Our motivation of our tautomerism-related work is thus to use all tools at our disposal, chemoinformatics analyses, QM computations, experimental work, and systematic extraction of results from literature, to provide a scientific footing for the recommendations how to improve handling of tautomerism in InChI V2. The starting point of these effort were based on the 21 rules incorporated in the chemoinformatics toolkit CACTVS. All rules are encoded in SMIRKS line notation. Based on Baldwin's well-known set of rules to predict the relative facility of ring forming reactions, we have added a set of about 50 rules describing ring-chain (RC) tautomerism. With these RC rules, plus additional prototropic and valence tautomerism rules, we now have a set of 120 tautomeric rules. In order to provide additional experimental data for tautomerism-related analyses and chemoinformatics work, we have created a database based on data extracted from experimental literature. This database consists of 1,873 entries which belong to n-tuples of tautomers studied in a particular set of experimental conditions (pH, solvent, temperature, technique), adding up to 3,898 records since the average of n is slightly >2. The data were extracted from 73 publications, many of them reviews, taken from a selection of ~200 papers. Our web service - called Tautomerizer - can be used to apply and test the transforms we have compiled from the above database and literature for the Redesign of Handling of Tautomerism in InChI(Key) V.2. The work of the IUPAC Working Group (headed by Dr. Nicklaus) about the transforms to be recommended for InChI V2 has been successfully completed. Exploratory coding for adding some of the new rules to the previous InChI code (v.1.05) were successful for 6 rules. A new version of InChI (v. 1.07) with these rules incorporated has just been publicly released. We collaborated with a precisionFDA Challenge on evaluating InChI for tautomer handling. A recent study has explored what impact tautomerism has on drug discovery and development.

project_title: Phase 2 study of Lu-177-DOTATATE in inoperable paraganglioma - pheochromocytoa
project_abstract_text: The goal of this project it to assess the safety and to evaluate the ability of Lu-177-DOTATATE to improve upon progression-free survival (PFS) at 6 months in patients with inoperable, SSTR positive PHEO/PGL by comparing PFS of patients treated with Lu-177-DOTATATE to historical controls from existing literature. This will be an early phase clinical trial of 90 patients which will seek to determine whether Lu-177-DOTATATE can be used to improved the PFS in the rare tumor metastatic pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma. This is a collaborative project with Dr. Karel Pacak of NICHD. There is ongoing accrual with this study.

project_title: Metabolic imaging of the effects of brain radiotherapy
project_abstract_text: The preclinical animal studies and preliminary studies in human tissue are ongoing. In the next year, we aim to develop metabolic signatures of radiation-induced memory dysfunction and recovery, exploring time as a variable as well as administration of radiation protectors and radiation mitigators for efficacy. Once effect is established we will establish the metabolic signature as a radiation response in tumor models. Pending positive results, these variable will be used to evaluate human subjects in future studies.

project_title: Exploiting DNA Replicative Stress for Novel Small Cell Lung Cancer Therapies
project_abstract_text: We have proposed that replication stress, a key driver of cancer progression which leads to stalled replication forks and genome instability, is a small cell lung cancer (SCLC) hallmark (Sci Transl Med 2016). Ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related (ATR) kinase is crucial in managing this stress by phosphorylating downstream kinases like CHK1. Disruptions in ATR signaling result in replication fork collapse, DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), and increased genome instability. Our cell-based screens identified ATR and TOP1 inhibitors as synergistic agents that exacerbate replication stress and genomic instability in SCLC (Cancer Cell 2021). In a Phase I trial, the ATR inhibitor berzosertib (M6620) combined with the TOP1 inhibitor topotecan showed promising pharmacodynamics, evidenced by ATR inhibition and increased DSBs, with no additional normal tissue toxicities (J Clin Oncol 2018). In a subsequent Phase II trial, this combination resulted in partial responses in 36% of patients with relapsed SCLC, especially those with chemo-resistant disease (Cancer Cell 2021). A subsequent randomized Phase II trial found that while progression-free survival was similar between topotecan alone and with berzosertib, the combination significantly improved overall survival and response rates (JAMA Oncol 2023). Transcriptomic analysis revealed that neuroendocrine (NE) SCLC tumors, characterized by high replication stress, were more responsive to this combination than nonNE tumors. We developed an 18-gene 'repstress score' to predict responses to replication-stress therapies, validated across 60+ SCLC cell lines, representing the molecular diversity of the SCLC (Cancer Research Comm 2022). High repstress-score cells, indicative of robust endogenous replication stress, showed increased sensitivity to topotecan, gemcitabine, and ATR inhibitors. Ongoing studies are expanding this approach to extra-pulmonary small cell cancers (2022 ASCO Annual Meeting) and exploring targeted TOP1 delivery using antibody drug conjugates (Clin Cancer Res 2023; NCT04826341) and patient selection strategies. Overall, our research highlights the transformative potential of targeting replication stress in SCLC and advances our understanding of tumor subtypes and biomarkers for predicting therapeutic responses. Leveraging Anti-Tumor Immune Responses: Despite the high mutation rate, durable SCLC responses to chemo-immunotherapy are rare, with only 12-18% of patients remaining progression-free after one year. We hypothesized that combining PARP inhibition with immune checkpoint blockade could enhance response rates. In a Phase II trial, the combination of the PD-L1 inhibitor durvalumab and the PARP inhibitor olaparib did not achieve efficacy benchmarks. However, biopsies revealed that tumor immune phenotypes play a crucial role in SCLC responses, with over two-thirds of tumors exhibiting an immune-excluded phenotype (J Thorac Oncol 2018). Further transcriptomic analysis demonstrated that the third of responses could be explained by Notch activation which induced a non-NE phenotype, enhancing tumor immunity (Nat Comm 2021). Additionally, our research into immunotherapy resistance in mismatch repair-deficient tumors identified defective JAK1 signaling as a key factor, highlighting the complex interplay between genomic instability and immune resistance (Cold Spring Harb Mol Case Stud. 2020). Building on these insights, we are exploring the use of epigenetic modifiers like EZH2 inhibitors to reprogram SCLC to a more immune-activated state (NCT05353439) and developing chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapies, which target specific tumor antigens independent of MHC molecules. SCLC Subtypes and Subtype-Specific Vulnerabilities: Molecular characterization of human SCLC has historically lagged, resulting in it being treated as a single disease. Our work has identified distinct SCLC subtypes and the associated vulnerabilities. Profiling pre-treatment tumors from patients undergoing replication-stress targeted therapies, we found significant enrichment of DNA damage response components in responsive tumors (Cancer Cell 2021). Ongoing studies aim to elucidate the mechanistic basis of high replication stress in NE SCLCs. Profiling pre-treatment tumors from patients undergoing immunotherapies revealed that responding tumors exhibited elevated Notch signaling and non-NE differentiation (Nat Comm 2021). These findings pave the way for future personalized treatment opportunities. We identified a new NE-v2-like subtype in patient tumors, associated with chemo-resistance and poor survival (Nat Comm 2022), and discovered that inherited mutations in cancer predisposing genes predict improved SCLC responses to chemotherapy and longer remissions (Sci Transl Med 2021), questioning the long-held notion of smoking being the sole SCLC risk-factor. These findings illustrate the potential of clinical observations, even from relatively small trials, to yield mechanistic insights irrespective of treatment outcome. More recently, we have started to learn about the drivers of SCLC heterogeneity and plasticity including tumor-intrinsic factors such as extrachromosomal DNA amplification which drive massive intra-tumoral heterogeneity and portends exceedingly poor outcomes (Cancer Discov 2023) and tumor-extrinsic factors from the tumor microenvironment that shape tumor cell states (Cell Rep Med 2024). Given the challenges of obtaining SCLC tumor biopsies, we are investigating many approaches to profile the SCLC molecular characteristics noninvasively from plasma, including circulating tumor DNA histone modifications (bioRxiv 2022), nucleosomal occupancy (bioRxiv 2023), and fragmentome patterns (2022 ASCO Annual Meeting). I place a strong emphasis on mentoring the next generation of physician-scientists and researchers. My trainees have advanced to thriving careers, receiving career development awards from foundations and federal agencies. For the past four years, they have been honored with the prestigious American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) Young Investigator Awards, which support high-quality research by early-career investigators transitioning to faculty roles.

project_title: Identification of genomic regulatory elements in pancreas cells
project_abstract_text: Using cutting-edge genomic technologies, we have mapped and categorized thousands of genomic elements that might be putative regulators of pancreas cell lineages. We identified chromatin regions that are associated with cell type-specific gene expression. Our work has revealed an enhancer logic that suggests a mechanism for the diversification of pancreas cell lineages during development. Our results also revealed previously unrecognized links between endocrine and exocrine pancreas in diabetes risk.

project_title: Engineering HCC-selective PET agent
project_abstract_text: Liver cancer is ranked second in cancer-related deaths worldwide. Unlike many other cancer types, the incidence and death rate of liver cancers is rising in the United States, with a 5-year survival of 18% (all stages). Treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma, the most common type of liver cancer, transplant and resection offer curative potential and have 5 year overall survival (OS) rates of 70%, and 40%, respectively. For palliative local treatments, 5 year OS rates fall to 20-35%. Classic imaging of HCC includes Tri-phasic CT scan and MRI, however, these modalities provide little biological information of the tumors, especially after local ablative therapies, compromising our ability to discern active from treated disease. Our goal is to engineer HCC-selective PET agents that will allow us to define the extent of disease to facilitate screening of in patients at high risk of HCC development, aide in treatment planning once HCC has been diagnosed, and help in selecting patients who may benefit from tumor-selective therapies (e.g. immunotherapy, molecular radiotherapy). To date, we have succesfully deisgned, engineered, and validated one full length antibody-based radiopharmaceutical agent for imaging and treatment in murine models of liver cancer. In addition, we have developed a novel single domain antibody-based PET agent for which we have submitted a patent and are looking to translate into first in human studies.

project_title: T cell regulation for intestinal barrier function
project_abstract_text: IELs are known to be important for regulating intestinal barrier function, considering their close association with intestinal epithelial cells. The specific microenvironment of intestine determines the unique cellular and molecular features of IELs which potentially impact IELs function. We found that CD101 is highly expressed on IELs. We also found the loss of CD101 causes disrupted intestinal barrier and elevated bacterial invasion, leading to increased risk of intestinal inflammation. We are interested in studying molecular mechanisms of how CD101 controls IELs function to regulate intestinal barrier function.

project_title: Discovery of genetic interactions in cancer
project_abstract_text: This approach provides a basis for new combination-based therapeutic strategies improving the effectiveness of existing cancer therapies by identifying and targeting drug resistance pathways. Going forward in this line of research, having just established our laboratory recently, we intend to explore two main paths: (a) precision medicine - inferring patient specific GI-mediated drug response by analyzing the transcriptomics of their tumors, and (b) drug development - identifying new SL-based drug targets, combined with their SL-derived patient stratification profiles.

project_title: Computational studies of cancer immunotherapy
project_abstract_text: In the last two years we have become actively engaged in collaborative studies in cancer immunotherapy, ranging from studying the role of urea cycle dysregulation in modulating the response to checkpoint inhibitors in different cancer types, studying the role of intratumor heterogeneity in shaping the immune response and its effectiveness, and very recently, building machine learning based predictors of patients' response to checkpoint therapies in melanoma. We also found CAPN1 is a novel binding partner and regulator of the tumor suppressor Neurofibromin 1 (NF1) in melanoma. We also found robust prediction of response to immune checkpoint blockade therapy in metastatic melanoma. Analyzing gene expression data from patients with neuroblastoma, we identified 15 checkpoint-related pairs of genes whose relative activity could be used to predict the effectiveness of the immune system's anticancer response, which we used to develop a predictive tool. When we applied this predictor to available data from patients with melanoma, it outperformed all other predictors of immunotherapy drug outcomes that had been reported so far.

project_title: Dual Blockade of IGF1R and MEK synergistically inhibits pediatric cancers
project_abstract_text: Activating mutations in the RAS/MAPK pathway are observed in relapsed neuroblastoma. Pre-clinical studies indicate these tumors have an increased sensitivity to inhibitors of the RAS/MAPK pathway such as MEK inhibitors. MEK inhibitors do not induce durable responses as single agents, indicating a need to identify synergistic combinations of targeted agents to provide therapeutic benefit. We previously showed preclinical therapeutic synergy between a MEK inhibitor, trametinib, and a monoclonal antibody specific for IGF1R, ganitumab in RAS-mutated rhabdomyosarcoma. Neuroblastoma cells, like rhabdomyosarcoma cells, are sensitive to inhibition of the RAS/MAPK and IGF1R/AKT/mTOR pathways. We hypothesized that the combination of trametinib and ganitumab would be effective in RAS-mutated neuroblastoma. This year, we showed that trametinib and ganitumab synergistically suppressed neuroblastoma cell proliferation and induced apoptosis in cell culture. We also observed a delay in tumor initiation and prolongation of survival in heterotopic and orthotopic xenograft models treated with trametinib and ganitumab. However, growth of both primary and metastatic tumors was observed in animals receiving the combination of trametinib and ganitumab. Therefore, more preclinical work is necessary before testing this combination in patients with relapsed or refractory RAS-mutated neuroblastoma. Because ganitumab is no longer available for clinical development, our current work is focused on identifying additional IGF1R inhibitors for clinical translation in combination with MEK inhibition.

project_title: Thymus biology
project_abstract_text: Since my laboratory moved from Japan in 2018, we have opened an experimental research laboratory to study thymus biology. In FY2023, we have demonstrated that CCL21-expressing embryonic thymic medullary epithelial cells (mTECs) carry a developmental potential to give rise to self-antigen-displaying mTECs including Aire-expressing mTECs, revealing that the sequential conversion of thymocyte-attracting subset into self-antigen-displaying subset serves to assemble functional diversity in the thymus medulla epithelium. We have also demonstrated that indispensable interplay among functionally diverse mTECs, including the cooperation between CCL21-expressing mTECs and Aire-expressing mTECs and between Fezf2-expressing mTECs and Aire-expressing mTECs, for the establishment of central self-tolerance.

project_title: Immunophenotyping by high-dimensional cytometry  and machine learning
project_abstract_text: We expanded our pipeline into PlateYPus in order to streamline immune profiling of blood and lymphoid tissues. Our pipeline allowed us to systematically analyze the variability in hematologic content between the bone marrow, blood and spleen of healthy mice. We collaborate with many labs to test-run our automatized blood preparation and tissue preparation, staining and acquisition on the CyTEK. Surprising results related to the large fluctuations in leukocyte numbers led us to introduce a model (based on previous work on cell-to-cell variability and response to cytokines) that accounts for all aspects of our experimental measurements, namely, fluctuations, correlation and chaos in the dynamics of hematopoietic cells at homeostasis. A comprehensive manuscript is being submitted

project_title: Role of ETS-Transcription Factors in Regulating Cell Fate
project_abstract_text: During FY2024 we have made great progress in this project, and we have this work accepted for publication in Sciences Advances. We have established the role of the transcriptional repressor ERF as the MAPK dependent switch that controls the exit from the naive state of pluripotency. For this, we have used inducible ESCs to genetically eliminate all RAS proteins and determined that, while differentiated RAS deficient cells remain trapped in an intermediate state of pluripotency, further absence of ERF overcomes the developmental blockage of RAS deficient cells from this intermediate state. We also performed RNAseq data and observed that deletion of ERF restored the overall gene expression profile to a wild type level in differentiated Ras deficient cells. Mechanistically, we have demonstrated that ERF ensures naive pluripotency by strengthen naive pluripotent transcription factor binding and accessibility at specific ESC enhancers. Moreover, we have also determined that ERF regulates negatively the expression of the de novo methylase DNMT3, essential for the extinction of the naive transcriptional program. Our data has revealed an essential role for ERF in the exit from rosette pluripotency as a regulator of the progression to primed pluripotency.

project_title: Identification of molecular pathways regulating quiescence in pluripotent cells
project_abstract_text: During FY2024 we also have made great progress in this project. Here, we are interested in understanding the molecular mechanisms inducing quiescence in pluripotent cells. For this, we generated two different reporter cell lines: 1) A pluripotent cell line expressing a fluorescently labelled p27-mutant form unable to interact with CDKs and only visible in quiescent cells (p27Mut-mCherry). 2) A pluripotent cell line expressing a recently described live cell sensor to measure CDK2 activity. This sensor included amino acids 994-1087 of the human DNA helicase B fused to the fluorescent protein mVenus (DHBmVenus). In addition, it contains four CDK consensus phosphorylation sites, a nuclear localization signal, and a nuclear export signal making this fusion protein able to shuttle between the nuclei and the cytoplasm. Cells in G0/G1 with low CDK2 activity will accumulate DHBmVenus in the nuclei while cells traversing through cell cycle will progressively export the chimeric reporter out to the cytoplasm. Using p27-mutant Cherry embryonic stem cell lines (ESCs), we assayed a chemical library of almost 1000 compounds, and selected 15 as potent inducers of quiescence based on p27-Cherry levels. After a secondary validation screen, we have further proceeded with 5 compounds. Currently, we are exploring the molecular mechanisms by which these compounds induce quiescence in ESCs. Using the same fluorescently labelled p27-mutant protein we have identified the existence of endogenous quiescent cells residing within mESCs cultures. We are currently identifying the proliferation dynamics by live cell imaging and transcriptional profile by single cell RNAseq of these cells. Finally, we generated similar fluorescently labelled reporter cell lines in human embryonic stem cell lines (hESC) to screen the same library of chemical compounds. Moreover, we set up a system to induce a gastrulation-like system in vitro using these reporter hESC lines to visualize changes in CDK activity as cells commit and differentiate. In addition, we targeted mESCs with one single copy of the CDK2 live-sensor described above in the ROSA26 loci. We have generated a mouse model containing this reporter to determine the spatiotemporal CDK2 activity landscape during early development. Using this CDK2 activity map we will evaluate the causal relation between cell cycle regulation and cell specification.

project_title: Canonical and non-canonical roles of Argonaute proteins in mammals
project_abstract_text: Argonaute 2 (AGO2) is a cytoplasmic component of the miRNA pathway, with essential roles in development and disease. Yet little is known about its regulation in vivo.We found that in quiescent mouse splenocytes, AGO2 localizes almost exclusively to the nucleus. AGO2 subcellular localization is modulated by the Pi3K-AKT-mTOR pathway, a well-established regulator of quiescence. Signaling through this pathway in proliferating cells promotes AGO2 cytoplasmic accumulation, at least in part by stimulating the expression of TNRC6, an essential AGO2 binding partner in the miRNA pathway. In quiescent cells in which mTOR signaling is low, AGO2 accumulates in the nucleus, where it binds to young mobile transposons co-transcriptionally to repress their expression via its catalytic domain. Our data point to an essential but previously unrecognized nuclear role for AGO2 during quiescence as part of a genome-defense system against young mobile elements and provide evidence of RNA interference in the soma of mammals.

project_title: CRISPR tools to dissect the coding and non-coding genome
project_abstract_text: We have established important principles to the use of CRISPR tools to dissect non-coding RNA sequences. These efforts are described in several publications either led by my lab or in which we are co-authors. These include 'CSC software corrects off-target mediated gRNA depletion in CRISPR-Cas9 essentiality screens' by Perez in Nature communications ; and 'Genome-scale exon perturbation screens uncover exons critical for cell fitness' by Xiao in Molecular Cell. In addition, we have a manuscript currently in revision which we expect will be accepted soon.

project_title: Molecular Determinants of Totipotency
project_abstract_text: To understand totipotency we used the recently described totipotent-like conversion induced by expression of the homeoprotein DUX. Expression of DUX induces most of features that characterize 2-cell embryos (transcriptional profile, loss of heterochromatin or activation of retroviral dormant sequences). Thus, we generated mESCs carrying a doxycycline (DOX)-inducible DUX cDNA using the KH2 mESC line (hereafter, ESCDux). We verified that DUX is expressed upon addition of DOX along with well-known DUX-dependent downstream ZGA-associated genes. We observed that sustained expression of DUX leads to DNA-damage, revealed by the increased levels of the gH2AX marker, and efficient cell death in a dose dependent manner correlating with the conversion into the 2C-like state. We determined that DNA-damage was taking place at a subset of CTCF-binding sites and hypothesized that CTCF was a barrier to totipotent-like conversion. Interestingly, we observed that CTCF depletion in ESC induced a 2C-like conversion in an spontaneous manner. Finally, we also showed that 2C-like conversion upon CTCF-depletion was dependent on the endogenous activation of the cluster of genes ZSCAN4. Taking all together, we made great progress in this project, and we have this work accepted for publication in Nature Communications. We are also interested in exploring the DUX-dependent induction of DUXBL, a gene that belongs to the DUX family of proteins only found intact in rodents. This gene is part of a triplicated region of the genome spanning more than 300kb with three identical copies of DUXBL. Using published ChIP-seq data for DUX we observed that all three DUXBL copies contain three binding sites for DUX. In fact, induction of DUX in ESCDux cells leads to elevated levels of DUXBL in a dose dependent manner. We performed Cut&Run to identify the putative binding sites in ESCs and found it enriched in different enhancer and promoters. Interestingly, by performing morpholino microinjections in zygotes to downregulate Duxbl, we observed that this protein is essential for development. Indeed, Duxbl-knockdown zygotes arrested at the 2C-stage of development. RNAseq analysis of wild-type and Duxbl-knockdown 2C embryos revealed strong defects in splicing. This project has moved forward during this past FY and these analyses will set the basis to further explore the role of DUXBL during embryonic development.

project_title: Identify modulators of telomerase activity
project_abstract_text: A critical factor in controlling cellular proliferation in mammalian cells is the balance between telomere erosion and telomere elongation. The expression of the enzyme telomerase (TERT) allows de novo telomere elongation in germ cells, some stem cell compartments, and the vast majority of human cancers. Outstanding questions regarding telomerase function and regulation include how this enzyme is recruited to chromosome ends and how cells determine the upper limit of telomere length. A major limitation that has hampered addressing these questions is the lack of a robust assay to measure telomerase activity at the single-cell level. We have overcome this limitation by utilizing a robust inducible system to express a mutant RNA template for telomerase, allowing direct visualization of TERT activity in cells. Using this approach, we are defining the role of telomere-associated factors in telomerase regulation, the properties of telomerase-mediated telomere elongation, and identifying novel telomerase modulators.

project_title: Determine the mechanism of ALT-mediated telomere elongation
project_abstract_text: A significant fraction (~15%) of human cancers maintain telomere length using a recombination-based mechanism termed ALT (Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres). Despite major breakthroughs in recent years on the molecular mechanisms driving telomere lengthening in ALT-positive cancers, we lack actionable therapeutic targets that could be used to treat this type of cancer. We embarked on a comprehensive genomic and pharmacological approach to identify novel vulnerabilities of ALT-positive cancer cells. We leveraged comparative genomics to identify genes required for the proliferation of human and canine ALT-positive osteosarcoma cell lines but dispensable for non-ALT osteosarcoma cell lines. Using this information, we performed secondary screens aimed at identifying novel targets and inhibitors that could selectively curb the proliferation of ALT-positive cell lines. Using this approach, we aim to develop novel potential therapies to target cancer cells based on their telomere maintenance mechanism as well as uncover molecular pathways that ensure the ALT process functions.

project_title: Mechanisms of multi-species bacterial interactions
project_abstract_text: Our research over the last year had three main directions. I) P. aeruginosa response to sensing S. aureus. Interactions between species can affect multiple bacterial behaviors, including antibiotic resistance, production of antibiotics, biofilm formation, and motility. We were interested in studying how S. aureus secreted molecules can affect P. aeruginosa motility, which molecules mediate this interaction, and the details of the P. aeruginosa motility response. II) S. maltophilia response to P. aeruginosa. We are testing how P. aeruginosa secreted molecules can affect lifestyle transitions in S. maltophilia III) Characterize the adaptation of S. aureus to P. aeruginosa secreted antimicrobials. P. aeruginosa produces multiple molecules with antimicrobial activity against several other species, but their mode of action, and the pathways by which other bacteria can adapt to them, are not well-defined. We are interested in delineating the effect these molecules have on S. aureus cells, and identifying the adaptive trajectories of S. aureus in their presence. We have evolved multiple populations of S. aureus against the P. aeruginosa redox-active phenazine molecule pyocyanin and have identified mutations in several genes that have not been previously implicated in pyocyanin resistance. We aim to characterize how these mutations confer pyocyanin resistance, test their relevance in clinical isolates, and better describe the cellular effects of pyocyanin on S. aureus.

project_title: Evolution of antibiotic resistance
project_abstract_text: We have identified that genomic amplifications provide an alternate evolutionary trajectory for the rise of antibiotic resistance. We are interested in characterizing two aspects of this process. I) What pathways are important for the formation of amplifications? We are currently testing panels of mutants to address this question. II) What role does genomic location play in the formation and selection of amplifications? We are also interested in developing a targeted long-read sequencing strategy to quantify the frequency of amplification formation.

project_title: Development of Novel Approaches to Optimize CAR T-cell Therapies for B-cell Malignancies
project_abstract_text: CD19-targeted immunotherapy, including CAR T-cells and T-cell engaging bispecific antibodies, has transformed the treatment of relapsed or chemotherapy refractory B-cell malignancies, with several therapeutic strategies now FDA approved for the treatment of B-cell leukemias and lymphomas. Despite high remission induction rates and the potential for durable remissions, growing experience, particularly in B-ALL suggests that 50% or more may relapse within the first year, with a substantial fraction emerging with CD19 loss as a mechanism of immune escape. For those with relapse retaining CD19 expression, second CD19 CAR T-cell infusions are frequently unsuccessful, further limiting options for salvage therapy in these highly refractory patients.Indeed, outcomes for patients with post CAR T-cell relapse is remarkably poor. Accordingly, the overarching goal of this project is to implement novel strategies to extend durable remission following CAR T-cells in children and young adults with B-ALL, thereby improving overall survival. This goal is addressed through the following three specific aims: 1) Evaluate the ability of combinatorial targeted strategies to prevent antigen negative relapse; 2) Test novel CAR T-cell constructs targeting non-CD19 antigens in B-ALL; 3) Develop a risk-stratified approach to improve long-term durable remission. With the hypothesis that dual-antigen targeting may overcome mechanisms of immune escape through antigen loss which occur following single antigen targeting, advancing combinatorial approaches represents one potential way to improve durable remissions following CAR T-cells. Building upon on the prior experience with effective CD19 CAR T-cell targeting and CD22 CAR T-cell targeting, the latter for which I authored a successful application to the FDA for 'Breakthrough Therapy Designation' in 2019, my team took the natural next step of testing a combinatorial treatment approach targeting both CD19 and CD22 simultaneously. Based on a construct developed in the POB where dual antigen targeting was achieved based on two scFvs configured in tandem,I developed a clinical trial testing a novel bivalent CD19/CD22 CAR T-cell construct (CD19.22.BBz CART) in children and young adults with B-ALL (NCT03448393). This built directly off our prior experiences with CD19 and CD22 single agent targeting. The trial began enrollment in 2018 and we published our initial experience in Blood in 2022 based on the experience of the first 20 children and young adults with B-ALL who were infused. We found that this construct was highly effective in inducing remissions. including in those patients who had received prior CAR T-cell therapy. Additionally, the toxicity profile was relatively mild with minimal rates of high-grade CRS or severe ICANS. Persistence, however, was limited despite the incorporation of a 4-1BB costimulatory domain prompting both further investigation and the utilization of this construct as a bridge to HSCT. Through additional laboratory-based experiments, we also found that CD22 targeting for this construct was suboptimal-limiting the ability to effectively dually-target CD19 and CD22 simultaneously. Through efforts led by the Taylor Lab, we explored these clinical observations through a reverse-translation approach and were able to: 1) compare differences in promoters used in CAR T-cell constructs and 2) explore the features of the bivalent CD19.22.BBz CART to several novel bicistronic CD19/CD22 CAR T-cell constructs that effectively expressed both CD19 and CD22 scFv independently on the cell surface. Based on preclinical efforts that identified a more optimal dual-antigen targeting strategy, we have successfully translated this effort to the clinic and enrolled our first patient to our CD19/CD22 bicistronic CAR T-cell trial for children and young adults with B-ALL in January 2023. Given the concern for antigen escape (loss of CD19 and/or CD22), exploring alternate antigens for CAR T-cell targeting remains imperative. A high-risk subgroup of B-ALL, termed 'Philadelphia-like, or Ph-like' has been associated with high rates of chemotherapy resistance and relapse. Approximately half of these childhood and adult Ph-like ALL cases harbor a rearrangement in cytokine receptor like factor-2 (CRLF2), which encodes one subunit of the thymic stromal lymphopoietin receptor (TSLPR) and heterodimerizes with the IL7Ra subunit. Given the high frequency of CRLF2-R in B-ALL across the age spectrum with detectable TSLPR overexpression by flow cytometry, an anti-CRLF2-TSLPR (TSLPR CART) CAR T-cell construct was created in the Fry Lab (former POB). Accomplishments: The preclinical, translational, and IND-enabling studies for a phase I dose-escalation study in children and young adults with CRLF2R (TSLPR expressing) B-ALL using the clinical vector have all been conducted by the Taylor Lab and the Center for Cellular Engineering. Regarding the trial design, dose-escalation will be conducted using a 3+3 design. Eligible participants for this trial will initially be young adult participants aged >18 years to <39 years of age with relapsed or refractory CRLF2-R (TSLPR expressing) B-ALL. After initial experience in adult participants to evaluate safety of this first in human target, an amendment with available data will be submitted to the FDA to include the participation of pediatric participants. Plans are to submit to the FDA by later this year, with the anticipation of enrollment beginning in early 2025. While novel constructs to improve upon the current limitations of single antigen targeting are in development, optimizing the utilization of CAR T-cell constructs that are currently available and being used for children and adults in real-time is of the utmost importance. In this regard, I have embarked on a series of studies (both retrospective and prospective) that will help to establish standards of care in risk-stratification in the peri-CAR T-cell timeline to improve outcomes for patients receiving CD19 CAR T-cells. Key efforts have focused on understanding the impact of sequential antigen targeting, identification of risk factors associated with relapse, and development of a prospective study that will serve to establish a post-CAR T-cell biomarker-based monitoring approach to optimally risk-stratify patients post-infusion. Based on a concern that sequential CD19 targeting (e.g., blinatumomab followed by CD19 CAR T-cells) could select for antigen escape, I led a multi-center retrospective effort to study the impact of sequential targeting, ultimately culminating in a dataset of 420 children and young adults who had received CD19 CAR T-cells (primarily on early phase academic studies). We identified that both high-disease burden and non-response to prior blinatumomab (before receipt of CD19 CAR T-cells) associated with poor event-free, relapse-free and overall survival post-infusion. In exploration of serial antigen expression, we also determined that ongoing modulation of cell-surface CD19 expression (bright to dim expression over time) could potentially predict loss of CD19 and that closer monitoring was needed for these patients. Additional retrospective analyses have identified risk factors associated with unique relapse phenotypes (e.g., antigen positive versus antigen negative disease and risk factors for lineage switch).

project_title: Protection of Salivary Gland in PSMA-targeted radioligand therapy
project_abstract_text: The goal of this project is to see if salivary gland uptake of PSMA injected systemically can be blocked selectively blocked by using local blocking methods at the salivary gland level. The desired end point would be blocking salivary gland uptake of PSMA without affected the tumor update. This is a collaboration with Dr. Blake Warner of the Dental Institute and involves the use of rodents as the pre-clinical model. If the pre-clinical approach is successful, the approach will be translated to humans in a future clinical trial. This study is now close to accrual.

project_title: Phase 1-2 study of Lu177-DOTATATE and olaparib in neuroendocrine tumors
project_abstract_text: The rationale behind using combination therapies in cancer stems from the potential of synergistic mechanisms of action of the involved agents. Olaparib is a PARP-inhibitor which blocks the repair of single-stranded DNA breaks and is especially effective when combined with other agents which induces DNA damage. We are nearing accrual for the Phase I portion of the trial, to look at the combination of olaparib with the targeted radionuclide agent Lutetium-177-DOTATATE (trade name: Lutathera, Novartis/Advanced Accelerator Appliations) in inoperable gastro-entero-pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (GEP-NET).

project_title: Hepatic organization and functions
project_abstract_text: We aim to identify the mechanisms maintaining cellular heterogeneity and spatial compartments in normal liver physiology and gain insights into how they are disrupted in liver disease and cancer. We use diet-induced metabolic stress either through overnight (ON) fasting or western diet (WD) to model the onset of Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD) in mice. In addition, primary Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) models are used to examine tumorigenesis. In complementary studies, biopsies from healthy or chemotherapy-treated patients shed light on compartmentalization in the human liver. We apply cutting-edge technologies, including Intravital microscopy (IVM) and volumetric electron Microscopy (vEM), combined with in-house developed cell isolation and AI-guided image analysis. The knowledge gained will lead to a better understanding of liver physiology, approaches for cancer prevention, tumor classification, and, ultimately, novel therapy approaches.

project_title: Control of cell cycle commitment by APC-C-Cdh1
project_abstract_text: In mammalian cells, DNA damage can trigger cells to arrest prior to entering into S phase to safeguard against replicating damaged DNA, which could lead to even greater defects. Cells were long thought to arrest right at the transition point between G1 and S phase, giving rise to the term G1/S checkpoint. However challenging this paradigm, my lab showed that individual cells take divergent paths after suffering DNA damage in G1 phase. Rather than cells arresting at the G1/S transition, my lab observed cells either reversing course and entering quiescence or seemingly ignoring the damage and entering S phase. The molecular mechanism underlying this bifurcation was due to the slow induction of the DNA damage-induced cell cycle inhibitor p21. Cells that induced p21 fast enough re-routed to quiescence, while cells that were too slow to induce p21 entered S phase with damaged DNA. This work showed that the long-standing model of the G1/S checkpoint was simply an artifact of bulk-cell measurements, and by using live-cell imaging and single-cell measurements was able to demonstrate that cells exhibit highly heterogenous responses to DNA damage.

project_title: The Role of Protein Methylation in Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head and Neck
project_abstract_text: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is the sixth most prevalent non-skin cancer in the world, causing 890,000 new cases and 450,000 deaths in 2018. HNSCC is categorized into two main pathogenetic types: human-papilloma-virus (HPV)-positive and HPV-negative, which has strong associations with tobacco use. HPV-negative HNSCC is associated with a worse prognosis and treatment is often multimodal and toxic, with the use of surgical intervention, platinum-based chemotherapy and radiation therapy. Despite this intense multimodality therapy, approximately 50% of patients with HPV-negative HNSCC recur either locoregionally or with distant metastases. Even with the advent of immunotherapy, patients with recurrent/metastatic disease have a dismal prognosis, with a median overall survival of approximately 13 months. Based on the above, novel therapeutic approaches are urgently needed. SET and MYND-domain containing protein 3 (SMYD3) is a protein lysine methyltransferase with oncogenic activity in multiple cancer types, such as colon, hepatocellular carcinoma, lung and pancreatic cancer. It methylates histone substrates, such as H3K4me3, enabling its function as a chromatin modifier, as well as non-histone substrates, such as MAP3K2, VEGFR1 and HER2, which mediates its cytoplasmic functions [Hamamoto et al, Nat.Rev.Cancer, 2016]. Over the past 2 years, our lab has focused on the function of SMYD3 as an oncogenic chromatin modifier and novel therapeutic target in HPV-negative HNSCC. We have found that SMYD3 is significantly overexpressed in ~60% of HPV-negative HNSCC tumors [Nigam et al, Cell Rep. 2023], and that SMYD3 depletion significantly decreases the proliferative and colony forming capacity, cell cycling and the invasive potential of HPV-negative HNSCC cell lines, while it also significantly reduces tumor growth in immunocompromised mouse models of flank tumor xenografts [Murali et al, 2024, under review, Sci. Rep.]. Our findings support that these phenotypes are mediated through a bifaceted transcription function, whereby SMYD3 binds to and acts as an activator or repressor of specific cell cycle and epithelial-mesenchymal transition genesets within the same cell context [Murali et al, 2024, under review, Sci. Rep]. Furthermore, we have reported that Smyd3 depletion using anti-sense oligonucleotides (ASOs), which degrade Smyd3 mRNA, sensitizes HPV-negative MOC1 flank mouse tumors to anti-PD-1 therapy by increasing the intratumoral influx of CD8+ T-cells, reinvigorating exhausted CD8+ T-cells and upregulating the protein levels of PD-1 on CD8+ T-cells, and H2-Kb on MOC1 cells in vivo. Combined Smyd3 depletion and anti-PD-1 therapy enhances IFN response signatures in MOC1 tumors and leads to cure of 50% of MOC1 tumors and significant shrinkage in 25% of the treated tumors [Tsai et al, 2024, iScience, Nigam et al, Cell Rep. 2023]. Mechanistically, we reported that loss of SMYD3 increases the sensitivity of HPV-negative HNSCC cancer cells to interferon-b (IFN-b) and induces transcriptional upregulation of multiple type I IFN response genes through the regulation of UHRF1, a major epigenetic H3K9me3 reader which binds on the promoters of key immune-related genes and recruits DNMT1, and through the deposition of the repressive mark H4K20me3 on the gene bodies of immune-related genes in human HPV-negative HNSCC cells [Nigam et al, Cell Rep. 2023]. Further, we found that SMYD3 overexpression is associated with decreased tumor CD8+ T-cell infiltration and poor response to neoadjuvant pembrolizumab in patients with HPV-negative HNSCC. Building upon the aforementioned findings, the goal of this research program over the upcoming 4 years is to elucidate the specific mechanisms through which SMYD3 exerts its bifaceted transcriptional effect in the nucleus of HPV-negative HNSCC cells, determine the cytoplasmic functions of SMYD3 in HPV-negative HNSCC, and to develop PROteolysis-Targeting Chimeras (PROTACs) targeting SMYD3. To this purpose, the following aims will be pursued: Specific Aim 1: Determine the epigenetic mechanisms through which SMYD3 exerts a bifaceted repressive and activating transcriptional effect in HPV-negative HNSCC. Hypothesis: SMYD3 mediates the formation of specific transcriptional complexes that enable its function as a repressor and activator in HPV-negative HNSCC cells. We have found that SMYD3 promotes the deposition of H4K20me3 on the gene bodies of immune-related genes, inducing their repression. We will conduct immunoprecipitation of the SMYD3 chromatin-bound fraction from nuclear extracts of HPV-negative HNSCC cells (HN-6 cell line), and then mass spectrometry analysis to identify interacting proteins of SMYD3 in its chromatin-bound form. The top 5 significant interacting candidate partners will be sorted and validated with co-immunoprecipitation in two cell lines. CUTandRUN assays of the validated partners will be conducted to confirm chromatin binding and evaluate co-occupancy patterns with SMYD3. Transient knockdown of each of these candidates will be conducted using siRNAs to assess their activating or repressive effect on transcription. CUTandRUN assays for repressive histone marks (H4K20me3, H3K27me3, H3K9me3) will also be pursued to assess whether SMYD3 affects the deposition of these histone marks. Specific Aim 2: Determine and dissect the functions of non-histone cytoplasmic substrate(s) of SMYD3 in HPV-negative HNSCC. Hypothesis: SMYD3 mediates oncogenic effects through a non-histone cytoplasmic substrate(s) in HPV-negative HNSCC. The SILAC method will be utilized to identify candidate non-histone cytoplasmic substrates of SMYD3 in HPV-negative HNSCC cells (HN-6 cell line). Using the top 5 candidate methylation substrates, in vitro methyltransferase assays will be conducted with recombinant proteins/peptides using tritium-labeled SAM, followed by mass spectrometry to identify the specific methylation site. A customized antibody will then be generated to further validate the induction of the specific methylation in cancer cells. Based on the known function of the specific substrate, loss- and gain-of-function experiments will be designed with the methylation-mutant substrate and enzymatically active or inactive SMYD3 CRISPR expressing cell lines to dissect the function of the methylated substrate in HPV-negative HNSCC cells. Specific Aim 3: Develop PROteolysis-Targeting Chimeras (PROTACs) targeting SMYD3. Hypothesis: SMYD3 targeting PROTACs are effective in degrading SMYD3 protein levels and are more efficacious than available SMYD3 enzymatic inhibitors in suppressing the oncogenic phenotypes of HPV-negative HNSCC cells in vitro and in vivo. Ten SMYD3 PROTAC lead compounds have already been generated and have manifested significant antiproliferative activity in multiple HPV-negative HNSCC cell lines. In vivo toxicity experiments, pharmacokinetic (PK) and efficacy studies using SCID mice will be conducted to identify compounds with the most favorable toxicity, PK and PD profile. These compounds will be further compared with the available SMYD3 enzymatic inhibitors to assess their effect on SMYD3-induced epigenetic and non-epigenetic pathways. An enzymatically-dead SMYD3 expressing cell line will be generated using CRISPR knock-in and its proliferative and colony-forming capacity, invasive capacity and type I IFN-responsiveness will be compared with that of an already available SMYD3 KO and a control wild type cell line.

project_title: Study cell cycle regulation in dormant tumor cells
project_abstract_text: Contrary to temporary quiescence, cells can respond to cellular stress by undergoing an irreversible cell cycle exit termed senescence. We sought to leverage of platform for long-term single cell tracking and quantitative analysis to understand the molecular mechanism underlying the irreversible cell cycle exit associated with senescence. Using an innovative strategy to induce senescence transiently, we discovered that constitutive MYC degradation was necessary to maintain cells in the senescent state. Importantly, our data revealed that inhibiting MYC in combination with clinically approved CDK4/6 inhibitors could switch cells from quiescence to senescence, a strategy that could greatly improve the efficacy of CDK4/6 inhibitors currently used as the front-line treatment for hormone receptor positive breast cancer.

project_title: Minimal Myc functional threshold for tumorigenesis
project_abstract_text: We designed a genetic test of the hypothesis that a minimum level of Myc function is required to 'amplify' the transcriptional programs necessary for promoting and sustaining tumor formation. We employed the mouse p53 null mutant (p53 KO) as a robust tumor model to test for Myc-dependency by introducing modest changes in the endogenous c-Myc level (c-Myc+/-). Tumor-free survival times were compared in genetically similar p53 KO sibling mice that were either c-Myc+/+ (Myc WT; p53 KO), or c-Myc+/- (Myc-Het; p53 KO). Median tumor-free survival times doubled in the Myc-Het; p53 KO relative to Myc-WT (significant at P 0.0001). This difference was independent of the tumor type, with hemangiosarcoma and thymic lymphoma being the most common (83%) tumor types in both groups. Analyses of c-Myc genomic alterations and expression levels in p53 KO tumors, using Spectral Karyotyping (SKY), FISH, and quantitative RNA ISH and immunohistochemistry, revealed that compensation for the initially reduced endogenous c-Myc dosage had occurred in tumors arising in Myc-Het;p53 KO mice. Notably, in hemangiosarcomas, genome amplification achieved by several rounds of genome tetraploidization was consistently higher in the Myc-Het;p53 KO than in the Myc-WT;p53 KO tumors. Although thymic lymphomas of either genotype showed no genomic amplification, expression of Myc RNA and Myc protein were nevertheless comparably elevated in both the Myc-WT and Myc-Het tumors, suggesting that compensation for reduced Myc gene dosage had occurred at the transcriptional level. These results indicate that reduced endogenous c-Myc dosage substantially delays tumor development in mice that are genetically predisposed to neoplasia and that, in order for Myc-Het;p53 KO mice to develop tumors, a compensatory increase in expression of Myc, which can occur by multiple mechanisms, is required. We have also used allografts using of thymic lymphomas from p53 KO mice carrying conditional c-Myc-floxed and tamoxifen-dependent Cre alleles and a dual-fluorescent reporter to monitor recombination efficacy, in order to test whether reducing c-Myc will adversely impact established tumors (i.e. growth, progression) and found that after recovery from recombination induced apoptosis, tumor growth rate is substantially slowed when endogenous Myc dosage is acutely reduced. Our results strongly suggest that a modest reduction in Myc can curtail cancer growth and has important implications, particularly for extending tumor-free survival in patients with Li-Fraumeni syndrome (germline mutations in p53), as well as sporadic cancers. This study provides a framework and model for future analyses of c-Myc role in tumorigenesis and tumor progression and can be readily extended to other tumor types using analogous strategies, and other tumor promoters, such as oncogenic Ras. We are currently testing whether p53-loss driven tumorigenesis can occur at all in the context of severely reduced or absent endogenous c-Myc expression levels using a conditional knock-out approach to model hemangiosarcomas by removing both p53 and c-Myc genes together, selectively from endothelial tissues (Cdh5CreER) in young (2-week age) mice. Surprisingly, we have found that hemagiosarcomas still occur in p53-KO mice with c-myc loss in endothelial cells; however, these develop at a much slower pace than in c-myc-WT mice, which suggests two likely possible explanations: 1) incomplete recombination with removal of p53, but not both copies of the c-myc allele in rare endothelial cells, 2) compensatory activation of another endogenous myc gene (eg. N-myc) in a small fraction of p53-KO endothelial cells that compensates for c-Myc loss. We are currently analyzing tumors that develop in these mice to determine the basis for tumor formation in the absence of c-Myc. Compensation by activation of another Myc gene would support the model that tumorigenesis absolutely requires a minimum Myc-threshold to occur.

project_title: Outcomes and Risk of Rare Tumors
project_abstract_text: Rare cancers are defined as those with <40,000 cases per year. There are over 130 separate types of primary CNS tumors, all of which meet the definition of a rare cancer. However, some CNS cancers have incidences of less than 1,000 cases per year. Because of its relative rarity, limited reports of the presentation and clinical course have been completed. An additional consequence of the relative rarity of these CNS tumors, studies to evaluate risk factors for the occurrence of these rare CNS tumors or predicting the clinical course of these rare CNS tumors are also limited. Rare CNS tumors like other cancers, occur when there are changes to genes that control the way cells grow and divide often as a result of exposure to other environmental risk factors. Therefore, exploring genetic changes in persons with rare CNS tumors will allow us to begin to understand what changes are associated specifically with these tumors. To date, these participants are often included as part of larger cohorts which include other types of brain tumors. We now understand that even among gliomas, the risk factors differ]. Therefore, identifying the risk factors specifically associated with rare CNS tumors is critical for primary prevention and early detection. This knowledge would allow scientists and physicians to eventually screen for these changes or target the genes or the processes they control for treatment purposes. Paper reporting self-efficacy and outcomes recently accepted for publication. Ongoing analysis looking at self-report versus chart review underway with planned publication in 2024

project_title: Mechanisms of resistance to treatment in aggressive prostate cancers
project_abstract_text: Our efforts to study the resistance mechanisms of lethal prostate cancer are rooted in three distinct studies. First, we are using immunocompromised and humanized models of prostate cancer metastasis focusing on organotropism and variable treatment resistant phenotypes upon metastasis establishment and recurrence. Second we are using clinical samples from patients treated with standard and novel therapies to assess the genomic, transcriptomic and proteomic determinants of treatment outcome. Finally, we continue to explore potential mechanisms in vitro.

project_title: Discovering novel therapies for glioma patients
project_abstract_text: To investigate the therapeutic vulnerability of IDH-mutant gliomas to ZTR, we performed extensive preclinical studies in patient derived cell models and in vivo glioma models. Our laboratory research demonstrated, for the first time, the ability of ZTR to disrupt mitochondrial function, suppress stress response pathways, and induce cell death specifically in IDH-mutant gliomas at a low concentration. In collaboration with NCI NCATS, we conducted a high-throughput drug screen of 2,481 FDA-approved and investigational drugs using six primary patient-derived glioma cell lines with IDH1 mutation, which demonstrated ZTR is one of the few available drugs showing both high efficacy of cell killing and capacity to penetrated BBB. ZTR exhibited selective growth inhibition across multiple IDH-mutant glioma in vitro and in vivo models. Mechanistically, ZTR at low doses suppressed CDK9 and RNA Pol II phosphorylation in IDH-mutant cells, disrupting mitochondrial function and NAD+ production, causing oxidative stress. Integrated biochemical profiling of ZTR kinase targets and transcriptomics unveiled that ZTR-induced bioenergetic failure was linked to the suppression of Provirus Integration site for Moloney Leukemia Virus (PIM) kinase activity. Continues with bench-to-bedside translational research, I have designed and launched a hypothesis-driven phase I/II clinical trial of zotiraciclib in recurrent IDH-mutant gliomas to evaluate the safety and efficacy of ZTR as a single agent in recurrent IDH-mutant glioma patients (NCT 05588141, NCI 000860). This is an open label, phase I/II study of ZTR in patients with IDH-mutant recurrent gliomas WHO grade 2-4. The primary objective is to estimate recommended phase II dose (RP2D) of ZTR in phase I; to determine PFS12 in participants with recurrent glioma, IDH1/2-mutant, WHO grade 3 treated with ZTR in phase II. Patients with clinically indicated need for surgical resection of their brain tumors will be enrolled to the surgical cohort of the study prior to the procedure following the screening. A dose of ZTR at RP2D will be given within 24 hours prior to surgery. Tumor tissue and blood sample will be collected during the surgery. Drug concentration and pharmacodynamic biomarkers, including CDK9 phosphorylation, gH2AX and other PD markers will be assessed using the tumor tissue. PK profiling will be performed for all study participants treated at all dose levels in phase I and those enrolled in surgical cohort during phase II. The PK profile at different dose level will assist the RP2D determination, as well as correlate plasma ZTR concentration with PD and PG analyses. Given the findings of polymorphisms in CYP3A4 and 1A2 in study NCI 17C0009, we will perform PG study in all study patients to further validate the previous findings. To expand the clinical trial portfolio in glioblastoma, my laboratory conducted preclinical studies that provided a proof of concept for the combined treatment with LMP400 and Niraparib in a subset of glioblastoma with PTEN deficiency. The preclinical data support the clinical investigation of a therapeutic strategy that should have a broad impact on precision medicine in a subset of GBM patients with PTEN deficiency. Moreover, our promising findings supported the designation of FDA Orphan Drug Designation of LMP 400 as treatment for GBM. Taking the laboratory findings to the bedside, I have designed a clinical trial The clinical trial is designed to test the hypothesis that combined inhibition of TOP1 and PARP using LMP400 and Niraparib is safe and results in better disease control in recurrent glioblastoma with PTEN deficiency. Primary objective for phase I is to determine the RP2D of LMP400 in combination with Niraparib in recurrent glioma, WHO grade 4; the primary objective for Phase II is to determine the efficacy of combined treatment in recurrent glioblastoma using PFS6. The key secondary objectives include the Objective Response Rate (ORR) as determined by RANO criteria; PFS, OS and OS12; and PRO measured by self-reported symptoms severity and interference with daily activities using the MDASI-BT. The clinical trial is currently going through the contracting and reviewing process.

project_title: Understanding IDH mutant gliomas
project_abstract_text: I have designed and implemented an observational clinical trial, NCI 19C0096, titled 'Studying the Biology of Higher-grade Transformation in IDH-mutant Gliomas via longitudinal Observation of Tumor Metabolic Reprogramming using Noninvasive Metabolic Imaging'. To date, 41 patients have enrolled in the study and about a hundred MRS scans have been performed. Many participants have undergone multiple scans longitudinally. Importantly, twenty MRS imaging were performed within two weeks prior to the clinically indicated tumor resection. Tumor samples within the imaging voxel have been procured, processed, and will be used for LC-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). This will enable us to correlate imaged-based determinations of 2HG and other metabolites level with the ex vivo measurement of the actual tumor tissue. In addition, the clinical trial protocol has been amended to include the HP 13C pyruvate MRSI for longitudinal disease monitoring in IDH-mutant gliomas. This study has been done through the intramural and extramural collaboration. This clinical trial will serve as the FDA IND enabling protocol for HP 13C pyruvate MRSI, allowing the first patient at NCI/NIH to be imaged using this technology. Recognizing the importance of 13C MRSI, allowing the monitoring of metabolic pathways, and the relevance of a-KG in IDH-mutant gliomas research, I am developing HP 13C a-KG MRSI as an additional metabolic imaging tool for my research program. Leveraging the resource at NCI, we generated GMP level [1-13C-5-12C]-a-KG as a HP 13C MRSI imaging probe via funding support from NCI Experimental Therapeutics (NExT) program. In collaboration with UCSF imaging program, we performed preclinical studies values of HP [1-13C-5-12C]-a-KG MRSI as an important non-invasive tool for monitoring disease and drug treatment response. Simultaneously, I designed 'A First-In-Human Phase I Study of Hyperpolarized (HP) [1-13C-5-12C]-a-KG Metabolic Imaging in Diffuse Glioma with IDH mutation' (IRB001558), which was planned as the FDA IND enabling protocol to establish another non-invasive approach to monitor disease and treatment response in IDH-mutant gliomas. To test the hypothesis that IDH-mutant gliomas with high TMB are better respond to immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICPI) therapy, I have designed and opened a Phase II clinical trial (NCI 19-c-0006, NCT03718767) titled: Nivolumab in Patients With IDH-Mutant Gliomas with and without Hypermutator Phenotype'. To date, accrual to NHMP cohort has been completed, while 8 have been treated in HMP cohort. I plan to reach to interim analysis for HMP cohort in the next 6 months, considering the rarity of the HMP case in IDH-mutant gliomas. Peripheral blood and tumor samples have been collected from study participants which will be used for correlative studies.

project_title: Identification and use of T-cell receptors recognizing common tumor mutations
project_abstract_text: We have used HLA transgenic mice to generate multiple TCRs recognizing common human tumor mutations in the context of human MHC presenting molecules. Several of these have no fully human TCRs with the same specificity. Although totally specific for the neoantigen versus the wild type epitope, many of these TCRs are of insufficient affinity to recognize most human tumor lines or organoids. We have screened multiple approaches to enhancing recognition through the introduction of co-receptor and TCR signalling moieties. These studies are continuing, with encouraging results found with a novel IL-12 construct in collaboration with Dr. Peter Kim.

project_title: Single-cell DNA methylation analysis of human cancer
project_abstract_text: We have used techniques in machine learning and deconvolution of methylation data to elucidate genomic profiles of several CNS cancers. In one study, we examined papillary tumor of the pineal region (PTPR), an uncommon tumor of the pineal region with distinctive histopathologic and molecular characteristics. Experience is limited with respect to its molecular heterogeneity and clinical characteristics. Here, we describe 39 new cases and combine these with 37 previously published cases for a cohort of 76 PTPR's, all confirmed by methylation profiling. As previously reported, two main methylation groups were identified (PTPR-A and PTPR-B). In our analysis we extended the subtyping into three subtypes: PTPR-A, PTPR-B1 and PTPR-B2 supported by DNA methylation profile and genomic copy number variations. Frequent loss of chromosome 3 or 14 was found in PTPR-B1 tumors but not in PTPR-B2. Examination of clinical outcome showed that nearly half (14/30, 47%) of examined patients experienced tumor progression with significant difference among the subtypes (p value = 0.046). Our analysis extends the understanding of this uncommon but distinct neuroepithelial tumor by describing its molecular heterogeneity and clinical outcomes, including its tendency towards tumor recurrence. In another study, we examined a newly proposed tumor type, CNS tumor with BRD4::LEUTX fusion, has been described. As only a few CNS tumors with BRD4::LEUTX fusions have been described, we herein characterize a cohort of 9 such cases (4 new, 5 previously published) to further describe their clinicopathologic and molecular features. We demonstrate that CNS embryonal tumor with BRD4::LEUTX fusion comprises a well-defined methylation class/cluster. We find that patients are young (4 years or younger), with large tumors at variable locations, and frequently with evidence of leptomeningeal/cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dissemination. Histologically, tumors were highly cellular with high-grade embryonal features. Immunohistochemically, 5/5 cases showed synaptophysin and 4/5 showed OLIG2 expression, thus overlapping with CNS neuroblastoma, FOXR2-activated. DNA copy number profiles were generally flat; however, two tumors had chromosome 1q gains. No recurring genomic changes, besides the presence of the fusion, were found. The LEUTX portion of the fusion transcript was constant in all cases assessed, while the BRD4 portion varied but included a domain with proto-oncogenic activity in all cases. Two patients with clinical follow up available had tumors with excellent response to chemotherapy. Two of our patients were alive without evidence of recurrence or progression after gross total resection and chemotherapy at 16 and 33 months. One patient relapsed, and the last of our four patients died of disease one month after diagnosis. Overall, this case series provides additional evidence for this as a distinct tumor type defined by the presence of a specific fusion as well as a distinct DNA methylation signature. Studies on larger series are required to further characterize these tumors.

project_title: Development and validation of a predictor of meningioma recurrence
project_abstract_text: An important clinical problem in the management of patients with meningiomas is the difficulty in predicting recurrence at the individual patient level, limiting appropriate selection of patients who would benefit from adjuvant therapy to delay recurrence. We have participated in new studies examining transcriptomic subtypes and heterogeneity. To approach this problem, we combined 13 bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) datasets to create a dimension-reduced reference landscape of 1,298 meningiomas. The clinical and genomic metadata effectively correlated with landscape regions, which led to the identification of meningioma subtypes with specific biological signatures. The time to recurrence also correlated with the map location. Further, we developed an algorithm that maps new patients onto this landscape, where the nearest neighbors predict outcome. This study highlights the utility of combining bulk transcriptomic datasets to visualize the complexity of tumor populations. Further, we provide an interactive tool for understanding the disease and predicting patient outcomes. We also participated in studies of CDKN2A in meningioma. The expression of CDKN2A was independently prognostic after accounting for copy number loss and consistently increased with WHO grade and more aggressive molecular and methylation groups irrespective of cohort. Despite the discordant and mutually exclusive status of the CDKN2A gene in these groups, both CDKN2Ahigh meningiomas and meningiomas with CDKN2A deletions were enriched for similar cell cycle pathways but at different checkpoints. High mRNA expression of CDKN2A was also associated with gene hypermethylation, Rb-deficiency, and lack of response to CDK inhibition. p16 immunohistochemistry could not reliably differentiate between meningiomas with and without CDKN2A deletions but appeared to correlate better with mRNA expression. These findings support the role of CDKN2A mRNA expression as a biomarker of clinically aggressive meningiomas with potential therapeutic implications.

project_title: Preclinical Modelling and Therapeutic Development for Other Cancer Indications
project_abstract_text: To support research advancements in Dr. Laurie Krug's lab at the CCR HIV and AIDS Malignancy Branch, CAPR has embarked on a project aimed at developing pdx modes from Kaposi sarcoma (KS) biopsies. As the clinical KS samples proven themselves to display very low take rate and slow proliferation in recipient mice, specific set of standard operating procedures have been developed for both clinical sample collections and pdx implantations to increase success rate in deriving stable pdx xenografts. In addition to optimizing the experimental protocols, we have performed evaluation of various growth factors and employed humanized IL-6 transgene expressing NSG recipient mouse sub-strain to implant 9 skin biopsies and 3 gastrointestinal tract colonoscopy biopsies from KS patients. Alternative procedures for more reliable and sustainable propagation of slowly growing in mice KS tumors are also being evaluated, such as implantation of biopsies into renal capsule. CAPR researchers successfully established and characterized several PDX models for both chemotherapy-naive and recurrent KS and compared anti-tumor efficacy of Doxil chemotherapy in such models. Comparative histopathology an IHC evaluation for established KS PDXmodels have been also completed and spatial transcriptomics studies are underway. Additionally, the established models are being employed to assess preclinical efficacy of two novel selective small molecule inhibitors of CDK4/CDK6 (abemaciclib) and Janus kinas 2/CD135 (pacritinib). CAPR pancreatic modelling group made progress towards developing an unmet need model for a rare pancreatic malignancy type known as pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma (PACC). To achieve this ambitious objective, we have either imported and characterized two constituent alleles of PACC model (Cela1-CreERT and APC-flox) or engineered in house using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing technology a conditional allele for Id3 gene which is currently in characterization stage. The final assembly of the tri-allelic PACC model has been established by intercrossing Cela1CreERT recombinase- expressing allele with conditional alleles for Id3 and APC tumor suppressor genes. Multiple tri-allelic animals bearing the full set of genetic alleles anticipated to develop PACC malignant lesions have been induced for carcinogenesis and are monitored by palpation and abdominal imaging tools for tumor incidence originating in pancreatic acinar cells and subsequent analyses of the disease course to validate the model vs. the corresponding clinical disease and prepare PACC animal cohorts for drug evaluation experimental activities. CAPR PDX modelling efforts resulted in establishing Program's first PDX model for gastric neuroendocrine tumor. We are currently propagating this gastric NET PDX tumor from passage 2 to passage 3 in recipient NSG animals to establish a biobank of PDX tissues suitable for subsequent experimentation in a variety of model evaluation and drug testing experiments. As one of the promising clinical avenues in treatment of advanced GEP_NET malignancies, we will subject mice carrying gastric NET tumors to a combination of epigenetic modifier therapeutics (such as HDAC inhibitor entinostat) and radioablation-based therapeutics targeting somatostatin type 2 receptor (SSTR2). SSTR2 molecule is expressed on early stage neuroendocrine malignancies but becomes epigenetically silenced in higher grade tumors. The availability of PDX models carrying tumors proven to express only low levels of SSTR drug target will facilitate the preclinical validation of this combinatorial therapeutic strategy.

project_title: Genomic Biomarkers of Cancer
project_abstract_text: We have made substantial progress on goal #3, where we have published a paper in Nature Medicine, showing that molecular genomic alterations can be predicted from histopathology in CNS tumors. Specifically, we developed Deep lEarning from histoPathoLOgy and methYlation (DEPLOY), a deep learning model that classifies CNS tumors to ten major categories from histopathology. DEPLOY integrates three distinct components: the first classifies CNS tumors directly from slide images ('direct model'), the second initially generates predictions for DNA methylation beta values, which are subsequently used for tumor classification ('indirect model'), and the third classifies tumor types directly from routinely available patient demographics. First, we find that DEPLOY accurately predicts beta values from histopathology images. Second, using a ten-class model trained on an internal dataset of 1,796 patients, we predict the tumor categories in three independent external test datasets including 2,156 patients, achieving an overall accuracy of 95% and balanced accuracy of 91% on samples that are predicted with high confidence. These results showcase the potential future use of DEPLOY to assist pathologists in diagnosing CNS tumors within a clinically relevant short time frame.

project_title: MyPART: My Pediatric and Adult Rare Tumor Network - Cures
project_abstract_text: The natural history of rare solid tumors study (19-C-0016) (NHRST) at CCR (PI Dr. Mary Frances Wedekind Malone) is the backbone of the MyPART program.
