The goals of the study are to 1) comprehensively and longitudinally evaluate rare tumors in children and young adults through 2) standardized evaluations, medical record extraction, patient reported outcomes, comprehensive clinical and research molecular profiling, with 3) return of results and recommendations including identification of suitable clinical trials after molecular tumor boards, with help of a genetic counselor. An annotated biospecimen repository is established and data are deposited in NIH approved databases led by Dr. Reilly's group. An important aspect of this study is that patients can enroll remotely or at the NIH Clinical Center. This allowed us to continue enrolling patients during the Covid 19 pandemic when patients could not travel to the NIH and also enabled international participation. Data collection includes standardized web-based forms for family and medical history, patient reported outcomes, tumor pathology, tumor treatment history, tumor imaging, and biospecimen collection. In addition, Dr. Abby Sandler leads efforts to engage patient advocacy and patients. Subprotocols have been developed for select rare tumors, such as chordoma, to allow collection of very tumor- specific information. This study (19-C-0016) opened for enrollment in January 2019 and has enrolled 602 participants as of 2/7/2024 with >68 histologies from 46 US states and 27 countries outside the US. For the most frequent histologies enrolled dedicated clinical disease champions have been identified: Chordoma (N=111), Dr. Wedekind Malon, gastrointestinal stromal tumor (non-kit or PDGFRA mutated) (N=98), Dr. Glod, neuroendocrine tumors (N=87), Dr. Del Rivero, adrenocortical carcinoma (N=72), Dr. Del Rivero, medullary thyroid carcinoma (N=26), Dr. Glod. Given pediatric and adult oncology expertise at CCR, patients of any age with these tumors can enroll, allowing the evaluation of biologic differences of tumors in children and adults. Making this protocol available to PIs in CCR, Dr. Alewine (CCR medical oncology) has been able to enroll participants with very rare pancreatic carcinoma without the need to develop a new study. The NHRST study will soon open to enrollment at Oregon Health Science University, Portland OR (PI, Dr. Shivaani Kummar) and at Texas Children's Hospital, Houston, TX (PI, Dr. Rajkumar Venkatramani). Our NHRST study is an integral part of the Cancer MoonshotSM funded MyPART. The study was developed by IRP staff (Drs. Del Rivero, Widemann, Reilly, and Sandler) but is also available to other CCR investigators as a platform to study rare tumors. During the conduct of the study, we have learned that focus on a limited number of rare tumors is needed to enroll cohorts, which may be sufficiently large and well characterized to serve as potential external controls for interventional clinical trials. This requires strong advocacy engagement and disease champions for specific rare tumors. A landscape analysis of national and international rare tumor research programs and literature review led by Drs. Sandler and Vivelo also indicated that while many efforts are ongoing, they are frequently isolated, and that the rare cancer community may especially benefit from collaborative efforts. We are thus working with the NCI Childhood Cancer Data Initiative (CCDI), the Children's Oncology Group (COG), non-COG investigators and advocacy towards the development of a CCDI-coordinated national strategy to study multiple rare tumors simultaneously. This will be an observational longitudinal natural history study for patients with rare solid tumors. Eligible patients will be identified through COG-APEC14B1 and community engagement. The foundational infrastructure of this study will be provided to disease champions across the country. A protocol is in development with the goal to open early 2025. The POB NHRST study will focus on studying fewer tumor types, in cases when there is a dedicated intramural disease champion. The study will also be open to patients not eligible for the CCDI coordinated study due to age (>25 years old). Finally, the POB NHRST will continue to host NIH rare tumor clinics for tumors of interest including tumors selected by the CCDI-coordinated effort.

project_title: CONNECT: Comprehensive Oncology Network Evaluating Rare CNS Tumors - Cures
project_abstract_text: Our NCI-CONNECT program includes a network of 33 institutions across the nation that has helped us enroll patients for clinical trials and studies. Our network was instrumental to the launch of two first of their kind multi-center clinical trials after a landmark agreement with Medical Science and Computing that provides unprecedented opportunity for intramural and extramural collaboration on clinical trials for the network. We have formal partnerships under an NCI Memorandum of Understanding with 9 patient advocacy groups to share educational content and raise awareness to improve outcomes for people with rare CNS tumors. We collaboratively host workshops, meetings, and webinars with partners to help share the patient perspective and have collaborated on seven events since 2018, including a Survivorship Care in Neuro-Oncology Symposium virtually in June 2021 with over 200 attendees. NCI CONNECT leadership also participates in advocacy lead events like the National Brain Tumor Society Quality of Life Research project convened in 2022 with the first workshop held in May 2023. The project brings together patient partners and stakeholders to establish a patient-centered brain tumor QoL research agenda. We host scientific workshops that bring together neuro-oncology experts and patient advocates worldwide to discuss the scientific progress and challenges of a selected rare CNS cancer and find ways to improve therapies and develop new clinical trials. We have published papers from these workshops and changed cancer care guidelines; notably in November 2020, the NCCN guidelines for medulloblastoma were updated due to our scientific workshop report. Our NCI-CONNECT website is an educational tool for patients, caregivers, and professionals. From June 2023 to June 2024, the website exceeded 1 million page views, which it has accomplished annually since 2022, and had 847,537 visits. NCI-CONNECT launched a Spanish-language version of its website in 2020 to reach a broader and underserved audience, and it averages 18,796 monthly as of June 2024. Our monthly NCI-CONNECT e-newsletter is delivered to over 19,000 subscribers. Our private Facebook group NCI-CONNECT Community, the first ever for NCI, has 715 members; our YouTube Playlist has 39 videos, accumulating 33,611 views; and our X account has 7,783 followers. All these platforms share educational and scientific information. We developed a symptom-burden app called My STORI in 2021 (available in the Apple and Google Play Stores) to facilitate patient symptom monitoring and tracking and launched a Spanish language version in 2024. Our NCI-CONNECT Clinic is dedicated to bringing together patients with similar rare CNS tumor types. We have seen 437 patients from January 2023 to July 2024, which is 57 percent of the clinic volume monthly. These patients receive genetic testing and counseling, a review of their diagnosis with advanced molecular testing, and participate in support group meetings with a dedicated Health and Wellness Counselor. During COVID-19, NCI-CONNECT added partnerships with local physicians to provide study drug, and telemedicine to expand access to care for our patients. Clinical studies launched and their progress through NCI-CONNECT include these treatment trials: PLX038 in Primary Central Nervous System Tumors Containing MYC or MYCN Amplifications (06161519); a basket trial testing the immune checkpoint inhibitor nivolumab for adults with rare CNS cancers (17C0102), progress includes a positive interim analysis in the heavily pre-treated patient cohort and the presentation on these results won an abstract Award for Excellence in Rare CNS Disease at the 2021 SNO Annual Meeting; a first-in-human study of oral ONC206 in recurrent and rare primary CNS neoplasms (20C0069); a study of nivolumab for patients with recurrent IDH mutant gliomas including oligodendrogliomas (19C0006); and an immune monitoring study for patients with gliosarcoma and glioblastoma (21C0015). Clinical and observational studies include one retrospective study of Tissue Outcomes and Pregnancy Sub Study (P194734); two Natural History Studies, a natural history and specimen banking study for adults with rare central nervous system (CNS) cancers (16C0151), research using data from our Natural History Study received an Abstract Award for Excellence in Survivorship at the 2021 SNO Annual Meeting, and based on study data, the 2021 WHO diagnosis book for ependymoma was updated; an online survey of outcomes and risk for patients with adult CNS cancers (17CN141); a trial using immersive Virtual Reality (VR) at the time of clinical evaluation to improve psychological distress and anxiety (20C0065), which the interim results were published in March 2023 and support feasibility and acceptability of the intervention to target psychological symptoms for primary brain tumor patients; a study on managing Cancer And Living Meaningfully (CALM) therapy in individuals diagnosed with a primary brain tumor; and a Sleep Observation Study. NCI-CONNECT is conducting extensive biomarker research as a part of the ongoing immunotherapy basket clinical trial using nivolumab for rare CNS cancers. Collaborating with the Translational Immunology Program in the Neuro-Oncology Branch, extensive monitoring of individual patient's immune response treatment is underway using serial blood collections. NCI-CONNECT is advancing science through the identification of new molecular subtypes of CNS tumors. For example, through intramural collaborations with the CCR Laboratory of Pathology team led by Dr. Kenneth Aldape, NCI-CONNECT importantly uncovered a new subtype of ependymoma characterized by MYCN amplification. Collaborations with other investigators in CCR led to the hypothesis that these cancers may be selectively sensitive to topoisomerase inhibitors, and a novel inhibitor, PLX-038, is being tested in a new clinical trial (launched 2024) for these and other tumors harboring MYCN amplification. NCI-CONNECT established a new collaboration with the Pediatric Oncology Branch, Radiation Oncology Branch, and the Surgical Neurology Branch to develop novel therapies for high-grade and radiation-induced meningioma. The NCI-CONNECT consortium has allowed us to expand our research efforts across the United States and provides a network for patient referrals to our NCI-CONNECT Clinics. We have led educational activities for NCI-CONNECT members several times per year, including virtual journal club sessions and live tumor board sessions that we videocast to NCI-CONNECT investigators in conjunction with our scientific workshops. In April 2020, we expanded our weekly multidisciplinary NIH Neuro-Oncology Tumor Board to include investigators and cases from participating NCI-CONNECT consortium sites, including 16 Comprehensive Cancer Centers. These educational efforts have been well-attended and engaging as exhibited by our data: 154 providers have presented 154 cases to participants from 47 external sites. In addition, NCI-CONNECT holds weekly lectures from visiting scholars and in May 2023 held its first in-person visiting scholar lecture on Survivorship in Neuro-Oncology with a Patient and Caregiver. Further, MyPART and NCI-CONNECT networks are collaborating on developing an AYA program at NCI. We held a collaborative workshop October 14, 2022, and since are holding regular meetings on clinical research ideas and survivorship care with plans for several clinical trials to be modified to expand to AYAs. With the information technology team led by Dr. Jason Levine, NCI-CONNECT is analyzing data from its patient outcomes surveys to dynamically display it online.

project_title: NCI Program for Natural Products Discovery - Cures
project_abstract_text: Overall Progress Towards Initiative's Goals: Aim 1. Create new technologies to build an enhanced NP pre-fractionated library amenable to modern high-throughput targeted screening programs. The NCI Program for Natural Products Discovery (NPNPD) has created a new high-throughput natural product chemistry laboratory at the NCI at Frederick campus including jointly-developed robotic systems for pre-fractionation, weighing, plating fractions, and storing the fraction library. The NPNPD has so far pre-fractionated >85,000 crude natural product extracts, produced >600,000 pre-fractionated natural product samples, and released 500,000 samples to the public. Additional pre-fractionated samples will be released in Q1 2024. The NPNPD has plated >27,000,000 wells of pre-fractionated samples into 384-well plates for release to the public (>1800 unique, 384-well plates, 35-50 replicates each). The NPNPD has engaged in outreach to the extramural community to aid other programs to adapt NPNPD technologies including labs in Brazil, S. Africa, S. Korea, Sweden, and the United States (VA, MS, MI, CA). The NPNPD has worked with commercial analytics companies (Bruker, Gilson, ACD Labs, MesrReNova, Perkin Elmer, etc.) to optimize commercially available software to enable automated high throughput natural products chemistry programs. Aim 2. Expand the chemical diversity available to the public from culturable microorganisms with new methods and libraries. The NPNPD has obtained a library of >24,000 non-duplicate (by sequence) soil fungi from the United States and an additional >6000 marine microbes from Australia. The NPNPD has sequenced ~1200 Australian marine actinomycete specimens include whole-genome sequencing on 20 unique organisms. We have also completed taxonomic ITS sequencing of >1200 Australian marine fungi. The NPNPD has performed >3,000 large-scale fungal fermentations and extractions. Thornburg CC, et al. National Cancer Institute (NCI) Program for Natural Product Discovery: Creation of A Diverse Fungal Extract Library for High-Throughput Screening. (submitted) Aim 3. Provide the pre-fractionated library to screening centers worldwide to accelerate drug discovery. The NPNPD has executed 74 Material Transfer Agreements since the pre-fractionated library became available in 2019 (>1 per month, Appendix A). In addition, the NPNPD has received another 30 requests for MTAs that have not yet been executed. To date, the NPNPD has shipped >8,000,000 samples to the research community since the first release of pre-fractionated extracts in 2019. The NPNPD has executed 22 collaboration agreements including those with NIAID, NCATS, NCCIH, NIDCR, WRAIR, Astra Zeneca, and Novartis and is in negotiations with Genentech (Appendix A). Aim 4. Provide high throughput screening support for researchers to enable targeted discovery efforts. The NPNPD has worked closely with both intramural and extramural researchers to productively screen NPNPD fraction libraries and identify novel anticancer compounds. The NPNPD has worked with NCATS, NCCIH, and extramural research groups to enable funding of screens of the NPNPD fraction libraries against NIH HEAL Initiative targets. The NPNPD worked with NIAID on a screen of >320,000 fractions for antimicrobial activity. In addition to the references below the NPNPD has several discoveries as yet unpatented and published. For example: - Modulators of the stability of beta-catenin (with William Kaelin, Harvard) - Selective cytotoxic terpenoids that shrink tumors in initial mouse studies (with Debananda Pati, Baylor College of Med.) Aim 5. Provide faster analytical resources (isolation, structure elucidation, re-supply) to expedite translational pipelines. The NPNPD has collaborated with numerous extramural and intramural research groups and has undertaken >4,300 active fraction purifications resulting in >95,000 highly purified sub-fractions, >200 active compound class identifications, and >130 active pure natural products shipped back to research labs. The NPNPD has worked with several extramural research groups in both the U.S. and overseas to help them replicate NPNPD automated purification procedures. Aim 6. Establish a public database and bioinformatics platform to broaden input and expand impact. The NPNPD has created a comprehensive database including plant collection data, taxonomy, extract and fraction production, shipping, targets proposed by screening groups, identified active fractions, second stage purifications and active compound identifications, and analytical chemistry data (NMR, FT-IR, LC-MS/MS). The NPNPD has and is partnering with research groups (Novartis, Meliora, Biometric Research Program, University of California San Diego, Simon Fraser University, etc.) to create and adapt bioinformatic strategies to identify potential molecularly-targeted natural products. In addition to the refences below, the NPNPD has also used these bioinformatic methods to discover, based on the prediction of a specific genetic signature in cancer cells, a novel anticancer compound that will be patented by the NCI.

project_title: Center for Cell-based Therapy - Cures
project_abstract_text: In the past year, NCI authorized the filing of patent applications for our clinically ready CT3-CD28 hinge/transmembrane CAR targeting GPC2 at the national stage in the US, Europe, Japan, Australia, Canada, and China. The NIH purchase agreement with Expression Therapeutics, LLC, for the GMP production of the CT3-CD28 hinge/transmembrane CAR vector, funded by the Cancer Moonshot Program, is being processed at the NCI contract office and expected to be signed by the end of the current fiscal year in September 2024. The clinical trial protocol has been written and has completed the SRC review. The DTM Center for Cellular Engineering at the NIH Clinical Center has established the GMP cell production protocol and will produce CAR T cells for the anti-GPC2 CAR-T clinical trial. We anticipate submitting the IND to the FDA by early 2025, with the clinical trial expected to open in the fall of 2025. In the project on the identification of key genes driving myeloid-mediated immune suppression during cancer progression, our aims are: a) Analysis of data from the three independent CRISPR screens we performed in 2023 and now have identified several positive and negative regulators of trogocytosis by monocytic cells; b) 400 gene validation CRISPR screen that we are conducting in THP-1 and then confirming hits mapping the drivers of tumor cell trogocytosis in primary human monocytes; c) Analysis of functional sequencing (Func-seq) studies in primary human monocytes has identified changes in the trogocytic process in the setting of CD47 which impacts lysosomal processing and may play an important role in antigen presentation and immune signaling; d) Clinical development of human IL12 genetically engineered myeloid cells. We have developed a clinical protocol for first in human IL12 genetically engineered myeloid cells that has underwent scientific review committee and is now being submitted to OSRO for review prior to the FDA submission. Working with Center for Cellular Engineering we have finalized our manufacturing protocol for the human genetically engineered myeloid cells expressing IL12 and truncated EGFR from healthy donor CD34+ myeloid progenitor cells using engineering grade lentiviral vector funded in part by the Cancer Moonshot Program. Moreover, an IND enabling studies are underway to include in IND submission planned for fall 2024 and Clinical grade lentiviral vector is being processed at the NCI contract office and expected to be signed by the end of the current fiscal year in September 2024. Anticipated first in human clinical phase I trial opening by the end of 2024 early 2025.

project_title: IMRRT for Locoregionally Recurrent Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
project_abstract_text: This study has completed accrual and the clinical and correlative endpoints are being developed. Radiation therapy is a major modality in treatment of patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Radiation therapy induces reactive oxygen species that mediate DNA damage, intrinsic death pathway activation, as well as TNFa that induces extrinsic death pathway activation. Remarkably, concurrent birinapant 15mg/kg every 3 days plus radiation 2 Gy/day M-F for 2 weeks followed by an additional 2 weeks of birinapant induced durable cures >100 days and potentiated expression of TNFa. Birinapant and radiation treated mice trended toward lower weight but showed no evidence of worse acute radiation dermatitis or decrease in mobility or contracture involving the irradiated limb. Together, these findings unveil a novel therapeutic approach for HNSCC harboring FADD/BIRC2 genomic alterations associated with worse prognosis. Current standard treatment for advanced stage III/IV HNSCC typically includes surgery with post-operative radiotherapy, or definitive concurrent chemo-radiotherapy alone. About 50% recur within 5 years. The majority of these are patients with HPV- cancers. Survival analysis of 243 TCGA patients with HPV- cancers harboring 11q13 amplification of FADD indicate they are enriched among those recurring in the first two years. Based on these observations, patients with local-regionally recurrent HNSCC who are otherwise unselected would thus be expected to be enriched for FADD-/+BIRC2 amplification. The treatment of such patients with recurrent HNSCC after prior surgery and irradiation or chemo-radiation presents a unique challenge, as many patients present with unresectable disease. Median survival with palliative chemotherapy is ~5-9 months, with 1-yr survival of ~20-30%. Reirradiation remains the only potentially curative treatment option. Salvage reirradiation with concurrent radiosensitizing chemotherapy is the current standard of care. The data supporting this approach are mainly derived from Phase I/II trials, and investigation of a number of different radiation and chemotherapy regimens have been considered acceptable in this setting. With targeting of re-irradiation to recurrent tumor, dosing to 60Gy or higher is associated with greater local control, and is usually feasible, with sparing of the spinal cord and acceptable toxicities (18). In a phase I study of bortezomib and re-irradiation at NIH, 15/17 patients completed re-RT to 60-70Gy. At Ohio State University, 60-70Gy re-RT is given as standard of care with acceptable toxicity. Local control rates for reirradiation with chemotherapy are nearly 50% at 1 year , and demonstrate improved overall survivals (OS) of 8-28 months, with 2-year OS rates of 15-38%, but greater toxicity when combined with cisplatin, highlighting the potential benefit for more efficacious and tolerable regimens. Based on our pre-clinical studies, birinapant plus radiation demonstrates anti-tumor activity and improved survival, but the dose, schedule and tolerability in human studies needs to be determined. We propose a phase I trial for patients with local-regionally recurrent HNSCC who are candidates for irradiation, to determine the feasibility, toxicities and maximally tolerated dose (MTD) and schedule of concurrent therapy with birinapant. The dose steps proposed include 5.6, 11, 17 and 24 mg/m2 IV, which in prior studies has been administered week 1 and 2 every three weeks, and tolerated in single agent and combination regimens with several cytotoxic chemotherapy agents. The starting dose of 5.6 mg/M2 is the lowest dose along the previously used dose escalation schedule predicted to be potentially therapeutically active, and the first dose below 1/6 the MTD of 47mg/M2 for single agent birinapant, considered a margin of safety for starting combination with radiation, for which toxicities are unknown. Doses above 24mg/M2 in chemotherapy combinations were associated with dose limiting toxicities. Weekly dosing is consistent with the prolonged half-life demonstrated in tumors. Dose limiting toxicities have included facial nerve and other cranial neuropathies, reversible with cessation or delayed dosing of birinapant. Because of the potential for the combination to exacerbate cranial neuropathy or mucosal toxicity, the schedule incorporating the 1 week break every 3 weeks and weekday visits to radiation oncology provides an added level of safety for observation and drug dose modification or cessation, if detected.

project_title: Evaluating outcomes for patients with primary-metastatic gastrointestinal cancer
project_abstract_text: Our efforts in this arena have uncovered numerous hypothesis-generating correlations for mechanistic interrogation in the laboratory. These findings extend across the gastrointestinal tract and encompass metastases from both adenocarcinomas and neuroendocrine tumors. This foundational work has led us to pursue spatial transcriptomic and phospho-proteomic profiling of metastatic neuroendocrine cancers, immuno-cytokine evaluations for metastatic adenocarcinomas to liver, and the development of means to evaluate the new targets unveiled by our work though novel ex vivo humor models.

project_title: Advancing RAS and RASopathy Therapies
project_abstract_text: I participated in the design and am a lead associate investigator of the Clinical, Genetic, and Epidemiologic Study of Children and Adults with RASopathies study at the NCI (NCT04888936). As part of this study, we have identified several novel variants of unknown interest in genes in the RAS/MAPK pathway in patients with RASopathies. We are using a multi-disciplinary approach to functionally characterize these novel germline RAS/MAPK variants. We are comparing the impact of RASopathy-associated variants on the enzymatic activities of RAS/MAPK proteins using biochemical assays with purified proteins. We are assessing the ability of RASopathy variants to stimulate the RAS/MAPK pathway by transfection of the RASopathy variants into mammalian cells. The effect on cell proliferation is determined in genetically engineered mouse embryonic fibroblasts that stably express only the variant RAS/MAPK protein. Similarly, the effect on myogenic differentiation is assessed in C2C12 mouse myoblasts. Finally, the impact of RAS variant expression on zebrafish development including early convergence and extension (CE) at the gastrulation stage is assessed. Our initial experiments evaluating the efficacy of RAS/MAPK targeted agents in animal models of non-NF1 RASopathies are focused on publicly available RASopathy mouse models. We have established a colony of the HrasG12S/+ mouse model of Costello syndrome and have shown that the HrasG12S/+ mice have decreased locomotor activity, progressive cardiomegaly, and decreased overall survival compared to littermate controls. In ongoing studies, we are testing the effects of long-term treatment with tipifarnib on these functional outcomes. However, the phenotypes of mouse models of the RASopathies are often subtle and do not fully recapitulate the phenotypes of RASopathy patients. We have also established a colony of the Mek1Y130C mouse model of cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome and were unable to identify an observable phenotype in those mice. Importantly, neither the HrasG12S or Mek1Y130C mice develop spontaneous tumors, limiting our ability to develop cancer prevention strategies for patients with RASopathies using these models. We are employing three complementary strategies to address this limitation 1) We are developing several novel mouse models of Noonan syndrome, NrasG60E/+, Raf1S257L/+, and Sos1R552G/+, 2) We plan to cross our novel mouse models as well as the HrasG12S/+ model with p53 KO mice, and 3) We are developing an inducible transgenic zebrafish line expressing HRASG12S. We will evaluate each of these models for tumor formation.

project_title: Liver Cancer Program
project_abstract_text: One of main reasons why survival for patients with primary liver cancer (PLC), including hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and cholangiocarcinoma (CCA), has not improved in the past twenty years is the lack of approved novel therapies, with the exception of the limited success of sorafenib. Multiple phase III studies have failed to demonstrate any survival advantage for patients with liver cancer. We believe that this situation will change dramatically with the advent of immunotherapy and biologicals and by the implementation of precision cancer management strategy. Our optimism is supported by recent findings in the field of HCC. CCR is in a unique position to utilize its expertise in the area of immunotherapy and biologics to test these novel treatment options in patients with liver cancer. Molecular subgrouping and biomarker-guided molecularly-targeted therapies are promising approaches that are being implemented in our ongoing and future studies. One of the key elements of the NCI-LCP is to build an infrastructure which allows intramural investigators to expand on their research and not only collaborate with each other but also with extramural investigators. Our first effort is to build an NCI IRP-based collaborative translational science network of liver cancer clinical trial data, with accompanying biospecimens and correlative laboratory data to determine why immunotherapy is effective in certain patients but not in others. This goal is encompassed in our funded Liver Cancer Study (NCI-CLARITY). In this study, we are building a national clinical network in liver cancer to 1) define at the molecular level which group of PLC patients respond to immunotherapy and which do not and why some patients develop resistance/tumor relapse and 2) to determine whether any similarities or differences in response to immunotherapy are observed in HCC versus CCA patients. This program is based on the creation of a unique and robust national information commons comprised of comprehensive clinical and molecular data which can be utilized by the cancer research community for future studies of PLC. To accomplish these aims, the NCI IRP is serving as the lead and coordinating hub to leverage ongoing immunotherapy-based clinical trials at major institutions treating PLC patients. We have partnered with clinical extramural collaborators across the U.S. to obtain biospecimens (biospy, blood, urine and fecal) and clinical data (medical chart data, treatment outcome and survival) from PLC patients in their ongoing clinical trials and/or standard of care patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors. We aim to collect biospecimens and clinical data from 500 PLC patients over a 5-year period across study sites. Comprehensive correlative data will be performed at NCI and NCI Frederick National Laboratory, along with our collaborators, including molecular (DNA and RNA-Seq), single-cell sequencing, metabolomics, microbiome, immunophenotyping by CODEX 3D-multiplex imaging (Optical Microscopy and Image Analysis Laboratory) and SNP/variant analysis. Radiogenomics, pairing data mined from comprehensive multi-modality imaging with genomics, by artificial intelligence/machine learning, will also be used to screen and predict patient response to immunotherapy. Comprehensive statistical, machine learning and bioinformatics analysis will be used to integrate correlative data and clinical data to molecularly characterize and define predictive signatures of treatment responders and nonresponders to immunotherapy in all cases or in the stratified analyses. In concert with this effort, we also initiated a pilot retrospective study of archival biopsy specimens collected before and after immunotherapy treatment (IO) from liver cancer patients from the NIH Clinical Center and Georgetown University. Samples from 89 patients undergoing immunotherapy treatment were assessed by DNA and RNA sequencing to identify mutations, transcripts and molecular signatures associated with patient outcome following IO treatment. A total of 230 primary HCC and CCA tumors and adjacent non-tumor tissues, largely stored as formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) and attained before and following immunotherapy treatment, using total RNA sequencing and whole exome sequencing were analyzed. We established a SOP and show feasibility to conduct molecular analytics to monitor patient response to immune therapy utilizing FFPE tissue. We identified four stable survival-related molecular subgroups defined by orthogonal axes of tumor aggressiveness and immune infiltration, the latter associated with immunotherapy response. Furthermore, although the underlying molecular status of tumors prior to immunotherapy treatment was largely maintained following treatment, some molecular responses tracked with patient outcome. Thus, outcome-related and intersecting molecular axes are apparent in FFPE liver tumors prior to immunotherapy treatment, components of which could serve as indicators of treatment response. The pilot arm of the study was recently published (Budhu et al, Cell reports Medicine, 2023). Additional samples from these and other collaborating sites are being incorporated and integrated with these analyses to further assess these data. The pilot data are also being utilized as validation samples or additional samples for several ongoing and published studies. This includes a phase II study of the combination of pembrolizumab with capecitabine and oxaliplatin (CAPOX) in patients with advanced biliary tract carcinoma (BTC) to assess response rate and clinical efficacy. We found that capecitabine and oxaliplatin in combination with pembrolizumab is tolerable and a potentially effective treatment for refractory advanced BTC (Monge et al, Oncologist, 2022). Other studies from this program include an assessment of genomic changes at the single-cell level at baseline and in response to therapy which have provided insight into tumor cell heterogeneity and the foundations of alterations which affect outcome in certain patient subgroups (Ma et al, Nature Comm, 2022). Another example includes the comparison of the bulk transcriptome data of the pilot study with single-cell transcriptomics conducted from samples of the same patient. In addition, we are exploring the differences in immunotherapy response between race. Health disparity is evident in HCC, however an understanding of the molecular features contributing to differences in clinical response are not known. Such studies aim to shed light on the differences in treatment response among African Americans and Hispanics compared to White patients. The LCP is also initiating collaborations with the Cancer Data Science Laboratory (CDSP) to create and test new and known bioinformatic tools for their ability to predict patient response and outcome utilizing our datasets. The prospective arm of NCI-CLARITY is underway with 115 patients enrolled and over 5000 biospecimens collected. Overall, we anticipate that these data will define specific subgroups of patients who are more likely to benefit from immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment. In addition, biomarkers and novel druggable targets may be identified to better determine or affect treatment response.

project_title: T-Cell Receptor Gene Therapy for Human Cancers-Cures
project_abstract_text: T cell receptor (TCR) gene therapy is a personalized, cancer treatment strategy that can precisely and potently target a wide variety of tumor antigens. It is based on the infusion of T cells that are genetically engineered ex vivo to express a TCR directed against a tumor antigen. This strategy enables tumor targeting with a large number of T cells that express a high affinity TCR. It also permits pretreatment host conditioning to enhance anti-tumor T cell engraftment and function. TCR gene therapy has shown encouraging results in melanoma, synovial cell sarcoma, and human papillomavirus-associated cancers. In contrast to antibody and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) therapy, TCR gene therapy can target intracellular antigens, which is important because many of attractive oncological therapeutic targets (e.g. mutated protooncogenes, viral oncogenes, driver chromosomal translocations, and cancer germline antigens) localize to the intracellular compartment. The goal of this NCI Moonshot Project is to catalyze the discovery and development of TCR gene therapy for a wide-array of cancers.

project_title: PSMA-PET Imaging of High Risk Prostate Cancer-Cures
project_abstract_text: This study has now started accrual. It is a multi-institutional trial involving the use of PSMA PET/CT in high risk patients. The PSMA PET agent, F18 DCFPyl, is provided to sites by Progenics. The American College of Radiology will assist in archiving imaging and pathology. Approximately 4 patients have been accrued at the NCI site to date and accrual was interrupted by the COVID pandemic. To date we have seen excellent performance of the PSMA PET agent and the surgery has been successfully performed without incident.

project_title: Graft-Versus-Host Disease Symptom Management-Cures
project_abstract_text: This multi-center non-interventional psychosocial trial addresses the study aims in two projects: 1) a qualitative project using cognitive interviewing to confirm the comprehension and ease of response to the PCSS, and 2) a quantitative project to evaluate test-retest reliability, construct validity and responsiveness of the PCSS, as well as to explore concordance of symptom ratings by patients and parent proxies. In Project 1, the study was designed tol conduct at least 20 cognitive interviews of patient and proxy dyads (parent/guardian) within each age group (5-7; 8-12; 13-17) for a sample of 60 pediatric transplant survivors with cGVHD to refine the symptom items and response choices to ensure that they resonate across the developmental spectrum. Cognitive interviews are being used to evaluate the clarity and comprehension of the PCSS items, the ease and accuracy of judgement of the response choices, and any errors in understanding the response choices, and will refine the PCSS in accordance with study data, before proceeding to Project 2. To date, 73 participants have been enrolled on the study and 63 participants have successfully completed Project 1 study procedures (16 5-7-year-olds, 21 8-12 year olds, and 26 13-17-year-olds. In Project 2, we will evaluate test-retest reliability, construct validity, and responsiveness of the PCSS, in association with the NIH Global cGVHD Symptom Severity Score, the Peds QL, clinician ratings of organ specific cGVHD severity scores and cGVHD severity using the NIH criteria, in a sample of 120 pediatric transplant survivors with cGVHD reflecting three age groups (5-7 years; 8-12 years; 13-17 years) of equal numbers. In subjects ages 13-17, we will also compare responses on the PCSS with those from the Lee Scale, to determine the youngest age at which adolescent respondents can comprehend the Lee Scale. We enrolled the first participant from an extramural site on June 24, 2020.

project_title: Establish Preclinical Model for IDH-mutated Glioma
project_abstract_text: We introduced ectopic gene expression/knockdown through the RCAS virus, because of its lineage specific delivery in a receptor dependent way. To do this, the gene expression cassettes were cloned into the RCAS genome as previously described. We adopted and validated the RCAS virus strains RCAS-IDH1WT-shTrp53 and RCAS-IDH1R132H-shTrp53 to allow the expression of IDH1 mutant and Trp53 genetic silencing. The RCAS-U6-gRNA-PDGFb construct was a kind gift from Dr. Squatrito, and it allows gRNA and PDGFb spontaneous expression in vivo. We will also optimize RCAS plasmids strategy for gene editing and IDH1-mutated glioma modeling. New vector strategies, such as RCAS-gRNA, RCAS-IDH1-2A-PDGFb will be developed for further tumor modeling. At this stage, we have confirmed the tumor induction by using the RCAS-PDGFb and RCAS-IDH1-shTrp53 constructs in Ntva+/+, Ink4a-Arf-/- mice with predictable disease outcome. Moreover, we have also established a gRNA targeting strategy based on RCAS-U6-gRNA-PDGFb construct and validate the targeting efficacy in mouse genome.

project_title: Immunological Analysis of Brain Cancer
project_abstract_text: Previously, we identified that human glioblastoma (high-grade glioma) cells have distinct lipid profiles from human low-grade glioma cell lines and normal human astrocytes. The glioblastoma-enriched lipids were recognized by and activated human NKT cells. These lipids induced the production of multiple cytokines. Interestingly, none of the glioblastoma-enriched lipids induced the production of Th1 cytokines that facilitate anti-tumor immune response; instead, they induced cytokines that have the potential to act against anti-tumor immune responses. These results suggest that glioblastoma produces lipids that modulate NKT cell function to suppress tumor immunity. We designed and synthesized multiple analogs of sulfatide, a self-glycolipid abundant in the brain, based on the structure of 7DW8-5, a previously reported human NKT cell agonistic lipid antigen. Previously, we demonstrated the binding of sulfatide analog loaded CD1d-tetramers to TCRs of an iNKT cell line using flow cytometry. Using healthy donor PBMC-derived iNKT cells, we confirmed that the sulfatide analogs activated iNKT cells. The sulfatide analogs also induced the production of multiple cytokines. The existence and functions of MAIT cells in glioblastoma are less understood than NKT cells. Using publicly available glioblastoma transcriptomic data sets from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and Chinese Glioma Genome Atlas (CGGA), we found that the expression levels of MAIT signature genes negatively correlated with disease prognosis, suggesting that MAIT cells contribute to immune suppression occurs in glioblastoma patients. Previously, we detected MAIT TCR transcripts in some patients using a TCGA glioblastoma data set, suggesting the existence of MAIT cells in glioblastoma tissues. Now, we identified MAIT cells using a single-cell RNA sequencing of CD45+ leukocytes extracted from multiple glioblastoma patient tissue samples. We found that more than half of the samples we examined contained MAIT cells. We also found a relatively higher frequency of MAIT cells among T cells than in the peripheral blood, suggesting that MAIT cells are enriched in glioblastoma tissues. Most MAIT cells in tumor tissues showed a highly skewed function that induces activation and chemotaxis of granulocytes. Together with our previous observation that MAIT cell signature-positive glioblastoma samples had higher expression levels of the signature genes for immunosuppressive myeloid cells, our data strongly suggested that MAIT cells enriched in glioblastoma tissues contribute to the formation of immunosuppressive environment through the induction of immunosuppressive myeloid cells. We are developing viral vector-based vaccines based on ChAdOx-1 and MVA vectors and testing their efficacy against mouse syngeneic glioblastoma in vivo. Using a syngeneic orthotopic glioblastoma model expressing a model tumor antigen, we demonstrated that prophylactic vaccination combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors induced significant protection. We found that the prophylactic vaccination induced significant memory T cell subsets in the brain. We also made vectors expressing tumor-associated antigens (TAAs) or neoantigens using the pipeline we invented (METRO), which we identified in the mouse glioblastoma cell lines we used in the project. We are currently testing the clinical efficacy of the vaccine in the syngeneic orthotopic mouse glioblastoma models. We are also optimizing vaccination strategy to induce protective effects in a therapeutic setting.

project_title: BRD4 Contributes to the Regulation of Alternative Splicing
project_abstract_text: We have established that BRD4 contributes to patterns of splicing both in normal cells in vivo and in cancer cells. Through its direct interaction with the splicing machinery on the genome, BRD4 acts preferentially by modulating exon usage. These findings lead to the model that BRD4 functions to integrate the processes of chromatin structure, transcription and splicing to ensure proper regulation of gene expression. The role of BRD4 in regulating alternative splicing in vivo was documented in the thymus where deletion of BRD4 resulted in marked changes in the patterns of alternative splicing. Furthermore, we have found that the transitions from one developmental stage to another - DN to ISP to DP to SP - are accompanied by changes in the patterns of splicing, indicating that splicing is developmentally regulated in the thymus. BRD4, which is expressed at approximately equal levels in each of these stages, contributes to this regulation since deletion of BRD4 results in changes in the splicing patterns at each stage of differentiation, preferentially affecting skipped exon events, but not affecting the expression of splicing factors. Consistent with its role in cancer, BRD4 also contributes to patterns of alternative splicing in T-ALL cells, largely affecting the genes involved in cell cycle regulation. Interestingly, degradation of BRD4 results in much larger changes in splicing patterns than the inhibition of BRD4 binding to chromatin through its bromodomains. This suggests that BRD4 mediated regulation of alternative splicing does not depend entirely on its binding to chromatin through its bromodomains. Further support for this perspective comes from the finding that BRD4's co-localization with splicing factors is not perturbed by JQ1, which prevents binding to chromatin. In addition, whereas degradation of BRD4 targets both promoters and gene bodies, blocking of BRD4 bromodomain-mediated interactions with chromatin by JQ1 is largely confined to the promoter regions of genes, lending further support to the conclusion that BRD4's interaction with the elongation and splicing machineries does not depend on its bromodomains. Our finding that BRD4 directly interacts with both FUS and HnRNPM, suggests that it can participate as an integral component of the splicing machinery. The precise mechanism(s) by which BRD4 contributes to the regulation of splicing remain to be determined. Based on the functional parallels between BRD4 and cohesin, we examined the possibility that cohesin also regulates alternative splicing, either alone or in combination with BRD4. We find that cohesin regulates splicing in cellulo and in vivo. Depletion of cohesin leads to altered patterns of splicing. Introduction of a single point mutation in the cohesin subunit, SMC1, in mouse embryonic stem cells, alters both its association with splicing factors and the pattern of splicing. Mechanistically, cohesin interacts with core components of the splicing machinery including U1-70, the regulatory factors FUS and HNRNPM. Importantly, in primary AML patient samples, cohesin mutations are associated with altered splicing patterns compared with either normal CD34+ cells or AML cells without cohesin or splicing factor mutations. Consistent with a direct role of cohesin in alternative splicing in AML, AML-associated cohesin mutations no longer interact with splicing factors. Strikingly, the alterations in splicing patterns associated with cohesin mutations in two distinct datasets of primary AML samples result in perturbations in metabolism. The patterns of splicing mediated by cohesin are distinct from those regulated by BRD4 alone. Importantly, cohesin and BRD4 together contribute to a pattern of splicing that is distinct from either factor alone. Consistent with their co-regulation of splicing, cohesin and BRD4 directly interact and exist in a complex in HCT116 cells. These studies establish a novel role for cohesin in regulating alternative splicing, either alone or in conjunction with BRD4 and have implications in the characterization of human AML cancer.

project_title: The dynamics of chromatin topology in human cells
project_abstract_text: We have characterized DNA supercoiling across the human genome and revealed the widespread existence of DNA supercoiling domains in human chromatin. These supercoiling domains are modulated by topoisomerase, co-localized with nuclear compartments but not topologically associating domains, and have important roles in human gene regulation. We are further investigating the formation mechanism of DNA supercoiling both at local regions including around genes and TAD boundaries and across the human genome. We are also studying the impact of DNA supercoiling on gene expression in human cells, as well as its regulation by topoisomerase activities and its role in chromatin and gene regulation during dynamic biological processes.

project_title: First in Human Trials of ProAgio, a Cytotoxin
project_abstract_text: AIM1 (ongoing): Test safety and pharmacokinetics (PK) of ProAgio in patients. A Phase I clinical study at the NIH Clinical Center was initiated in previously treated patients with advanced solid tumor malignancies (PI Alewine). Patient accrual began in 12/2021 and accrual to the dose escalation phase of the study completed January 2024 (n = 29) with identification of ProAgio single agent RP2D. Accrual of the dose expansion phase of the study (including biopsy cohort) is ongoing. AIM 2 (ongoing): Identify the specific cell subsets in the PDAC TME that are targeted by ProAgio and characterize its effect on TME structure over time. Our current data indicate that short-course ProAgio treatment does not deplete PDAC TME cell subsets that express integrin alphaV-beta3 despite causing significant retardation of tumor growth in an autochthonous mouse model of PDAC. These data have been presented at the AACR Special Conference on Pancreatic Cancer. We are continuing to study the affect of ProAgio on the murine PDAC TME after longer courses of treatment and anticipate submission of a manuscript later in 2024. AIM 3 (ongoing): Assess bioactivity of ProAgio in patients. Tumor biopsy samples are being collected from patients on the ProAgio study. Correlative studies to assess ProAgio effect on stromal density, blood vessels and tumor cellular components will begin when all samples are collected.

project_title: Cancer Stem Cells in Cholangiocarcinoma
project_abstract_text: This year we reported our findings on how single-cell RNA sequencing reveals cancer stem-like cells and dynamics in tumor microenvironment during cholangiocarcinoma progression. Cholangiocarcinoma is a malignancy of the bile ducts that is driven by activities of cancer stem-like cells and characterized by a heterogeneous tumor microenvironment. To better understand the transcriptional profiles of cancer stem-like cells and dynamics in the tumor microenvironment during the progression of cholangiocarcinoma, we performed single-cell RNA analysis on cells collected from three different timepoints of tumorigenesis in a YAP/AKT mouse model. Bulk RNA sequencing data from TCGA (The Cancer Genome Atlas program) and ICGC cohorts were used to verify and support the finding. In vitro and in vivo experiments were performed to assess the stemness of cancer stem-like cells. We identified Tm4sf1high malignant cells as cancer stem-like cells. Across timepoints of cholangiocarcinoma formation in YAP/AKT mice, we found dynamic change in cancer stem-like cell/stromal/immune cell composition. Nevertheless, the dynamic interaction among cancer stem-like cells, immune cells, and stromal cells at different timepoints was elaborated. Collectively, these data serve as a useful resource for better understanding cancer stem-like cell and malignant cell heterogeneity, stromal cell remodeling, and immune cell reprogramming. It also sheds new light on transcriptomic dynamics during cholangiocarcinoma progression at single-cell resolution.

project_title: Data-driven inference of regulators for cytokine-mediated tumor killing
project_abstract_text: As a major progress this year, we have validated the effectiveness of four secreted proteins prioritized by our computational models on immune checkpoint blockade in mice, emphasizing our top hit: AOAH. AOAH exhibits advantages in potentiating immunotherapy in multiple models and T-cell activation by depleting arachidonoyl-phosphatidylcholine, particularly in tumors with inferior antigen strength and density. Together, our computational platform offers a comprehensive resource to advance oncoimmunology research, and its utility and reliability are validated by experiments. We also indicate that AOAH can be exploited as an immunotherapy enhancer against both immune-inflamed and immune-excluded tumors, overcoming a major clinical challenge.

project_title: Computational approaches for the analyses of spatial profiling technologies
project_abstract_text: As a major progress for this year, we developed the SecAct computational framework for inferring secreted protein activities at bulk, single-cell, and spatial levels. The human genome contains about 1900 genes coding secreted proteins, mediating intercellular communications. However, no systematic approaches exist to characterize their activities in biological samples. We postulate that spatial transcriptomics data from human clinical samples can reveal the physiological impact of diverse secreted proteins in tissues. Here, we introduce the Secreted Activity (SecAct) computational framework. SecAct infers intercellular activity for 1248 secreted protein-coding genes from gene expression data at bulk and single-cell levels by harnessing their intercellular signatures trained from 618 genome-wide spatial transcriptomics profiles from 28 tumor types. With spatial transcriptomics input, SecAct further infers secreted proteins' signaling velocities from source to sink spots. By applying SecAct to 42 cancer immunotherapy cohorts, we discovered new secreted proteins associated with anti-PD-1/CTLA4 efficacy. Using in-vivo mouse models, we validated the potential of LY86, whose functions were previously unknown in cancer, as a promising immunotherapy target.

project_title: Targeting RAS in Pediatric Cancer
project_abstract_text: One method to improve the clinical efficacy of MAPK-targeting drugs is the use of combinations of drugs that inhibit the pathway at different nodes, termed 'vertical pathway inhibition', which prevents rebound ERK activation. In collaboration with Dr. Angelina Vaseva at OHSU, we have identified that the combination of a MEK inhibitor and a pan-RAF inhibitor inhibits tumor growth in xenograft models of FN-RMS. To clinically translate this work, I participated in the study design and development of a multi-center phase I/II basket study (ADVL2421) with myself as Study Chair. The primary endpoint of the phase 2 component of the study will be the objective response rate (ORR) of the tovorafenib (DAY101)/selumetinib combination in four histology or biomarker specific cohorts: 1) patients with low grade glioma that has progressed on MAPK pathway inhibitor monotherapy, 2) patients with solid tumors with BRAF/RAF1 alterations, 3) patients with solid tumors with H/K/NRAS alterations, and 4) patients with solid tumors with NF1 alterations. Directly targeting mutant RAS in pediatric solid tumors would decrease signaling through both the RAF/MEK/ERK MAP kinase pathway as well as the RAS-activated PI3K/AKT pathway. However, the identification of direct RAS inhibitors was thought to be impossible. RAS membrane localization, which is achieved through post-translational prenylation, is required for proper biological activity of all RAS proteins. The farnesyltransferase inhibitor, tipifarnib, prevents the prenylation and thus activation of HRAS specifically. In a collaborative project with Dr. Christine Pratilas, we have shown that tipifarnib inhibits tumor growth in HRAS-mutated xenograft models of FN-RMS. This work resulted in a multi-center phase II clinical trial, conducted through the COG as an arm of the pediatric MATCH study, which I helped to design and conduct as lead associate investigator. The study recently closed to accrual and data analysis is ongoing. Excitingly, a new class of drugs that covalently modify KRASG12C and prevent this oncoprotein from undergoing guanine nucleotide exchange have been developed. Two of these inhibitors, sotorasib and adagrasib, have been FDA approved for the treatment of adult malignancies. We have identified patient-derived neuroblastoma and FN-RMS models with G12C alterations in H-, K-, or NRAS and show that sotorasib is effective in these models. We plan to clinically translate our finding with sotorasib. We will also evaluate the new class of RAS-ON inhibitors in pediatric solid tumor models. Additionally, we have identified pediatric solid tumor models with novel mechanisms of adaptive resistance to direct RAS inhibitors. Future studies will be aimed at identifying effective combinations of RAS inhibitors and other molecularly targeted agents to prevent adaptive resistance, using both candidate gene and unbiased approaches.

project_title: Behavioral Correlates in Mouse Model of CNS radiation-induced hypersomnia
project_abstract_text: Radiation therapy is the standard of care for both primary and secondary central nervous system tumors tumors. A majority of patients experience radiation induced hypersomnia (RIH) which may impact life quality and treatment tolerance. Currently, there is no mouse model of RIH that measures behavioral sleep and activity. Previously, we demonstrated that Ethovison software can be used to effectively monitor differences in the sleep behavior of mice. Here we test the dose effect of radiation in mice using our system prior to introducing tumor. Aims: Establish the optimal radiation dose to recapitulate symptoms experienced by patients who receive cranial irradiation, such as heightened daytime sleep and reduced activity. Experimental Procedure: Animals: Male young (6wk) C57BL/6 mice were individually housed in Phenotyper cages Monitored for 10 days pre-irradiation and 11 days post irradiation under 12:12 light dark conditions. 24 non-tumor bearing C57BL/6 mice received whole brain radiation at one of 4 doses (sham, 2Gy, 5Gy, and 15Gy) using a single fraction Ethovision XT Software automatically generate general activity data as total distance travelled over time. Mouse Behavior recognition module scored Sleep/Rest, Walking, Grooming and Eating. Data Analysis: General activity was examined for total activity across 24 hours for 11 days between doses.Behaviors were compared between doses for three days (Day 8-10). Groups were analyzed between high (5&15Gy) and low (0&2Gy) doses. Baseline Analysis: Baseline activity was not significantly different between groups (F(3.23) = 0.649, p=0.593). As expected, activity levels are higher during the dark period (active period), while sleep is higher during the light period (inactive period). Post-Irradiation Activity Analysis: Activity levels were unchanged, less than 5% difference, for sham and 2Gy, however high doses 5Gy and 15Gy were suppressed by ~10% Suppression of activity started after 2 days in 15Gy and 5 days in 5Gy mice. Data was corrected to baseline, which is represented by zero in the graph Post-Irradiation Behavioral Analysis: Across three days (8-10), 5Gy and 15Gy (19,87sec) had more sleep during their active phase (t=2.27, p=0.03) than sham or 2Gy (17,618 sec). Grooming was significantly higher (t=2.588, p=0.017) for low radiation dose during the active phase. There are no effects on amount of time spent eating or the amount of time spent walking Animals had no significant difference in baseline activity or sleep between groups. Shams and 2Gy had activity levels similar to baseline, while 5 and 15Gy had decreased activity levels post-radiation. Mice exposed to 15Gy radiation had an earlier onset of radiation induced hypersomnolence, with decreases starting three days before 5Gy mice. Significant effects for sleep and grooming were observed during the active phase with animals exposed to high radiation doses having more sleep and less grooming. No changes were observed for eating or total walking time between groups. Our study demonstrates that cranial irradiation causes a clear increase in sleep during the active period and decrease in activity, both factors that recapitulate the human RIH experience. Activity and sleep are impacted by irradiation in patients. A good behavioral model to observe these changes has not yet been developed in rodents. Here we demonstrate a reliable system to collect and analyze activity and sleep parameters in mice exposed to irradiation that will serve as the foundation for ongoing experiments

project_title: Biology of Virus-associated Cancers
project_abstract_text: To experimentally study the interplay between BKPyV and urinary diseases, such as bladder cancer and hemorrhagic cystitis (HC), we've utilized a spontaneously immortalized urothelial cell line (HBLAK), which retains a normal morphology and ability to differentiate into stratified urothelium, to study virus infections in three dimensions. In one project, we treated these cells with low-dose genotoxic agents commonly used as immune conditioning drugs in bone marrow transplant recipients and identified that these greatly amplify BKPyV genome replication, which may contribute to the development of HC in these patients. Ongoing work is evaluating patient specimens for hallmark mutations caused by these agents. We have also engineered bladder cells to remove the primary mutagenic enzymes responsible for the somatic mutations observed in bladder cancer and in BKPyV evolution (APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B). Preliminary data from these lines have confirmed that APOBEC host mutagenesis happens during BKPyV infection and is abolished in the KO cells. We are in the process of establishing derivatives of these lines that express viral oncogenes to study both host and viral mutagenesis and carcinogenic potential in greater detail. In the above-mentioned cellular models, we are also using chromatin conformation sequencing in conjunction with knockdown of factors that control chromatin looping (CTCF, WAPL, RAD21) to study how these affect polyomavirus replication and erroneous integration into the host genome. While these models are used to study events prior and during integration, we are using newly derived virus-positive Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) cell lines to study how integrated viral DNAs in established cancers interact with host chromatin and affect cellular gene expression and chromatin conformation. These data are being combined with substantial sequencing data from patient-derived specimens to identify clinically relevant and important factors. A manuscript summarizing our findings from these patient-derived specimens on novel mutagenic processes and their relative timing in MCC is in preparation. Lastly, we have completed a study using total RNA sequencing and whole genome sequencing to characterize sebaceous neoplasm specimens, another cancer highly enriched in immunosuppressed patients, but without a clear infectious etiology. A manuscript for this study identifying key mutagenic processes and transcriptional changes affecting cellular metabolism has been revised and is under consideration at Clinical Cancer Research. Additional analysis of these data suggests there are distinct viral genera present at different stages of tumorigenesis. This analysis and manuscript are in progress.

project_title: Improving PSMA-based radioligand therapy via combination radioligand therapy
project_abstract_text: Study is in the process of opening for enrollment but is currently not open yet. The study has been approved by the National Institutes of Health Central Institutional Review Board but is awaiting other site-initiation activities. We expect the study to be open to participant enrolled towards the end of the calendar year 2024. This project is in collaboration with our industry partner Perspective Pharmaceuticals. Once the study opens, we expect to reach full accrual within three to five years approximately.

project_title: Evaluation of novel treatments in biochemically recurrent prostate
project_abstract_text: This aim has seen the first clinical trial to investigate a radiopharmaceutical alone in recurrent prostate cancer and has demonstrated novel findings of responses in a subset of patients. This aim has seen the first prostate cancer trial to combine an immuncytokine and androgen receptor pathway inhibitor in recurrent prostate cancer and will report the first findings PSMA changes after short-course enzalutamide. This aim has seen the first clinical trial to demonstrate that vaccines can cause PSA declines that are associated with changes on PSMA PET imaging.

project_title: Evaluation of Immune-based Combinations in Prostate Cancer
project_abstract_text: We are evaluating novel immune therapeutic strategies in prostate cancer. Much of our previous work has involved cancer vaccine strategies which we have shown can impact early recurrent (biochemically recurrent) prostate cancer. These studies have demonstrated declines in serum prostate specific antigen and now have also demonstrated improvements in PSMA PET Imaging. This combination of findings has never been demonstrated before in a clinical trial. We have also conducted the first prostate cancer trial combining docetaxel and a necrosis targeting immunocytokine. The phase 1 study of this combination demonstrated safety and proof of concept of synergy relative to previous trials. Phase 2 evaluation of this combination continues.

project_title: Targeted Therapy in Neuroendocrine Cancer
project_abstract_text: Our prior work at the NCI led to the FDA approval of a PET-imaging agent, Ga-68 DOTATATE, a high affinity ligand that binds somatostatin receptor (SSTR). These cancers are very rare and are unique in that they have characteristic surface receptor repertoire, the somatostatin receptors 1-5 (most prevalent SSTR2), that not only help identify them as neuroendocrine tumors, but also represent key pro-growth and pro-survival pathways. In aggressive or metastatic neuroendocrine tumors, that are not amenable to surgical resection, a novel radiolabeled SSTR2 analogs for the therapy of metastatic lesions (Lu177-DOTATATE) has been used. Unfortunately, with dedifferentiation, the tumors lose SSTR2 expression, and renders them invisible or not amenable for targeted therapy. SSTR2 expression is controlled by epigenetic mechanisms. OUr laboratory work was publishe in 2023, validating the upregulation of SSTR2 using HDAC inhibitors. THis led to a successful Lasker award submission. We have continued laboratory work to establish SSTR2 regulation. This project is currently beeing advanced to move into a clinical trial. We are awaiting industry approval. Furthermore, with collaborations we have started defining NET cell compositions and cell of origins.

project_title: Pilot Study of Avelumab in Thymic Epithelial Tumors
project_abstract_text: Forty-seven subjects with recurrent thymic tumors have been enrolled and treated with avelumab (24 thymoma; 23 thymic carcinoma). The objective response rate is 11% and disease stabilization was observed in 78% of participants. Immune related adverse events (irAEs) were observed in 57% of participants; most of these were mild to moderate in intensity and manageable. Preliminary results from immune correlative studies show the presence of lower levels of B cells and plasmacytoid dendritic cells at baseline among responders and higher levels of CD4 cells and lower NK-T cells at baseline among subjects that develop irAEs.

project_title: New regulatory mechanisms of WNT signaling in development, stem cells and cancer
project_abstract_text: Through forward genetics screens in haploid human cells harboring a fluorescent reporter of WNT signaling, we discovered new regulators of ligand-induced signaling and regulators selectively required to sustain hyperactive, oncogenic signaling. This study (Lebensohn et al., eLife 2016) comprised seven genome-wide screens systematically interrogating the pathway, including screens for positive, negative and attenuating regulators of ligand-induced signaling, as well as suppressor screens following disruption of key regulators commonly mutated in WNT-driven tumors, such as the tumor suppressor APC. A comparative analysis of the screens revealed new regulatory mechanisms for ligand reception, signal transduction and transcriptional activation, as well as new gene regulatory elements (Patel, Lebensohn et al., PLoS One 2019). Our current goal is to elucidate the molecular underpinnings of these new regulatory mechanisms, understand their physiological functions and evaluate their potential as therapeutic targets. The following sub-projects are aimed at elucidating some of these new regulatory mechanisms and evaluating their therapeutic potential. 1) The transcription factor TFAP4 is a new positive regulator of WNT signaling. Our genetic screens uncovered a basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper transcription factor called TFAP4 as a potential regulator of WNT signaling (Lebensohn et al., eLife 2016). We found that TFAP4 regulates b-catenin, the principal transcriptional co-activator in the WNT pathway, and is a limiting component for WNT/b-catenin signaling activity. Furthermore, excess TFAP4 can promote ectopic activation of WNT signaling during Xenopus laevis development, causing the formation of a secondary body axis. Interestingly, TFAP4 expression is tightly linked to malignancy in gastrointestinal cancers: TFAP4 is upregulated in colorectal cancer, where it mediates epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and metastasis, and its down-regulation in gastric cancer cells inhibits proliferation, induces cell cycle arrest and promotes apoptosis. We are dissecting the molecular mechanism by which TFAP4 regulates b-catenin and evaluating its potential as a therapeutic target. 2) A new function of the b-catenin destruction complex regulating WNT signaling through the ubiquitin ligase HUWE1. HUWE1 is a HECT-domain ubiquitin ligase involved in dozens of cellular processes through the ubiquitination of diverse substrates. Both oncogenic and tumor suppressive functions have been ascribed to HUWE1. HUWE1 has been postulated as a negative regulator of WNT signaling through at least two distinct mechanisms. However, in our unbiased forward genetic screen for mediators of hyperactive WNT signaling induced by loss of the b-catenin destruction complex kinase casein kinase 1a, we identified HUWE1 as a positive regulator of the WNT pathway (Lebensohn et al., eLife 2016). We also demonstrated that HUWE1 potentiates WNT signaling in cells and in Xenopus laevis embryos. We have now found that HUWE1 promotes WNT/b-catenin signaling by regulating both b-catenin abundance (McKenna et al. bioRxiv 2024) and sub-cellular localization. The second mechanism is independent of the control of b-catenin protein stability and can shift the balance between two distinct cellular functions of b-catenin - one as a transcriptional co-activator in the WNT pathway and the other as a structural component of adherens junctions involved in cell-cell adhesion. Control of b-catenin localization and WNT signaling by HUWE1 requires its ubiquitin ligase activity and a subset of b-catenin destruction complex components. These results reveal a new role for some destruction complex components in regulating b-catenin sub-cellular localization and WNT signaling downstream of HUWE1, distinct from their established activity in controlling b-catenin stability. We are further investigating the molecular mechanisms by which HUWE1, acting through the destruction complex, regulates b-catenin subcellular localization and function.

project_title: Anetumab in Thymic Carcinoma
project_abstract_text: This multicenter trial evaluated the mesothelin-targeting antibody-drug conjugate, anetumab ravtansine in subjects with thymic carcinoma. This clinical trial was based on a preclinical study conducted by our group that showed strong, membranous expression of mesothelin in thymic carcinoma. Three patients were treated at the NCI. One patient experienced a durable complete response and two patients had durable stabilization of disease. Adverse events associated with anetumab were manageable and included peripheral neuropathy and development of corneal microcysts, which were reversible with interruption of treatment. This study is complete and closed to accrual.

project_title: Synthetic bacteria as a targeted delivery system for small molecule therapeutics
project_abstract_text: The goal of cancer therapeutics is to ensure that the therapies only target the cancer cells resulting in tumor eradication without deleterious side effects to the patient. Patients with ovarian cancer show poor prognosis if testing revels an overexpression of a cell surface marker HER2. As this is on the cell surface and expressed at lower levels in normal cells, it is an attractive drug target. In this work, we apply a biocompatible bacterial spore-like particles, termed 'SSHELs.' Here, SSHELs are modified with an affibody directed against HER2 and loaded with the chemotherapeutic agent doxorubicin. Thus, providing a combinatorial treatment. We observed that drug-loaded SSHELs reduce tumor growth and increase survival with lower toxicity in a mouse tumor xenograft model compared with free drug and with liposomal doxorubicin by preferentially accumulating in the tumor mass. Cancer cells actively internalized and then trafficked bound SSHELs to acidic compartments, whereupon the cargo is released to the cytosol in a pH-dependent manner. We propose that SSHELs represent a versatile strategy for targeted drug delivery, for targets that are located at cancer cells with potential in clinical settings.

project_title: Assay development and screening for molecular targets and discovery
project_abstract_text: Assay development and screening section (ADSS) driven collaborations with MTP and other NCI scientists results in the development and implementation of large scale screening campaigns for the discovery and characterization of translationally relevant modulators of a variety of disease related targets. Some examples for the current reporting year include an assay designed for the identification of novel protein 'degraders' important in the context of prostate cancer, a differential cytotoxicity screen designed to identify compounds with pleural mesothelioma specific cytotoxicity, and a cell-based screen for specific inhibitors of a bifunctional RNA/DNA repair enzyme important in viral infection, neural development, and cancer. In addition to these and other cell-based screens, several biochemical and biophysical assays (in collaboration with the MTP Protein Chemistry and Molecular Biology Section) were also developed and executed as part of this project. As part of a novel drug discovery pipeline, ADSS developed assays are utilized in support of natural product chemistry efforts, i.e., purification and characterization of active compounds from natural product extracts identified from HTS campaigns. These include hundreds of productive chemistry projects resulting from cell-based and biochemically targeted screens. Finally, the section collaborates extensively with NCI scientists to characterize active compounds that arise from HTS and natural products chemistry. These efforts include intracellular and biochemical evaluation to elucidate both on target phenotypes of compound treatments as well as potential off-target liabilities of discovered agents. Recent significant publications resulting from work done for this project include active compounds targeting the oncogenic fusion transcription factor PAX3-FOXO1, Merkle cell carcinoma, and the oncogenic fusion kinase DNAJB1-PRKACA. In addition, ADSS has continued to support MTP anti-HIV protein discovery and development directions with continued whole-cell/live-virus anti-HIV assays as well as SARS-CoV2 specific projects developed during the pandemic.

project_title: Anti-PD-L1-TGFb antibody (M7824) in advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
project_abstract_text: Bintrafusp alfa is a bifunctional monoclonal antibody targeting programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) and transforming growth factor-beta. The use of this drug represents a form of combination immunotherapy. Fourteen patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer were enrolled and treated at the NCI. No new signals of clinical activity or toxicity were observed. A subset of patients derived long-term benefit with ongoing objective responses after 12 months of treatment. The study has been completed and the results have been published. Please refer to the associated paper for details.

project_title: CV301 and Anti-PD-1 Therapy in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
project_abstract_text: CV301 consists of a poxvirus-based immunotherapy encoding transgenes for B7.1, intercellular adhesion molecule-1, leukocyte function-associated antigen-3, Carcinoembryonic Antigen and Mucin-1 based on a non-replicating Modified Vaccinia Ankara (MVA) vector. Five subjects with recurrent non-small cell lung cancer following platinum-based chemotherapy were treated at the NCI with CV301 in combination with Nivolumab (four subjects) or pembrolizumab (one subject). The study has been completed and published.

project_title: Durvalumab in Combination with Olaparib in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
project_abstract_text: Increased DNA damage by PARP inhibition will complement the anti-tumor activity of the immune checkpoint inhibitor, durvalumab. Eighteen patients with recurrent non-small cell lung cancer have been enrolled, including patients previously treated with immunotherapy. Accrual to the non-small cell lung cancer expansion cohort has been closed. No new signals of clinical activity or toxicity have been observed. Immunological analyses are ongoing to identify predictive biomarkers in individuals with durable benefit.

project_title: Molecular Biology of Lymphoma
project_abstract_text: We aim to study the molecular biology of lymphoma subtypes in the context of each of our trials. These lymphomas include diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, follicular lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma, and EBV-driven lymphomas. We perform baseline tissue biopsies on all patients and perform comprehensve molecular profiling including WES, RNA sequencing, and copy number alteration profiling. This precision medicine approach allows us to understand mechanisms of resistance and response to targeted agents. Most recently, we have added noinvasive profiling by circulating tumor DNA, an emerging technique.

project_title: Pathway inhibitors in Lymphomas
project_abstract_text: We have been studying BTK inhibitors in primary CNS lymphoma, secondary CNS lymphoma, and aggressive B-cell lymphomas. We employ window of opportunity designs to elucidate the molecular differences betwedn tumors that are BTK-responsive and which tumors are BTK-resistant. We observe in SCNSL that tumors that are BTK-responsive can have durable remissions with TEDDI-R and that is potentially curative. We have seen the same results in patents with relapsed or refractory PCNSL. In DLBCL, the story is more complicated but we have observed BTK responsive tumors from both ABC origin and GCB origin suggesting that BCR signaling in DLBCL may be influenced by factors other than those we have previously described. PI3K inhibitors have shown remarkable activity in untreated FL and we have seen durable CR with a combination of copanlisib and rituximab as well.
