Completion of accrual is expected later in 2024. Aim2) Multiple researchers have shown transcriptional between the basal and classical subtypes of PDAC. Basal subtype is associated with a squamous phenotype and confers poor prognosis. By using forced expression of a squamous differentiation program in human pancreatic cancer cells, we have investigated whether these cells A) preferentially metastasize in mice and B) are enriched following chemotherapy treatment. B) PACC- Improving outcomes for patients with pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma (PACC). PACC is an ultra-rare tumor type that is histologically and genetically distinct from PDAC. Aim1: Investigate the Natural History of PACC. We have accrued >10 PACC patients to Rare Solid Tumor Natural History Study (PI: Wedekind-Malone) and are following these patients. Aim 2: Develop pre-clinical models of PACC. We have initiated a collaboration with CAPR Frederick (S. Kozlov) to engineer a PACC GEMM. Aim 3: Identify new treatments for PACC. We have initiated a Phase 2 trial to test olaparib in patients with PACC based on research by us and others suggesting that PACC is an ID3 deficient tumor and that deficiency of ID3 leads to PARP inhibitor sensitivity.

project_title: Transgenerational Epigenetic Inheritance Mediated by a Core Promoter Element
project_abstract_text: Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance is defined as the transmission of traits or gene expression patterns across multiple generations that do not derive from DNA alterations. The effect of multiple stress factors or metabolic changes resulting in such inheritance have been documented in plants, worms and flies and mammals. The molecular basis for epigenetic inheritance has been linked to histone and DNA modifications and non-coding RNA. In this study, we show that mutation of a promoter element, the CCAAT box, disrupts stable expression of an MHC Class I transgene, resulting in variegated expression among progeny for at least 4 generations in multiple independently derived transgenic lines. Histone modifications and RNA polII binding correlate with expression, whereas DNA methylation and nucleosome occupancy do not. Mutation of the CCAAT box abrogates NF-Y binding and results in changes to CTCF binding and DNA looping patterns across the gene that correlate with expression status from one generation to the next. These studies identify the CCAAT promoter element as a regulator of stable transgenerational epigenetic inheritance. Considering that the CCAAT box is present in 30% of eukaryotic promoters, this study could provide important insights into how fidelity of gene expression patterns is maintained through multiple generations.

project_title: Structural biology of host-pathogen interactions
project_abstract_text: This year we have published two key results, both in Nature Microbiology. In the first we have revealed how bacteria control the direction of rotation of their flagella via massive conformational changes in the super-structure assembled in the cytoplasm. The magnitude of conformational change seen is unprecedented and alters how we view the possibilities for protein conformational change. The second key result provides the first snapshots of how translocation of substrates is achieved by the type 9 secretion system - again involving massive conformational changes to achieve a biologically important process. Additionally we published work describing how Helicobacter pylori assembles a key enzyme essential for its ability to survive in the GI tract.

project_title: TCR engineered T cell therapies for hematologic malignancies
project_abstract_text: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapies transformed the field of hematology and oncology by enabling HLA-independent targeting of cancer cells. However, CAR-T resistance remains an obstacle to cure. CAR-T cell therapies so far have been most successful against B-cell malignancies, but even in these disease subtypes, sustained remission is achieved in less than half of treated patients. Therefore, effective strategies to overcome CAR-T resistant is needed. One of the well-established mechanisms of resistance to CAR-T cell is loss, reduction, or modulation of cell-surface antigen expression. Natural T cell receptors (TCR) recognize intracellularly processed and presented antigens in the context of HLA and do not require cell-surface antigen expression, and thus may be able to recognize CAR-T-resistant tumors. To test the premise TCR-T cell can recognize CAR-T resistant low-antigen tumors, we discovered a TCR that recognize intracellularly digested peptide fragment of CD22 that is presented in the context of HLA-A*02:01 (International Patent Application No. PCT/US2022/016561). T cells transduced to express the CD22 TCR recognized B-cell leukemia and lymphoma cell lines in both CD22- and HLA-A2-restricted manner. The CD22 TCR-T cells mediated in vivo anti-tumor activity in xenograft models. Importantly, the CD22TCR-T cells were able to kill low-antigen tumors that escaped CAR-T cells. Furthermore, the CD22 TCR-T cells mediated leukemia clearance without triggering systemic inflammation, while CAR-T cell (both CD19 CAR-T cells and CD22 CAR-T cells) therapy resulted in high levels of circulating proinflammatory cytokines. Cross-reactivity of the CD22 TCR was ruled out using our recently developed systematic multi-tiered screening strategy (Ishii K et al., Science Advances. 2023), which confirmed that the risk of off-target toxicity would be unlikely. These preclinical data support the pre-clinical anti-tumor activity and safety of the CD22 TCR-T for the treatment of CD22+ lymphoma/leukemia, including those that resisted existing CAR-T cells. We are in the process of clinical translation of the CD22 TCR-T cells. The GMP-grade vector manufacturing was supported by the NExT Program of the NCI. We are also developing the strategies to combine the CD22 TCR with the existing CAR-T cells to achieve synergy against lymphoid malignancies that carry heterogenous resistance mechanisms.

project_title: Neuroblastoma Tumor Microenvironment: tumor growth and immune regulation
project_abstract_text: Deep genomic sequencing reveals considerable tumor cell heterogeneity even in clonally derived tumors. Heterogeneity is influenced by the stochastic nature of molecular interactions as well as genetic, environmental and cellular interactions. In tumors this is compounded by genomic alterations driving oncogenesis as well as therapy-induced changes. To decipher molecular mechanisms contributing to heterogeneity and develop interventional strategies we have developed orthotopically generated PDX xenograft models and isogenic in vitro cell line models. In addition to a new NCIPDX-AJ PDX, we received from St. Jude's 6 PDX NB tumors with varying genetic alterations and developed them into orthotopic NB PDX tumors. From 4 of these we have developed companion isogenic cell lines and in 3/4 we have parental as well as MESEN and ADRN cell lines cultured in both serum-free and serum containing media. We performed genomic analyses including DNA sequencing, RNAseq, scRNAseq, and proteomic analysis on these PDXs with initial studies completed for SJNBL012407(MAST97) and SJNBL013762(MAST109). This set of NB PDXs and matched cell lines are used by POB researchers interested in evaluating therapeutic interventions in murine xenograft models. How tumor cell heterogeneity and cellular plasticity contribute to the chemo-refractory nature of NB tumors or their propensity to relapse? Our hypothesis is that a subset of NB tumor cells is epigenetically poised to adapt or lineage switch during tumor growth in complex tissue environments and in response to therapy. This epigenetic plasticity combined with the stochastic nature of molecular interactions leads to a wide range of cellular phenotypes that contribute to therapy resistance or relapse. Understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying NB heterogeneity will yield insights that should be therapeutically tractable. In detailing NB tumor heterogeneity we will aim to: Subaim 1: Develop models to study NB tumor cell heterogeneity. Subaim 2: Study genetic basis of tumor cell evolution under therapeutic pressure Subaim 3: Develop targeted therapies for NB tumor subtypes. Current studies are using scRNAseq and scATACseq to detail changes in phenotype that occur under therapeutic pressure using PDXs grown orthotopically in SCID-beige mice. We have generated barcoded cells to be able to track NB cells and their progeny as cells grow in a complex model system and under therapeutic pressure. We have developed an in vitro model to study phenotypic switching and are screening drugs that will prevent phenotypic switching.

project_title: Virus host interactions in clinical samples
project_abstract_text: In collaboration with Drs. Yarchoan, Ramaswami, Lurain, and Krug from HAMB, we have been exploring the expression patterns of human and viral genes in normal tissues, Kaposi sarcoma (KS), and other pathological tissues infected by KSHV. There is limited knowledge about the RNA transcripts of cells and viruses in KS lesions and how these are affected by previous treatments, concurrent KSHV-associated diseases, or the specific tissue location of KS lesions. Our goal was to compare human gene expression and viral transcripts in KS versus normal tissue using matched patient samples. This study included participants with well-documented clinical characteristics, investigating both skin and gastrointestinal (GI) KS to discern differences in viral and host transcripts. We analyzed samples from 19 participants, focusing on both cutaneous and GI KS. Most participants were also HIV-positive, with some having additional conditions such as KICS, MCD, and PEL. Our analysis revealed that GI KS samples had higher KSHV viral loads than skin KS samples, and HIV viral loads were also higher in individuals with GI KS. However, CD4+ T cell counts were similar in both types of KS samples. Examining gene expression patterns, we found significant differences in differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between the two types of KS lesions. We also found differences in genes associated with inflammatory response and cytokine dysregulation based on KS location. For instance, IL6 and IL10 RNA levels were increased in skin KS but not significantly altered in GI KS. Additionally, VEGF receptors, crucial for angiogenesis, were upregulated in skin KS, while VEGFR3 was increased in both skin and GI KS. There were varied expression changes in IFN-gamma, known for combating KSHV infection. Examining KSHV gene expression in both GI and skin KS lesions revealed heterogeneity in KSHV expression patterns, with three distinct patterns observed across multiple lesions. ORF75 was significantly present in 91% of all KS lesions, a surprising finding given less detection of many other lytic genes. Finally, we explored the expression of STC1 and FLT4, both upregulated in GI and skin lesions. Using the lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) model, we confirmed increased STC1 and FLT4 expression with KSHV infection or reactivation. Suppressing STC1 led to decreased viral gene expression and virion production. Targeting STC1 or FLT4 reduced the number of tubules formed (angiogenesis markers) in a cell culture assay, suggesting that increased expression of these genes may enhance angiogenesis within KS lesions. Our study revealed significant differences in gene expression between skin and GI KS lesions, providing valuable insights into the pathogenesis of Kaposi Sarcoma. These findings could guide future research and treatment strategies, with further investigations into the roles of STC1 and FLT4 in KSHV infection and angiogenesis potentially leading to novel therapeutic approaches. These results were published in September of 2023. In our subsequent analysis, we observed differences in skin and GI KS lesions compared to their normal counterparts, using a method that examines bulk RNA expression and compares it to gene expression in purified cells to predict cell type distributions in bulk RNA expression data. Macrophages play key roles in antigen presentation, inflammation and phagocytosis. M1-classically activated macrophages are pro-inflammatory and promote cell killing while M2-alternatively activated macrophages are anti-inflammatory and promote tissue healing. We found dysregulated macrophages and higher resting memory CD4+ T cells particularly in GI KS lesions. One hypothesis was that increased IFN-g expression in KS lesions might promote M1 polarization. However, IFN-g secretion levels decreased with KSHV infection in our experiments using LECs. Using conditioned media from KSHV-infected LECs, we did find an increase in the M1 macrophage marker CXCL10. These results suggest that factors other than IFN-g in the conditioned media from KSHV-infected cells may be promoting M1 polarization. In actual KS lesions, infiltrating cells capable of secreting various cytokines and chemokines beyond KSHV-infected endothelial cells may contribute to overall changes in immune cell populations, including macrophages. Correlational analysis suggested that these differences might be related to site-specific immune environments between the skin and GI tracts rather than broadly associated with KSHV or HIV infection. In GI KS, but not in skin KS, KSHV total gene expression levels were positively correlated with regulatory T cells, which promote M2 macrophage differentiation. Conversely, skin KS showed a preference for M2 differentiation over M1 in tumor samples compared to matched normal skin. We also acknowledge the limitations of this bulk RNA-Seq study and the need for single-cell and spatial analysis to further explore the role of immune cells in regulating the tumor microenvironment. Overall, we demonstrated KSHV's ability to dysregulate immune cells like macrophages in vitro, with correlatives in clinical specimens.

project_title: Zebrafish model of blood-brain barrier to improve drug delivery to the brain
project_abstract_text: Not only are ABC transporters responsible for drug resistance in cancer, but they are a major component of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and blood-placental barrier. The three most prominent transporters at the blood-brain barrier are ABCB1, ABCC2/C4, and ABCG2. We previously developed a murine model for analysis of ABCG2 expression at the blood-brain barrier based on the fact that luciferin is an ABCG2 substrate and its entry into the brain is prevented by transporter expression. In this model, firefly luciferase is under the expression of the GFAP promoter, leading to its expression in the astrocytes. When mice are injected with luciferin, no light signal from the brain is detected due to ABCG2 preventing luciferin from crossing the blood-brain barrier. However, when luciferin is co-administered with an ABCG2 inhibitor, it can cross the blood-brain barrier and react with luciferase expressed in the astrocytes to produce light which can be quantitatively measured. Because studies of the BBB in mice are time-consuming and expensive, we are developing homologous models in the zebrafish, as components of the zebrafish BBB appear to be very similar to those of the mammalian BBB. We have developed and characterized a transgenic zebrafish line with NanoLuc, derived by Promega from a deep-sea shrimp, under the control of the GFAP promoter. In this model, NanoLuc is expressed in the developing zebrafish brain and spinal cord. Coelenterazine is one of the substrates for NanoLuc and is transported by both ABCB1 and ABCG2. Furimazine, a coelenterazine derivative with very high yield of light, is an ABCG2 substrate. Thus, this model can be used to study the role of transporters at the blood-brain barrier, but could also be used to screen compounds that might increase permeability of the barrier regardless of the mechanism. We have shown that addition of a substrate, such as furimazine, and an Abcg2 inhibitor to the water containing larval zebrafish result in light generation consistent with penetration of furimazine across the BBB. If zebrafish are to be considered an appropriate model for study of transporters at the blood-brain barrier, the zebrafish homologs of human transporters must be carefully characterized. Zebrafish do not have a direct homolog of human ABCB1 but instead have 2 similar variants-Abcb4 and Abcb5. Expression of these transporters in heterologous systems has enabled their detailed characterization and inhibition properties. In collaboration with Matthew Hall at NCATS, we have found that zebrafish Abcb4 is nearly identical to human ABCB1 in conferring resistance to 90 known ABCB1 substrates. Abcb5 is also a functional transporter and confers resistance to many ABCB1 substrates but has a slightly narrower substrate specificity. While zebrafish Abcb4 is the only homolog that localizes to the BBB, Abcb4 and Abcb5 are expressed at other barrier and excretory sites in zebrafish, such as the gut, liver, and kidneys. Zebrafish also have 4 homologs of human ABCG2-Abcg2a, Abcg2b, Abcg2c and Abcg2d. We have functionally categorized these zebrafish ABCG2 orthologs and determined the brain tissue distribution of zebrafish ABCG2 homologs. To determine substrates of the transporters, we stably expressed each in HEK-293 cells and performed cytotoxicity and fluorescent efflux assays with known ABCG2 substrates. We found Abcg2a had the greatest substrate overlap with ABCG2, and Abcg2d appeared to be the least functionally similar. Using RNAscope in situ hybridization we identified abcg2a as the only homolog expressed at the adult and larval zebrafish BBB, based on its localization to claudin-5 positive brain vasculature. We also generated an antibody to specifically detect Abcg2a, and found it to stain brain endothelial cells, thus confirming the results with RNAscope probes. We also found reactivity in the liver and gastrointestinal tract similar to the ABCG2 expression pattern in humans. These results demonstrate the conserved function of zebrafish Abcg2a and suggest that zebrafish may be an appropriate model organism for the studying the role of ABCG2 at the BBB. Having identified zebrafish Abcb4 and Abcg2a as the homologous transporters at the zebrafish BBB, we characterized the ability of NanoLuc substrates to be transported by zebrafish and human transporters at the BBB. We examined several coelenterazine derivatives as well as some furimazine derivatives and found that furimazine was the brightest NanoLuc substrate tested and was transported by human ABCG2 and zebrafish Abcg2a. Coelenterazine h was the brightest coelenterazine derivative and was also transported by human ABCG2 and zebrafish Abcg2a. Thus, these compounds could be used to study the role of ABCG2 at the BBB. As context to our own inhibitor studies, and to enable characterization of the BBB in the complete absence of Abcb4 and Abcg2a, we have generated knockout zebrafish models for these genes which are viable and currently under study.

project_title: Developing ACC patient-derived organoids to identify therapeutic vulnerabilities
project_abstract_text: Our project has two aims: 1) Identification of novel therapeutic vulnerabilities in adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) by large-scale drug testing of adrenocortical carcinoma patient-derived organoids (ACC PDOs). We hypothesize that large-scale drug screening will identify compounds with efficacy in ACC PDOs that could be used for future combination studies and ultimately translated to the clinic. 2) Develop patient-derived organoids that encompass tumor heterogeneity of adrenocortical carcinoma. We hypothesize that we can develop ACC PDOs which represent the major molecular subtypes of ACC identified by the TCGA.

project_title: Vaccine strategies for HIVAIDS
project_abstract_text: The strategies above involve several steps that together comprise a push-pull approach, to optimize antigen structure, improve quantity and quality of the response, and remove regulatory barriers. Blocking negative regulation in HIV and vaccine strategies: We carried out epitope enhancement (sequence modification to improve MHC binding) to increase MHC binding of epitopes from several viral antigens including HIV, and showed these improved vaccine efficacy. We have pioneered the use of anti-TGFb as a novel checkpoint inhibitor, given that TGFb is one of the most immunosuppressive cytokines known. We even showed preliminary evidence of efficacy and safety in a clinical trial in melanoma patients. We have also compared combinations of checkpoint inhibitors and anti-TGF-b in enhancing vaccine efficacy in mice, and found preliminary data for synergy among anti-TGFb, anti-LAG3, anti-TIGIT and anti-PDL1. These strategies are applicable to both HIV and cancer. Cytokines as vaccine adjuvants for HIV and induction of high avidity T cells: Our earlier work first showed that high avidity T cells were more effective at clearing viral infections. We found ways to induce them with cytokines and TLR ligands, including expressing IL-15 in the vaccine, and inclusion of costimulatory molecules, in collaborations with Tom Waldmann and with Jeff Schlom, respectively. The quality of response proved more important than the quantity. We recently found, using a novel adjuvant, CAF09, that we could lower the vaccine dose sufficiently to induce higher avidity CD4 T cells to better clear HIV-gp160-expressing virus infection in mice. We also found that IL-1b induces Th17 helper cells that do not help Tc1 CD8 T cells that protect against vaccinia virus expressing HIV gp160. Rather, they skew the CD8 response to Tc17 cells that make IL-17 and do not protect. TGF-b blockade can prevent this problem, as TGF-b is involved in Th17 induction. We are examining the epigenetic and transcriptional mechanisms behind high avidity T cells by carrying out a single-cell RNAseq study of high vs low avidity T cell lines generated against the same antigen. T cells from OT-I TCR-transgenic mice were grown with high or low concentrations of antigen to produce low or high avidity lines, respectively, with the identical TCR, to exclude effects of intrinsic TCR affinity. These were stimulated with the same SIINFEKL peptide, and subjected to RNAseq. Also, T cells were generated against the same SIINFEKL peptide and subjected to concurrent TCR and RNAseq analysis, and high and low avidity lines with the same clonotype were compared. Promising genes are being tested in knock-down studies. We also found that IL-21 synergizes with IFN-g to induce IFN-stimulated genes and clear Citrobacter colitis through an effect on STAT1. We also examined combinations of cytokines and TLR ligands as vaccine adjuvants and found greatest efficacy of IL-15 + TLR3 and TLR9 agonists, but also some efficacy of IL-12 + GM-CSF. We are comparing these for qualitative differences in the immune response as well as quantity. Mucosal immunity, microbiome and HIV/SIV vaccines: About 85% of HIV transmission is mucosal. We found that a mucosal T cell vaccine can impact the initial mucosal nidus of infection. We are studying induction and trafficking of T cells, DCs, and MDSCs among mucosal compartments to optimize mucosal vaccine efficacy. In mice, we found that T cells could be directly primed in the vaginal mucosa, despite lack of organized lymphoid structures, contrary to textbook dogma. We also discovered that colonic DCs can imprint CD8 T cells to home back to the colon preferentially, based on differential retinoic acid expression vs. small intestine DCs. We are currently examining the mechanism of this effect in terms of chemokine receptor expression and homing activity, and by using an RNAseq comparison of clonal OT-1 T cells stimulated by DCs from the small vs large intestines, as well as single-cell RNAseq of DCs from the colon vs small intestine. We discovered that altering a cathepsin S cleavage site could protect an immunodominant epitope of HIV gp120 from degradation in endosomes during cross-presentation, providing proof of concept for a novel mechanism of virus escape for HIV that infects mostly non-APCs. Using NHP models, we found that activated mucosal T cells determine susceptibility to SIV/HIV infection (transmission), eclipse time prior to systemic viral detection, and acute viral load. We found that even in naive animals, gut microbiota can strongly affect susceptibility to transmission, by immune activation, and also affect vaccine efficacy. We are exploring the mechanisms by testing the effect of antibiotics on multiple cell subsets in the large compared to the small intestine. Further, we found that vaccines can induce MDSCs that counteract vaccine protection, and also infection can affect trafficking of MDSCs. We also demonstrated for the first time that MDSCs could be infected by SHIV in vivo. As most HIV transmission is through mucosal surfaces and HIV homes to the gut mucosa, we have designed and invented a nanoparticle vaccine delivered orally in mice but coated to pass through the stomach intact and to be released selectively in the large intestine where it induces CTL responses in the large intestine and vaginal mucosa and protects against rectal or vaginal challenge with a virus. We translated our oral nanoparticle (NP) approach to macaque SIV vaccines, finding reduced risk against SHIV rectal acquisition in 2 studies. Surprisingly, we discovered that protection against SIV acquisition in 3 studies can occur without anti-envelope antibodies. While T cell immunity was induced, it did not correlate with protection, and protection was not abrogated by CD8 T cell depletion. Rather, protection correlated with trained innate immunity, involving monocyte 'memory' for SIV in induction of cytokines maintained by epigenetic changes. We have carried out RNAseq to determine what changes occur in monocytes after immunization, leading to new mechanistic hypotheses including an unexpected role for platelets and their production of platelet factor 4 (PF4), also known as CXCL4. This is manifested by platelet-cell aggregates in which platelets actually coat cells. Also, we are combining an SIV vaccine and mucosal NP boost to increase mucosal immunity with a microbicide to reduce the viral inoculum in an OAR-funded study. Our hypothesis is that priming and boosting with mucosally delivered nanoparticles containing V2 loop antigens will both increase mucosal immunity to protect against intrarectal SIV challenge, and selectively expand immune responses against the V2 loop that have been shown to correlate with protection in the RV144 phase III human trial. Initial results show that priming and boosting orally with NPs containing a V2-loop pentamer can increase protection compared to the base vaccine alone consisting of SIV gag and env DNA, ALVAC expressing gp120, and deltaV1 gp120 protein in alum. Immune correlates of improved protection, include mucosal IgA, stronger ADCC especially targeting the V2 loop, mucosal gp120-specific plasma cells and plasmablasts, and T cell responses. However, some aspect of empty control NPs counteracted some of the protective benefits, in part by activating gut mucosal CD4 T cells that can be targets for SIV infection. Thus, the NP strategy needs to be adjusted to avoid this unwanted counterproductive effect.

project_title: Anatomical and gene expression resource for Macrostomum lignano
project_abstract_text: The Macrostomum lignano (Mlig) postembryonic anatomical atlas is a collaborative team effort. Dr. Matthew Voas has optimized cell dissociation, vital nuclear dye staining, and fluorescence activated cell sorting protocols required for sample preparation, and he is producing pilot 10x scRNA-Seq data sets in conjunction with Dr. Sevilay Turan and Dr. Bao Tran's team at the CCR Sequencing Facility at the NCI-Frederick Advanced Technology Research Facility. Postdoctoral Scientist Dr. Xintao Fan conducted QC and preliminary analysis of the data prior to his departure in April 2024. Dr. Francisco Pereira Lobo has taken over as lead analyst for the project and we have rebuilt the analysis and clustering with him. Dr. Matthew Voas is now conducting in vivo validation of cluster-enriched biomarkers while cross-species cluster annotation and trajectory analysis are ongoing. Finally, we will work to create an interactive Shiny app that integrates digital and spatial gene expression data for differentially expressed genes defining anatomical entities captured in our analysis.

project_title: Identification of immune evasion mechanisms in the osteosarcoma microenvironment
project_abstract_text: Our current research aims to further investigate the processes associated with immune evasion of metastatic osteosarcoma and to identify therapeutic vulnerabilities for clinical translation. We have successfully completed spatial transcriptomic and proteomic profiling of metastatic osteosarcoma specimens to thoroughly characterize the molecular landscape of this disease. Our integrated data analysis approach revealed that, despite the genomic heterogeneity that has long defined osteosarcoma, these tumors illicit a conserved cellular and molecular response in the non-malignant cells surrounding the tumor core. We hypothesize that this conserved peritumoral response is responsible for excluding lymphocytes from infiltrating into the metastatic tumor lesions. Current research efforts are focused on identifying and functionally validating therapeutic agents that can target this peritumoral response using murine models of disease. We hypothesize that by targeting the mechanism driving lymphocyte exclusion, we will increase the infiltration of lymphocytes into the tumor, thereby sensitizing these tumors to different immunotherapeutic modalities. We have also identified several immunoregulatory biological processes that are active within the core of the metastatic lesions. We are currently investigating the functional significance of these pathways using a combination of genetic (CRISPRa/CRISPRi) and pharmacological approaches in murine models of metastatic osteosarcoma. Lastly, we have completed single nuclei multi-ome sequencing of 26 metastatic osteosarcoma specimens where both RNA and ATAC sequencing are simultaneously performed on individual nuclei. We are currently in the process of analyzing these data and anticipate that by combining both RNA and ATAC sequencing data, we will be able to identify both cellular populations and different cell states within those populations. These data will be used to identify and functionally validate cellular targets associated with disease progression and immunosuppression.

project_title: Leveraging RNA and synthetic lethality in germline BRCA-mut breast cancer
project_abstract_text: BC-SELECT is a computational algorithm that is a breast cancer-specific adaptation of SELECT, with a focus on predicting response to competing targeted therapies or immunotherapy used in early-stage breast cancer. The training component involves use of large-scale datasets to identify clinically relevant genetic interactions through 3 steps - a cell line-based gene essentiality test to identify interacting gene pairs, a screen for relative gene expression levels in existing breast cancer clinical data, to identify pairs associated with statically improved survival, and a phylogenetic screen to assess preserved genetic interactions across species. Tuning of parameters in this step was performed using 3 breast cancer clinical trials. The inferred genetic interaction partner genes from this testing step are used to generate a patient's predicted response score. The testing/validation component involves generating individual-level predicted patient response scores with 11 unseen breast cancer clinical trials (testing HER2-directed therapies, PARP inhibitors, and immunotherapy), then assessing the performance of the predicted score versus actual patient responses. BC-SELECT predicted treatment response in 11 clinical trials in breast cancer (not used for training), with 5 out of 8 targeted therapy trials (including PARP inhibitors) showing ROC-AUCs > 0.6, and all 3 immunotherapy trials showing ROC-AUCs > 0.7. BC-SELECT showed empirical statistical significance and surpassed our 2.5% cutoff threshold compared to chance in 6/11 datasets. The algorithm outperformed the original SELECT for immunotherapy prediction in breast cancer. This project was presented at the AACR 2024 conference and the manuscript is currently being finalized.

project_title: Identifying Treatment Options using RNA-Based Synthetic Lethality and Rescue
project_abstract_text: This clinical trial is undergoing regulatory approval. It has been approved by the WMB Branch, the CCR Scientific Review Committee, and is now being presented to the FDA for risk assessment and determination before final review by the IRB prior to opening. Funding has been allocated for this study. The total enrollment of the study will be 66 participants in 2 cohorts. The objectives of the trial will be as follows: 1) To assess the feasibility of using the ENLIGHT algorithm to match heavily pretreated participants with metastatic breast cancer to off-label therapies and 2) To assess the objective response rate (ORR) of participants with advanced breast cancer using treatment recommended by the ENLIGHT algorithm. Our Secondary Objectives are: 1) To determine the overall frequency of the ENLIGHT algorithm in recommending matches of targeted therapy or immunotherapy for participants who would otherwise be ineligible per existing biomarkers associated with FDA-approved, on-label treatments, 2) To assess the duration of clinical benefit for treatments recommended by the ENLIGHT algorithm, 3) To determine the specific agents for which ENLIGHT demonstrates the best predictive performance in the context of breast cancer, 4)To determine extent of therapy-associated toxicity burden for participants who are matched to a therapy through the ENLIGHT algorithm Exploratory Objectives, 5)To assess progression-free survival (PFS) of participants who receive treatment as recommended by the ENLIGHT algorithm, 6)To assess overall survival (OS) of participants who receive treatment as recommended by the ENLIGHT algorithm, 7) To identify how ENLIGHT recommendations correspond to or differ from current guidelines-based recommendations in metastatic breast cancer 8)To assess correlation between baseline RNA-seq, clinical data, and data types used in clinical molecular pathology (germline DNA, whole-exome DNA from tumor, methylation), 9) To assess correlation between baseline RNA-seq, clinical data, and data types used in translational research after start of treatment (e.g., spatial transcriptomics, tumor microenvironment, circulating tumor DNA, peripheral blood RNA, and peripheral blood/serum immune features), 10) To identify changes in above clinical and translational data types between baseline / after initiation of ENLIGHT-selected treatment as observed from tissue biopsy of consenting participants, 11) To assess the ORR / duration of clinical benefit for participants undergoing an additional iteration of treatment as recommended by the ENLIGHT algorithm, 12) To assess patient-reported outcomes (PROs) through the metrics of feasibility of response to assessments, tolerability of treatments, longitudinal clinical impact of treatments on study, and meaningful change in disease / treatment-related symptoms while on study, 13) To identify shared clinical characteristics, if any, for participants not matched to an ENLIGHT therapy.

project_title: Study of CAR T cells and mechanisms of resistance in pediatric brain tumors
project_abstract_text: Trastuzumab-based HER2 CAR T constructs have demonstrated preclinical efficacy in medulloblastoma and are currently being evaluated for use in children and young adults with recurrent or refractory CNS tumors. Preliminary results demonstrate immune activation but no objective tumor response in three patients, including two patients with posterior fossa ependymoma (PF)-EPN. A key finding in the serum and CSF of all three patients was very high levels of the inflammatory chemokine CCL2 following treatment with CAR T cells. Preclinical studies suggest that high levels of CCL2 may impede T cell mediated anti-tumor activity in CNS tumors. The role of CCL2 to enhance or diminish CAR T cell efficacy for CNS tumors is unknown. We evaluated a second generation trastuzumab-based HER2 CAR construct with a 4-1BB co-stimulatory domain in two ultra-high-risk patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models that faithfully recapitulate PFA-EPN. In contrast to preclinical studies in other cancers, treatment with trastuzumab-based HER2 CAR T cell alone causes only partial regression of tumors and robust infiltration of immunosuppressive monocytes in PFA-EPN PDX mouse models. We studied constitutive NF-kB activation because it is a hallmark of PFA-EPN that drives dysregulation of inflammatory genes and forms an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Upon tumor recognition, CAR T cells produce high amounts of the cytokine tumor necrosis factor-alpha, which is an extracellular stimulus that propagates NF-kB activation in PFA-EPN. We show that HER2 CAR T cell treatment causes increased nuclear translocation of the RELA NF-kB subunit, which induces CCL2 gene transcription and chemokine release. This results in CCL2-CCR2 ligand/receptor mediated influx of inflammatory monocytes and regulatory T cells, impairing CAR-T cell effector function. Inhibition of CCR2 restores anti-tumor CAR T cytotoxicity against bulky orthotopic tumors by decreasing the infiltration of inflammatory monocytes and regulatory T cells. Combinatorial strategies addressing tumor mediated immunosuppression should be evaluated in upcoming CAR T cell trials for patients with high-risk CNS tumors. Submitted to Nature Communications in Fall, 2023. Currently completing major revisions with planned resubmission in Fall, 2024.

project_title: Imaging, image guided biopsy and treatment of prostate cancer
project_abstract_text: The project titled 'Imaging, Image Guided Biopsy, and Treatment of Prostate Cancer' aims to develop novel imaging techniques, both Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and molecular imaging, along with image processing (artificial intelligence) techniques to detect prostate cancer and estimate disease burden. Significant advancements have been made, including improved MRI resolution, automated evaluation of MRI with AI, use of TULSA system for focal therapy and guiding prostate biopsies and treatments using AI. These innovations have enhanced diagnostic accuracy and guided biopsy and treatment procedures. AI integration has automated the identification of suspicious areas, resulting in precise biopsies and more accurate cancer staging. Image-guided focal therapies, such as high-intensity focused ultrasound, have been implemented, targeting cancerous tissues while sparing healthy ones. Challenges like imaging artifacts and patient variability are being addressed with refined algorithms and adaptive imaging protocols. Future plans include clinical trials and continued research to enable personalized treatment plans and transfer technologies to clinical practice. These advancements promise to revolutionize prostate cancer care, offering more accurate diagnostics and less invasive treatments, ultimately improving patient outcomes.

project_title: Reduced toxicity allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation in malignancies
project_abstract_text: In this fiscal year, a study of reduced-intensity transplant for patients with peripheral T cell lymphoma has re-opened to accrual after a period of data analysis. The study results have been presented in oral form at the American Society for Transplantation and Cell Therapy and should be published in manuscript form by the end of 2024. The correlative studies of the project, including the study of horse ATG pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics are nearly completed. The study for patients with hematologic malignancies requiring allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation and who are living with HIV has enrolled two patients before being placed on a clinical hold, but is in process of review by the data safety monitoring board with an amendment aimed at re-opening the study.

project_title: Development of new therapies for neuroblastoma
project_abstract_text: Harnessing tumor-targeting antibodies and NK cell activity in pediatric solid tumors: We developed immunocytokines and demonstrated that they have anti-neuroblastoma activity in preclinical models. We are in the process of translating our findings from these studies into a CTEP-sponsored trial in the POB. Developing cellular immunotherapies for neuroblastoma: We optimized a GPC2-targeted CAR T-cell therapy for the treatment of neuroblastoma. This work is actively being translated into an investigator-initiated first-in-human clinical trial for patients with neuroblastoma in the POB. To further optimize CAR T cell therapy, our laboratory focuses on CAR engineering to manipulate the CAR structure, conditionally alter CAR expression, and exploit the use of transgenic cytokines. We use genome-wide CRISPR screens to understand the mechanisms of tumor response to and evasion from adoptive CAR T therapy. Altogether, these efforts are geared towards finding new adoptive therapies to treat patients with neuroblastoma.

project_title: Eukaryotic Protein Maturation and Transport
project_abstract_text: Working with this protein technology core at the CSB we have been developing high-affinity binders to enable purification of complexes from native cellular expression. This work is allowing us to access the functionally most relevant forms of our targeted systems in a prior-knowledge blind fashion. Early work on the systems involved in control of protein folding at the ER membrane lead to complexes with novel components and suggest that there is much still to be learnt about the native functioning of these systems.

project_title: Structural biology collaborations
project_abstract_text: Key outcomes this year have been the determination of a series of structures giving insight into the mechanisms used by pathogenic bacteria to export virulence determinants (published in Nature Microbiology) and a series of drug-bound human receptor proteins that reveal key details of drug-inhibition (in revision for publication). Other projects are being prepared for publication and describe mechanisms by which folded RNAs are recognised by protein-binders in health and disease states and how RNA switches control activity in novel cells engineered for therapeutic benefits.

project_title: Dialogue between genomic instability and metabolism in diseases
project_abstract_text: Homologous recombination (HR) and poly ADP-ribosylation are partially redundant pathways for repair of DNA damage in normal and cancer cells. In cell lines that are deficient in HR, inhibition of poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP1/2) is a proven target with several PARP inhibitors (PARPi) currently in clinical use. Resistance to PARP inhibitors often develops, usually involving genetic alterations in DNA repair signaling cascades, but also metabolic rewiring particularly in HR-proficient cells. We surmised that alterations in metabolic pathways by cancer drugs such as Olaparib might be involved in the development of resistance to drug therapy. To test this hypothesis, we conducted a metabolism-focused CRISPR knockout (KO) screen to identify genes that undergo alterations during treatment of tumor cells with PARP inhibitors. Of about 3000 genes in the screen, our data revealed that mitochondrial pyruvate carrier 1 (MPC1) is an essential factor in desensitizing NSCLC lung cancer lines to PARP inhibition. In contrast to NSCLC lung cancer cells, triple-negative breast cancer cells do not exhibit such desensitization following MPC1 loss and reprogram the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation pathways to overcome PARP inhibitor treatment. Our findings unveil a previously unknown synergistic response between MPC1 loss and PARP inhibition in lung cancer cells. Metabolic pathways fuel tumor progression and resistance to stress conditions including chemotherapeutic drugs such as DNA damage response (DDR) inhibitors. Yet, significant gaps persist in how mammalian cells sense stress induced by DDR inhibition to initiate resistance mechanisms. Here, we employed a focused CRISPR knockout screen and identified metabolic vulnerabilities to DDR inhibitors. We unveiled Peroxiredoxin 1 (PRDX1) as a synthetic lethality partner with Ataxia Telangiectasia Mutated (ATM) kinase. Tumor cells depleted of PRDX1 displayed heightened sensitivity to ATM inhibition in vitro and in mice. The p53 status dictates the tumor cell response. Mechanistically, we discovered that the ribosomal protein RPL32 undergoes oxidation on Cysteines 91 and 96 upon disulfide stress induced by ATM inhibition promoting p53 stability and impaired cell survival. Our findings reveal a new death pathway whereby RPL32 senses disulfide stress and induces p53 activation impairing tumor cell survival.

project_title: Early Detection of Cancer Patients with Germline SDH Deficiency
project_abstract_text: We have now developed methods of collection and analysis of metabolic data for patient samples from patients with SDH-deficient GIST and patients with gremlin SDH subunit mutations and no evidence of GIST. We are beginning to compare the metabolic profiles of these patients and compare to available data on patients without germline SDH subunit mutations. We have collected cfDNA samples from these patients and are developing methods of cfDNA methylation analysis for patients with SDH-deficient GIST.

project_title: Implementation of telehealth and health technology to improve patient outcomes
project_abstract_text: We have recently initiated three clinical trials using telehealth and health related technologies to improve patient experience for those with primary brain tumors (PBTs) or primary central nervous system tumors (PCNSTs): The first trial will use describe sleep disturbances and circadian disruption in people with PBT using Fitbits to learn more about sleep disruptions caused by tumors. Participants in this trial will receive a Fitbit, which they will wear for one month to track sleep, heart rate, and activity, they will keep a sleep diary for one week, and complete 4 surveys with questions about the patient's quality of sleep, their ability to fall asleep and stay asleep, how the quality of their sleep affects their daily activities, and their sleep hygiene and preferences. We will assess the feasibility of using smart wearable devices to measure the impact of oncologic therapy on sleep and circadian rhythms in the PBT population. We will also assess if reported quality of sleep collected with the PROMIS Sleep Indices are comparable between clinical evaluation and collection at-home, if patient chronotype, as measured by the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ), are more pronounced in individuals with circadian disruption or sleep disturbances as measured by smart wearables, or if circadian rhythm variables (Amplitude and Phase onset/offset) are dampened or phase shifted in patients with moderate to severe levels of sleep disturbances (as measured by the MDASI-BT, score of >=5). This trial has begun enrolling participants by invitation. The second trial will assess whether a type of therapy called CALM can help patients with PCNST manage distress symptoms and the emotional challenges experienced with a tumor diagnosis. Participants will fill out 7 electronic surveys asking about physical and emotional symptoms, depression, feelings about death and dying, feelings about close relationships, and general well-being. Participants will be assigned to a CALM therapist and will have 3 to 6 individual therapy sessions in 6 months. To assess the effects of the CALM intervention in reduction of depressive symptoms we will compare PROMIS-Depression scale results in PCNST participants from baseline to 6 months. We will also assess the effects of CALM intervention on death anxiety at both 3 and 6 months using the Death and Dying Distress Scale (DADDS), and the feasibility of implementing CALM remotely in a PCNST population. This trial has begun enrolling participants by invitation. The third trial will assess if virtual reality (VR) technology can help reduce stress and improve mood in people with PBTs. Participants will receive a VR headset by mail, which they will use to view computer-generated environments, and they will complete questionnaires at 4 timepoints during the study. At the end of the study we will assess the number of participants who completed the study, the effects of a VR intervention on self-reported mood disturbance (as measured by PROMIS -Anxiety PROMIS -Depression Short Forms) and symptom burden and interference (as measured by the MD Anderson Symptom Inventory Brain Tumor [MDASI-BT]), if the effects VR has on distress and anxiety are more pronounced in those with high distress (based on DT cut-off score of greater than or equal to 5) compared those with to low distress (based on DT scores of 0 4) Measurement of Distress, the effects of a VR intervention on self-reported acute and subacute distress (as measured by the NCCN Distress Thermometer [DT]) and anxiety (as measured by the State Anxiety Inventory [STAI-6]) in PBT patients, and if the effects VR has on distress and anxiety are more pronounced in those individuals not on systemic corticosteroids (CS) compared to those who are not. This trial has begun recruiting participants. Interim analysis of both use of smart wearables (fitbit) and virtual reality headset have demonstrated that use is feasible in the primary brain tumor patient population.

project_title: CAR-T Therapy of Mesothelin Expressing Cancers
project_abstract_text: Bispecific antibodies targeting human mesothelin kill human cells expressing hMSLN in presence of human T cells and have anti-tumor activity in NSG mice in which a human mesothelioma cell line, RH63 is growing. The anti-tumor activity does not produce and complete responses. In a mouse model in which there are mouse T cells in the tumor, and the anti-CD3 recruits these cells and causes complete remissions after one dose. We attribute this response to the presence of mouse T cells in the tumor which are activated and bind to the tumor cells when BiTe is administered.

project_title: Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant for VEXAS
project_abstract_text: In our trial 'A Phase II Study of Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant for Subjects With VEXAS Syndrome' NCT05027945 in August 2021 our research objectives are: To determine whether allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) results in sustained donor engraftment at day 100 and one-year post-HSCT. To determine whether allogeneic HSCT results in reversal of the clinical phenotype of VEXAS at one year and two years post-HSCT without requiring interval prednisone at greater than 0.5 mg/kg per day for reasons other than graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). Eligibility: Recipients ages 18-75 year-old with or without a somatic mutation in UBA1 who have: 1) the clinical phenotype for VEXAS with refractory cutaneous, pulmonary, musculoskeletal, and/or other recurrent acute inflammatory manifestations, and 2) require greater than 0.5 mg/kg per day of prednisone for inflammatory manifestations OR have cytopenia (transfusion dependent anemia, transfusion dependent thrombocytopenia/platelets less than 75,000, neutropenia less than 1,000/uL) or myeloid neoplasm (by WHO criteria) or being intolerant or refractory to use steroids. Have an 8/8 or 7/8 HLA-matched related or unrelated donor, or a haploidentical related donor. Design: For Recipients with 8/8 HLA Matched Donors: Participants will receive reduced intensity conditioning with the following regimen: fludarabine 40 mg/m2 IV once daily for four days on days -6, -5, -4, -3 and Busulfan IV for three days on days -6, -5, -and -4 followed by HSCT on day 0. The busulfan dose will be based on pharmacokinetic levels from the test dose or real time PKs and will be targeted to an AUC of 3600-4800 microMol*min/L (52-65 mg*h/L) (3.2 mg/kg IV per day will be the default dose). For Recipients with 7/8 HLA Matched Donors or Haploidentical Related Donors: Participants will receive reduced intensity conditioning with the following regimen: fludarabine 30 mg/m2 IV once daily for five days on days -6, -5, -4, -3, and -2, cyclophosphamide 14.5 mg/kg for two days on days -6 and -5, 200 cGy total body irradiation (TBI) on day -1, busulfan IV once daily for two days on days -4 and -3, and HSCT on day 0. The busulfan dose will be based on pharmacokinetic levels from the test dose or real time PKs and will be targeted to an AUC of 3600-4800 microMol*min/L (52-65 mg*h/L) (3.2 mg/kg IV per day will be the default dose). For Post-Transplant GVHD Prophylaxis: Post-transplant GVHD prophylaxis in all groups will consist of cyclophosphamide 50 mg/kg IV once daily for 2 days on days +3 and +4, along with mycophenolate mofetil from day +5 to approximately day +35 and sirolimus from day +5 to approximately day +180.

project_title: Tumor heterogeneity in liver cancer
project_abstract_text: We understand tumor heterogeneity by single-cell and spatial profiling of liver tumors. With co-detection by indexing (CODEX) imaging technologies, we analyzed the interactions between tumor cells and immune cells based on their spatial proximity. Through this approach, we identified four subtypes of liver cancer patients with distinct clinical outcomes. This study was published in Hepatology. Additionally, we authored a review article discussing the heterogeneity in the liver cancer immune microenvironment from single-cell and spatial perspectives.

project_title: Tumor evolution in response to treatment
project_abstract_text: Tumor evolution is a major hurdle for effective cancer interventions. We understand tumor evolution by single-cell transcriptome profiling of longitudinal tumor biopsies from liver cancer patients. We determined a lineage score of malignant cells and an ecological score of their microenvironments. Using the two features, we classified tumors into four main states, which are associated with patient outcomes. This study was published in Cell Reports Medicine. We also contribute to review articles on immunotherapy for liver cancer patients.

project_title: DNA Replication and Repair
project_abstract_text: In our previous study, we have solved X-ray crystal structures of the FAM111A serine protease domain (SPD). Our biochemical and structural studies suggested that FAM111A SPD forms a homodimer through the alpha-1 helix at the N-terminus, where two subunits are held together through hydrophobic interactions to form an active dimer enzyme. To extend these studies to full-length FAM111A, we have produced and purified recombinant full-length FAM111A protein and examined its oligomerization status. Our study using size exclusion chromatography and mass photometry suggested that full-length FAM111A protein also forms a homodimer. Importantly, mutations at the dimerization interphase within the SPD disrupted this dimerization, suggesting that the alpha-1 helix at the N-terminus of SPD is the major dimerization site. These new data reveal the architecture of the FAM111A homodimer formation and raise a new concept that chemicals that can block dimer formation could be used as an inhibitor of FAM111A. These structural studies will facilitate the development of FAM111A inhibitors as a sensitizers of anti-cancer therapeutics including topoisomerase inhibitors.

project_title: Unsupervised image processing methods for cryoEM analysis in real time
project_abstract_text: Traditionally, imaging experiments involve a linear workflow with sample preparation followed by data acquisition and analysis. In this workflow, data acquisition is often conducted manually-a researcher sits at a microscope and decides which particle, cell or tissue section to image. These procedures not only make imaging experiments incredibly time and labour intensive, they also limit the volume of data that can be acquired and can create biased data sets. With the advent of robotics for sample preparation and completely automated microscopes, it is now time to upscale imaging experiments to generate larger and better data sets through integration of analysis during data acquisition.

project_title: Algorithms for atomic-resolution structure identification of nanocrystals
project_abstract_text: Ensembles of synthesized ligand-protected nanocrystals, each with a unique atomic structure, can be imaged tumbling in solution using Graphene-Liquid Cell Electron Microscopy (GLC-EM). Projection images of differently rotated nanocrystals are acquired using a direct electron detector with high temporal (< 2.5 ms) resolution. The analysis of time-series data of nanocrystals imaged in solution to obtain 3D structural information is an emerging field of research with great potential for improving our understanding of the physiochemical properties of nanocrystals, which thermodynamically deviate from the expectations derived from the bulk material. We previously developed a 'one-particle 3D reconstruction method' based on imaging of individual Pt nanocrystals rotating in solution and the use of Single-Particle Analysis (SPA) to obtain an ensemble of 3D reconstructions (Science 2015 and 2020). However, the standard SPA workflow cannot straightforwardly be applied to reconstruct atomic- resolution 3D density maps of the nanocrystals. A number of critical steps need to be addressed: (1) the individual nanocrystals need to be accurately tracked throughout the time-series and robust tracking algorithms have proven difficult to develop, (2) the strong interfering background of the GLC needs to be subtracted, (3) low-quality images that result from the nanocrystals moving vertically out of the narrow depth of focus of the aberration-corrected microscope need to be identified and rejected and (4) tailored strategies for 2D and 3D alignment and averaging that differ from those used in biological cryo-EM are needed.

project_title: Neoadjuvant Photoimmunotherapy in Head and Neck Cancer
project_abstract_text: We currently have the following clinical protocol ongoing: Phase 2, Open-label, Single-arm, Window of Opportunity Study of ASP-1929 Photoimmunotherapy with Fluorescence Imaging in Patients with Operable Primary or Recurrent Head and Neck or Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma. This is a phase 2 study, in which treatment is based on the application of ASP-1929 640 mg/m2 by intravenous (IV) infusion followed approximately 24 hours later by illumination (also termed as photoimmunotherapy [PIT]) of tumor(s) using the PIT690 Laser System with a 690 nm light dose of 50 J/cm2 for superficial illumination and 100 J/cm of diffuser length for interstitial illumination. During the illumination procedure, fluorescence of the IR700 portion of ASP-1929 will be imaged at a wavelength in the vicinity of 830 nm with a Shimadzu Fluorescence Imaging System camera. The camera is non-invasive and has no therapeutic effect. The light dose for tumor illumination is fixed and will not be altered in this study. Patients will undergo standard of care surgery approximately 21 days after ASP-1929 PIT treatment. To be eligible for the study, patients must be diagnosed with resectable primary or recurrent locoregional head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) or cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cuSCC) that is eligible for standard of care surgical resection. At least one target tumor must be amenable to photoimmunotherapy with the PIT690 Laser System and imaging with the Fluorescence Imaging System. Approximately 22 patients will be enrolled. The total study duration for an individual patient is approximately 25 months and consists of a Screening Period (up to 28 days). A treatment period consisting of ASP-1929 PIT treatment and standard of care surgery approximately 21 days later, and a post-surgery Follow-up Period consisting of a 30-day safety evaluation, efficacy assessments for 12 months, and survival assessments for 12 months after the efficacy follow-up period. The study will enroll patients with operable primary or recurrent HNSCC or cuSCC who will be treated with one ASP-1929 PIT treatment followed by standard of care surgery approximately 21 days later. This trial is designed as a 22-patient study. The key objectives are to determine the (1) efficacy and safety of ASP-1929 PIT treatment in the preoperative/window-of-opportunity setting and (2) ability of the Shimadzu Fluorescence Imaging System camera to capture and measure fluorescence loss of IR700 during light treatment of tumors. Patients with operable primary or recurrent HNSCC or cuSCC will be referred from area medical facilities. Eligibility for enrollment of patients in the study will be determined by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Principal Investigator. Each patient will be admitted as an inpatient at the NIH Clinical Center in Bethesda, MD for approximately 3 days and will be treated with a single ASP-1929 PIT treatment. The inpatient status is necessary to facilitate the testing required on study. Patients will return to their referring medical facility to receive standard of care surgical resection with or without chemotherapy or radiation approximately 21 days after ASP-1929 PIT treatment. The experimental procedure will only be performed at NIH, and standard of care treatment, which is not part of this protocol, will be performed at the referring sites. A safety assessment will be performed 30 days after surgery by the Investigator, and efficacy follow-up visits with tumor imaging will be performed every 3 months (Q3m) for up to 12 months. After the patient has completed or withdraws from the 12-month efficacy follow-up period, patient will be followed for survival (eg, by phone, public record, medical record) Q3m for up to 12 months. Safety data will be captured for all 22 patients through 30 days after surgery. Early stopping of this study will occur if more than 1 patient experiences a study treatment-related delay in standard of care surgery of greater than 28 days from the initially planned surgery date. Non-study treatment-related events that delay surgery will not necessitate trial stoppage. If a patient declines surgery after receiving ASP-1929 PIT treatment, trial stoppage will not occur. A statistical test is planned for the primary endpoint, the proportion of patients with pathologic tumor response-2 (pTR-2) based on the sample collected from resected ASP-1929 PIT-treated lesions at Day 21 in the Treated Population. The 95% Clopper-Pearson confidence interval of the proportion of pTR-2 will be calculated. If the lower-limit of the 95% Clopper-Pearson confidence interval is greater than 5%, then the null hypothesis that the proportion of pTR-2 is . 5% expected for patients without neoadjuvant PIT will be rejected. The primary objective of this study is to assess the efficacy of ASP-1929 PIT treatment prior to standard of care surgical tumor resection in patients with operable HNSCC or cuSCC by evaluating the proportion of pathologic tumor response-2 (pTR-2). pTR-2 is defined as the overall tumor bed having . 50% tumor-cell necrosis and keratinous debris with giant cell/histiocytic reaction (Uppaluri, 2020). The secondary objectives include determining efficacy of ASP-1929 PIT treatment in combination with standard of care surgical tumor resection on recurrence and survival, determining safety of ASP-1929 PIT treatment as neoadjuvant by evaluating proportion of patients with surgery delay due to study treatment, and the frequency of treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) related to ASP-1929 PIT treatment. Another secondary objective is to determine the feasibility of using the Shimadzu Fluorescence Imaging System for real-time recording of the fluorescence of the IR700 portion of ASP-1929 while the tumor is being illuminated with the PIT690 Laser System by determining time to maximal fluorescence loss (TMFL) of IR700 and evaluating the proportion of patients with an index lesion successfully imaged. Successful imaging of IR700 fluorescence is defined as obtaining serial fluorescence images from the PIT-treated lesion over time. Statistical hypothesis test is planned to detect the proportion of pTR-2 that is greater than the minimally expected threshold (5%).

project_title: Investigating mechanisms of bladder tumorigenesis and therapeutic resistance
project_abstract_text: The focus of my research program is to explore molecular mechanisms and delineate therapeutically actionable pathways in bladder cancer. Aim 1: Molecular and phenotypic characterization of genomic alterations. We are using high-throughput CRISPR-mediated DNA editing, activation, and interference tools for massively parallel genetic manipulations of cells in vitro and in vivo to understand the role of genomic alterations in malignant cell transformation, tumor subtype speciation, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, metastasis, and interaction with therapies. Aim 2: Mechanisms that cause genomic alterations. To this end, we specifically focus on the role of innate immunity involving antiviral enzymes such as APOBEC3s. These deaminases have been implicated as major drivers of mutagenesis and other genomic alterations in certain cancers, including bladder cancer. We are using integrative multi-omics and functional approaches to: a) Identify extrinsic and intrinsic factors that prevent or promote the APOBEC-mediated mutational process; b) Investigate the role of these enzymes in driving tumor evolution, heterogeneity, and resistance/response to therapies; c) Test whether these enzymes are druggable.

project_title: Using artificial intelligence and MRI to address limitations in glioblastoma
project_abstract_text: This project has several facets: 1) tumor segmentation and progression which has been partially completed and has been published (Belue, M.J.; Harmon, S.A.; Chappidi, S.; Zhuge, Y.; Tasci, E.; Jagasia, S.; Joyce, T.; Camphausen, K.; Turkbey, B.; Krauze, A.V. Diagnosing Progression in Glioblastoma-Tackling a Neuro-Oncology Problem Using Artificial-Intelligence-Derived Volumetric Change over Time on Magnetic Resonance Imaging to Examine Progression-Free Survival in Glioblastoma. Diagnostics 2024, 14, 1374.). 2) linking imaging features to molecular features (MGMT methylation status) in local and publicly available data sets. 3) the conversion of cone beam CT acquired on the linear accelerators when patients get treated with radiation, to conventional CT and possibly to MRI to enlarge available data sets. This work is being currently presented at American Association Of Physicists In Medicine (AAPM). 4) data sharing towards federated learning efforts with the Federated Tumor Segmentation (FeTS) initiative. We have now successfully segmented our imaging scans post full de-identification and verified this. We will also be contributing our data towards the post operative segmentation challenge in gliobalstoma.

project_title: Proteogenomic characterization and biomarker discovery in glioblastoma
project_abstract_text: Work on this is ongoing with our collaborators. We have completed our work on valproic acid as a clinical feature with impact on the serum proteome. This work was published (Krauze, A.V.; Zhao, Y.; Li, M.-C.; Shih, J.; Jiang, W.; Tasci, E.; Cooley Zgela, T.; Sproull, M.; Mackey, M.; Shankavaram, U.; et al. Revisiting Concurrent Radiation Therapy, Temozolomide, and the Histone Deacetylase Inhibitor Valproic Acid for Patients with Glioblastoma-Proteomic Alteration and Comparison Analysis with the Standard-of-Care Chemoirradiation. Biomolecules 2023, 13, 1499.). Work is now ongoing on newly acquired metabolomic data for the same patient cohort.

project_title: Prognostic and predictive clinical and proteomic biomarker discovery in GBM
project_abstract_text: This work is ongoing with two specific directions: 1) Analysis the relationships between serum measured proteomic and metabolomic signals and patient outcomes ( overall survival and progression free survival) - this is work we are carrying out collaboration with Computational and Systems Biology Branch (CSBB). New metabolomic data has now become available and we are now linking this to proteomic data. This data type is novel, with biological annotation evolving and thus linkages will represent a major steps in understanding how to handle the data and how to interpret results from a clinical lens. 2) Aanalysis of the relationships between serum measured proteomic and metabolomic signals and patterns of tumor progression as defined using volumetric segmentation on MRI of the brain. - this is work we are carrying out with Computational Genomics and Bioinformatics Branch (CGBB). Using AI methodology we volumetrically segmented MRI brain for tumor volumes and calculated the rate of the volumes over the natural history of the disease. This was published (Belue, M.J.; Harmon, S.A.; Chappidi, S.; Zhuge, Y.; Tasci, E.; Jagasia, S.; Joyce, T.; Camphausen, K.; Turkbey, B.; Krauze, A.V. Diagnosing Progression in Glioblastoma-Tackling a Neuro-Oncology Problem Using Artificial-Intelligence-Derived Volumetric Change over Time on Magnetic Resonance Imaging to Examine Progression-Free Survival in Glioblastoma. Diagnostics 2024, 14, 1374.) Now we are linking the imaging patterns observed in the aforementioned analysis to omic signals measured in the serum of patients with glioblastoma.

project_title: Generating a multi-channel data framework for AI analysis in Radiation therapy
project_abstract_text: This project is ongoing has made progress this year in that we were able ,with the help of several collaborators, to surface radiation therapy data from the radiation therapy treatment planning system. Several barriers of siloed data had to be overcome to achieve this. The data is now surfaced but given that it spans 20 years, significant variability exists . The organisation of this data to ensure structuring for computational analysis is present or can be derived, is ongoing. We are also in the process of computational structuring to allow the data to be robustly queried for dose to organs at risk and dose coverage in various malignancies treated at NCI NIH over time.

project_title: Advancing clinically meaningful AI algorithms to improve oncologic outcomes
project_abstract_text: The aim of this project is two fold:1) to generate algorithms with superior performance that specifically target complex, multidimensional data and 2) to evaluate and optimise algorithmic interpretability. Both items are unmet needs in oncology. The data available to us at NCI NIH makes the study of both possible by providing unprecedented data depth for each subject on study and allowing evaluation of specific findings for clinical and statistical interpretability. To this end my lab has focused on item 1) by employing known molecular prognostic features (MGMT methylation status) or promising evolving biomarkers (CD133) in relationship to both known and novel proteomic features measured in the serum of patients with glioblastoma to determine which features (measured molecules) in large scale proteomic data are directly linked MGMT methylation status or in the case of CD133, cancer stem cell presence. MGMT status is a clinical feature, captured in tumor tissue at the time of resection. It was evaluated towards serum altered molecules with concurrent chemoirradiation which is standard of care and biological signaling pathways to address item 2) - interpretability both with knows clinical data and with publicly available proteomic data from tumor tissue in the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC). This work was published earlier this year (Tasci, E.; Shah, Y.; Jagasia, S.; Zhuge, Y.; Shephard, J.; Johnson, M.O.; Elemento, O.; Joyce, T.; Chappidi, S.; Cooley Zgela, T.; et al. MGMT ProFWise: Unlocking a New Application for Combined Feature Selection and the Rank-Based Weighting Method to Link MGMT Methylation Status to Serum Protein Expression in Patients with Glioblastoma. Int. J. Mol. Sci. 2024, 25, 4082. ). In addition, we wanted to explore how specific signals which we already know are associated with tumor aspects and biological behaviour, eg the presence of stem cells, may be linked to each other and outcomes when captured in serum as noninvasive means of biospecimen acquisition. This work was carried out for serum CD133 and has been accepted for publication but is not yet in print.

project_title: Control of Oncogenic Signaling Through Spatial Organization of Kinases and mRNAs
project_abstract_text: Our research is organized into two inter-related subprojects. First, we are characterizing perinuclear, ER-tethered signaling endosomes containing oncogenic kinases that are observed in all cancer cells. We found that oncogenic RAS induces perinuclear translocation of the effector kinases ERK1/2 and CK2 and their signaling scaffold, KSR1. These proteins form signaling hubs termed perinuclear signaling centers (PSCs) on endosomes embedded within the perinuclear ER network. PSCs are observed in all tumor cell lines and tissues examined but not in normal cells, suggesting that PSCs function as key signaling platforms. We showed that an endosomal adapter, TOLLIP, is required for perinuclear localization of RAB11A+ endosomes harboring CK2 and KSR1 but not ERK. ERK resides on a distinct endosomal population. TOLLIP associates with KSR1 through conserved domains on each protein, recruiting signaling complexes to endosomes. Phospho-proteomic studies revealed that TOLLIP-dependent perinuclear CK2 phosphorylates distinct substrates, including proteins involved translation and ribosome biogenesis. Thus, perinuclear CK2 plays an important role in generating onco-phosphoproteomes in tumor cells. Cancer cell lines carrying KRAS or NRAS oncogenes but not mutant HRAS, BRAF or PTEN require TOLLIP for proliferation/survival. Accordingly, KRasG12V-driven lung tumors in Tollip KO/KO mice displayed reduced progression to malignant adenocarcinomas. TOLLIP is therefore a key signaling adaptor selectively required by K/NRAS tumor cells whose inhibition is a potential liability of these cancers. We are currently engaged in drug discovery studies using TOLLIP as a target for small molecule inhibitors. Although cancer cells carrying oncogenes other than K and NRAS are TOLLIP independent, they nevertheless display perinuclear CK2, suggesting that another adapter provides a redundant function. Moreover, ERK does not co-localize with TOLLIP and remains perinuclear in its absence. Initial results indicate that ERK2 associates with another endosomal adapter that anchors ERK endosomes to the ER. Future studies will focus on identifying additional adapters for ERK, CK2 and other kinases, as these may be dependency genes for specific cancers or oncogenes and could be targets for anti-cancer drugs. Secondly, we are studying the mechanisms by which 3'UTRs in mRNAs can regulate the activity of the encoded protein. 3'UTR regulation of protein activity (UPA) was first demonstrated by our observation that the CEBPB 3'UTR inhibits RAS-induced post-translational activation of C/EBPb in tumor cells. UPA constrains the pro-senescence activity of C/EBPb and its ability to induce pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) genes such as IL6. UPA requires a G/U-rich element (GRE) in the CEBPB 3'UTR and its cognate binding protein, HuR. These components exclude CEBPB mRNAs from perinuclear ERK1/2 and CK2 signaling endosomes, preventing newly translated C/EBPb from accessing its activating kinases. Using GRE affinity purification, we identified the RNA decay proteins Upf1 and Staufen as essential UPA factors enriched within the perinuclear cytoplasm. Together with HuR, these proteins promote perinuclear decay of CEBPB transcripts. UPF1 or STAU1/2 depletion in tumor cells increased the abundance of perinuclear CEBPB mRNAs, coinciding with activation of C/EBPb and senescence. These perinuclear transcripts were often adjacent to CK2 foci, suggesting that when UPA is disabled the proximity of CEBPB transcripts and activating kinases facilitates phosphorylation of locally translated C/EBPb. We identified a Staufen binding site (SBS) adjacent to the GRE which, when deleted, activates the pro-senescence function of C/EBPb and phosphorylation by CK2 without appreciable induction of SASP genes. Deleting the GRE also stimulates senescence but not phosphorylation by CK2 or SASP gene expression. These observations indicate that multiple distinct 3'UTR sequences are involved in repressing specific C/EBPb functions, probably by inhibiting different phospho-modifications. STAU1/2 and UPF1 colocalize prominently with CK2 endosomes in tumor cells, suggesting that mRNA decay factors are tethered to signaling endosomes. Thus, particular 3'UTR elements could promote mRNA decay near (or transport from) distinct signaling endosomes and thus inhibit phosphorylation on specific sites. Future studies will expand on the relationship between individual 3'UTR motifs, mRNA decay/transport near perinuclear kinases, and inhibition of PTMs on the encoded protein. We are particularly interested in characterizing the CEBPB 3'UTR sequence that suppresses expression of pro-inflammatory genes. To test the in vivo relevance of UPA, we generated mice carrying a deletion of the Cebpb GRE region and challenged the animals in a KrasG12D model of lung tumorigenesis. Although delGRE mice had normal levels of benign adenomas, malignant adenocarcinomas were strongly reduced, coinciding with increased senescence in tumor areas. These findings provide the first in vivo evidence that UPA constrains C/EBPb tumor suppressor activity to facilitate malignant progression in cancer. A key goal is to determine whether UPA is a general mechanism that regulates other proteins. p53 is one such candidate, as it undergoes activation by oncogenic RAS in OIS cells and its 3'UTR contains a U-rich element that binds HuR. We found that the TP53 3'UTR suppresses the cytostatic activity of p53 in tumor cells. Similar to C/EBPb, the TP53 3'UTR excludes transcripts from the kinase-rich perinuclear region and inhibits p53 phosphorylation on an activating CK2 site, Ser392. Endogenous TP53 transcripts localize away from the perinuclear kinase-rich region in tumor cells but become perinuclear in senescent fibroblasts and in cancer cells treated with chemotherapeutic DNA-damaging agents, correlating with increased phosphorylation on Ser392. Silencing of the p53 ubiquitin ligase and oncoprotein, MDM2, also caused p53 transcripts to become perinuclear and induced p-Ser392. indicating that MDM2 restrains p53 activity both directly (through protein degradation) and indirectly (via UPA). In summary, two pro-senescence transcription factors, C/EBPb and p53, are inhibited by 3'UTR-dependent mRNA localization in cancer cells. We propose that the UPA mRNA localization mechanism is a promising target for development of novel anti-cancer agents.

project_title: Interrogating genetic interactions  dependencies in renal cell carcinoma
project_abstract_text: We have established our Cas9-Cas12a CHyMErA combinatorial screening system in various patient-derived renal cell carcinoma (RCC) cell lines.
