Expression of Cas nucleases have been verified by western blotting and editing efficiency of the cell lines has been confirmed. Screens with genome-scale gene knockout libraries have been performed to identify fitness genes across various environmental and genetic backgrounds. Validation and follow-up analysis of screen hits in progress. Furthermore, we have generated and screened a focused genetic interaction library. Data analysis and follow-up analysis is under way.

project_title: Combinatorial CRISPR transcriptional perturbation screening platform
project_abstract_text: We have successfully cloned transcriptional repressor and activator domains into lentiviral expression vectors carrying various catalytically inactive CRISPR-Cas nucleases (Cas9 and Cas12a variants). Various cell lines have been transduced with CRISPRi & CRISPRa constructs and nuclease expression has been verified by western blotting. Editing efficiency of individual effectors have been verified by assessing expression of cell surface markers by flow cytometry. Current work focuses on systematic comparison of different modes of effector domain expression as well as single vs. combinatorial targeting of genes.

project_title: Establishing combinatorial screening platform coupled to single-cell analysis
project_abstract_text: We have iteratively optimized our hybrid guide RNA expression cassette and sequencing library protocols to enable efficient capture of Cas9 and Cas12a guide RNAs using 10x Genomics reagents during single-cell analysis. The guide design and sequencing library protocols have now been fully optimized and we are in the process of perform large-scale genetic screening with single-cell transcriptomic readouts, thereby allowing us to gain mechanistic insights into the cellular rewiring in response to single or combined genetic perturbations.

project_title: Improving editing efficiency and guide design of CHyMErA screening platform
project_abstract_text: We have developed cell lines expressing various Cas12a variants and screened them using our Cas9-Cas12a CHyMErA platform combined with a hgRNA library. This approach allowed us to compare the editing efficiency and precision of different Cas12a variants within our screening system. Our findings demonstrated significant editing improvements with new Cas12a variants, which were further validated through focused experiments. Subsequently, genome-scale screens were conducted using the enhanced screening platform to identify fitness exons and genes across diverse cancer cell lines. In addition to optimizing Cas nucleases, we conducted screens to enhance and diversify the hgRNA scaffold, facilitating guide multiplexing necessary for higher-order genetic interaction mapping. We are also working on improving our guide design algorithms, focusing on more accurate on-target scoring to achieve higher genome editing efficiency and precision. Parallel to these efforts, we compiled a comprehensive collection of potential Cas9 and Cas12a target sites in the human and mouse genomes. Guide sequences were scored for on- and off-target properties, and these data, along with genomic features and scores, were uploaded to an online database. Our ongoing work aims to make these databases searchable in a time-efficient manner, providing an online tool that enables easy and efficient design of individual or large-scale guides for Cas9 and Cas12a nucleases, supporting numerous genome editing applications.

project_title: The role of structural variation in promotion, evolution and treatment of various tumor types
project_abstract_text: Recently we used long-read sequencing to characterize complex amplification patterns in cervical cancer cell lines, in collaboration with Michael Dean's lab. Cervical cancer is caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, has few approved targeted therapeutics, and is the most common cause of cancer death in low-resource countries. We characterized 19 cervical and four head and neck cancer cell lines using long-read DNA and RNA sequencing and identified the HPV types, HPV integration sites, chromosomal alterations, and cancer driver mutations. Structural variation analysis revealed telomeric deletions associated with DNA inversions resulting from breakage-fusion-bridge (BFB) cycles. BFB is a common mechanism of chromosomal alterations in cancer, and our study applies long-read sequencing to this important chromosomal rearrangement type. Analysis of the inversion sites revealed staggered ends consistent with exonuclease digestion of the DNA after breakage. Some BFB events are complex, involving inter- or intra-chromosomal insertions or rearrangements. None of the BFB breakpoints had telomere sequences added to resolve the dicentric chromosomes, and only one BFB breakpoint showed chromothripsis. Five cell lines have a chromosomal region 11q BFB event, with YAP1-BIRC3-BIRC2 amplification. Indeed, YAP1 amplification is associated with a 10-year-earlier age of diagnosis of cervical cancer and is three times more common in African American women. This suggests that individuals with cervical cancer and YAP1-BIRC3-BIRC2 amplification, especially those of African ancestry, might benefit from targeted therapy. In summary, we uncovered valuable insights into the mechanisms and consequences of BFB cycles in cervical cancer using long-read sequencing.

project_title: Examining IL-15 and IL-7 as an immunotherapy agent in cancer and AIDS
project_abstract_text: Understanding the cellular mechanisms controlling gene expression shed new light in the biology and regulation of IL-15, led to the identification of the bioactive heterodimeric form of IL-15 and provided methods for the efficient production (Bergamaschi, J. Biol. Chem., 2008; Blood 2012) and first-in-human clinical trials of hetIL-15 in metastatic cancers (Conlon, J. Immunother. Cancer, 2021), and also in combination with anti-PD-1 check point inhibitor (NCT02452268; collaboration with Novartis; Leidner, J Immunother Cancer, 2023). We have shown that hetIL-15 greatly increases lymphocyte infiltration in several tumors in mouse models and in macaques, suggesting a general method to increase lymphocyte infiltration, which is associated with anti-tumor activity. hetIL-15 is extensively studied in mouse tumor models where we demonstrated the rapid interaction of lymphoid and myeloid cell networks resulting in changes in numbers and migration of different cell populations. Extensive transcriptomics and proteomics analysis has revealed additional pathways affected by hetIL-15 (Bergamaschi, J. Immunother. Cancer, 2020; Cancers, 2021). We have studied the effects of hetIL-15 on the number and properties of Dendritic Cells (DC) in tumors of mice. DC participate in a network of cells that are induced during hetIL-15 treatment and in turn support more recruitment of effector cells in tumor sites. Locoregional monotherapy with hetIL-15 in a triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) orthotopic mouse model resulted in tumor eradication in 40% of mice, reduction of metastasis and induction of immunological memory against breast cancer cells (Stellas, Karaliota, Cell Reports, 2023). hetIL-15 reshaped the tumor microenvironment by promoting the intratumoral accumulation of cytotoxic lymphocytes, conventional type 1 DC (cDC1s) and a DC population expressing both CD103 and CD11b markers. These CD103intCD11b+DCs share phenotypic and gene expression characteristics with both cDC1s and cDC2s, have transcriptomic profiles, similar to monocyte-derived DCs and correlate with tumor regression. Thus, hetIL-15, a cytokine directly affecting lymphocytes and inducing cytotoxic cells, has also an indirect rapid and significant effect on the recruitment of myeloid cells, initiating a cascade for tumor elimination through innate and adoptive immune mechanisms. The intratumoral CD103intCD11b+DC induced by hetIL-15 may be the target for the development of additional cancer immunotherapy approaches. Our studies showed that DC populations correlate with tumor regression and reveal additional beneficial effects of hetIL-15 in inducing or enhancing long term protective immune response against tumors. We evaluated the therapeutic efficacy of hetIL-15 immunotherapy as monotherapy and found tumor eradication in 40% of mice and increased survival. Analysis of intratumoral lymphocytes showed they have reduced metabolic fitness caused by the tumor microenvironment and hetIL-15 was able to improve their metabolism. To further strengthen the cytotoxic function of the tumor-infiltrating cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, we tested combination with Fenofibrate, a PPAR-alpha agonist in the murine EO771 orthotopic breast cancer model. Monotherapy with Fenofibrate (FF) had no effect on tumor growth in this model, whereas the Fenofibrate/hetIL-15 combination resulted in complete eradication of the tumors in 85% of mice. We found that the combination treatment increased the mitochondrial function, Fatty Acid uptake and oxygen consumption rate, supporting a more metabolically active phenotype. Combination therapy reshaped the tumor microenvironment. Our data suggest that metabolic reprogramming of tumor specific CD8+T cells using FF is a promising strategy to overcome T cell 'exhaustion' and to promote survival in a metabolically hostile tumor microenvironment. We are further dissecting this mechanism. In addition to cancer immunotherapy, IL-15 has generated strong interest for clinical use to treat HIV infection, especially in protocols targeting viral eradication or a functional cure in the macaque model. This is based onIL-15's effects as a growth factor and key regulator of cytotoxic responses mediated by both the innate (NK cells) and the CTL. Importantly, hetIL-15 promotes the entrance of cytotoxic (GrzB+) CD8+ T cells in the B cell follicles, areas within the LN where CTL are typically excluded and where SIV/HIV infected follicular helper CD4+ T cells reside. hetIL-15 treatment led to significant decrease in cell-associated viral RNA within the LN and in plasma viremia in SHIV infected macaques (Watson, PLoS Pathog., 2018). In a collaborative effort, we further reported that an IL-15 transcriptional signature response to a viral RhCMV/SIV vaccine strongly correlated with protection (Barrenas, PLoS Pathog, 2021). We expanded this concept and are testing the contribution of a combinatorial treatment including hetIL-15 in reducing reservoir in the SIV infected ART-treated macaques, together with several Martin Delaney collaboratories supported by NIAID including ERASE-HIV, BEAT-HIV, and PAVE. Our studies showed that a combinatorial treatment including anti-PD-1 and NAb led to reduction of the viral reservoir. Detailed underlying mechanisms are being investigated and treatment regimens are being improved in on-going study. These pre-clinical data demonstrate that harnessing the immune system using different immunological interventions during ART-treatment can play a critical role the reduction of the reservoir and the control of viremia. We continue to work on optimizing this proof-of-concept study. IL-7 is also a homeostatic cytokine, belonging to the gamma-chain family. Similar to IL-15, we employed a dose-escalation regimen in rhesus macaques to deliver bio-produced purified fully glycosylated macaque IL-7, a cytokine critical for development and maintenance of T lymphocytes (Pandit, iScience, 2023). We showed that IL-7 increased proliferation and survival of T cells and triggered several chemokines and cytokines. Induction of CXCL13 in lymph nodes (LN) led to a remarkable increase of B cells, proliferation of germinal center Tfh cells and elevated IL-21 levels inducing in turn an increase in follicle activity. Transcriptomics analysis showed induction of IRF-7 and Flt3L, which was linked to increased frequency of circulating pDC upon IL-7 treatment. These pDC expressed higher levels of CCR7, homed to LN, and were associated with upregulation of type-1 interferon gene signature and increased production of IFN-alpha2a with TLR stimulation. Together, our results indicate that IL-7 therapy acts at different levels in the immune system involving both lymphoid and myeloid compartments. T cell immunity could be strengthened by promoting redistribution, survival, and proliferation of T cells, whereas the influx of B cells and Tfh activation can result in improved humoral immune responses. The role of IL-7 at the interface of cell and humoral adaptive immunity can be exploited in vaccine strategies and in immunotherapeutic regimens. Because IL-7 functions at the apex of lymphopoiesis in the bone marrow and is crucial for LN activation, our findings demonstrate the importance of delineating the systemic effects of IL-7 beyond its direct targets, which is part of on-going work. Together, IL-7 treatment promoted proliferation of T cells and increase of B lymphocytes in LN together with activated Tfh cells and pDC producing type-1 interferon, an immune landscape that is the potential to enhance cellular and humoral adaptive immune responses. The combination of IL-7 and hetIL-15 treatment is currently under evaluation in our group, and also in collaborative macaque experiments with extramural investigators and consortia.

project_title: A Phase II Trial of PT-112 in Subjects with Thymoma and Thymic Carcinoma
project_abstract_text: PT-112, an inhibitor of ribosomal biogenesis, offers a unique set of properties of both cellular interaction and molecular antitumor mechanisms, including resistance to DNA repair pathways and induction of immunogenic cell death. In phase I trials, PT-112 has demonstrated clinical activity in patients with recurrent TETs. This single-arm phase II trial has been designed to evaluate the safety and clinical activity of PT-112 in patients with recurrent TETs. After a recent protocol amendment PT-112 is administered intravenously on days 1 and 15 of a 28-day cycle at a dose of 360 mg/m2 (Cycle 1) followed by administration on day 1 of subsequent 28-day cycles at a dose of 250 mg/m2, until disease progression or development of intolerable adverse events. Fourteen patients have been enrolled to date. One partial response has been observed in a participant with recurrent thymoma, disease stabilization has been observed in 9 participants and progressive disease in 4 participants. Treatment is well tolerated and adverse events such as nausea, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia are manageable. Peripheral neuropathy was a common adverse event with the original dosing schedule (days 1, 8 , and 15 at 360 mg/m2), but the frequency and intensity of peripheral neuropathy is much reduced with the new dosing schedule NCT05104736.

project_title: Classification and Ontology of Macromolecular Complexes in Liquid Biopsies
project_abstract_text: This is a continuing project, started in 2021-2022 in response to ongoing requests from researchers across the biomedical research space to provide input on the design and interpretation of 'exosome' studies, pertaining to various diseases. This large, collaborative initiative, encompassing the EV biology and Liquid Biopsy/Molecular Diagnostics communities, and will engage with regulatory communities working with 'exosome' metrology, diagnostics, and therapeutics resulted in 1) an updated extracellular ontological framework in the 2023 MISEV Guidelines, Welsh JA et al, JEV 2024, and 2) ongoing ontology harmonization efforts across international working groups.

project_title: New algorithms for long-read cancer genomics
project_abstract_text: We are now actively working on two new algorithms for structural variant and copy-number variant detection using long-read tumor sequencing data. Severus is a method for the accurate detection of different types of somatic SVs using a phased breakpoint graph approach. To benchmark various short- and long-read SV detection methods, we sequenced five tumor/normal cell line pairs with Illumina, Nanopore, and PacBio sequencing platforms; on this benchmark Severus showed the highest F1 scores (harmonic mean of the precision and recall) as compared to long-read and short-read methods. We then applied Severus to three clinical cases of pediatric cancer, demonstrating concordance with known genetic findings as well as revealing clinically relevant cryptic rearrangements missed by standard genomic panels.

project_title: Population-scale, long-read characterization of human genome and microbiome
project_abstract_text: NIH CARD center is currently aiming to sequence thousands of human brain samples with nanopore sequencing technology, to explore structural variation and methylation distribution on a population scale. My group is developing algorithms to analyze the generated sequencing data. Our group have developed and maintain multiple software packages, such as Flye and Hapdup. In another collaboration, we are exploring the mechanisms of structural variation in bacteria from the human gut microbiome. Bacterial strains or clones may be distringuished by complex recombination regions with arrays of inversions and deletions. We are developing assembly-based algorithms to detect these rearranged regions from long-read metagenomic sequencing data.

project_title: Chromatin Regulation in Brain Development and Disease
project_abstract_text: During FY2024, we made significant progress on this research project. In one part of the research project, we are using molecular and genomic approaches to understand the function of the neuron-specific forms of DNA methylation, mCA and hmCG. We are investigating why these modifications accumulate in neurons, what proteins associate with these modifications, how these modifications regulate transcription and genome integrity, and how mutations in regulators of DNA methylation lead to neurodevelopmental disorders and cancer. During FY2024, we made significant progress investigating how mCA affects protein binding in neurons. MeCP2 was the only known mCA-binding protein, and it was unknown whether mCA blocks the binding of proteins to DNA, like mCG does. We identified new proteins that bind to mCA DNA as well as proteins that are blocked by mCA from binding DNA, many of which are implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders and cancer. We also gained new insight into why mCA accumulates in neurons but not in other cell types. A second part of the research project is focused on a specific methyl-DNA-binding protein, MeCP2. Loss-of-function mutations in MeCP2 cause the neurodevelopmental disorder Rett syndrome, and MeCP2 is overexpressed in multiple cancers. To investigate the function of MeCP2, we developed an approach to rapidly degrade the MeCP2 protein in the mouse brain. We are using this approach to distinguish the primary consequences of MeCP2 loss from the secondary consequences of neurological impairment. During FY2024, we performed RNA-seq at timepoints after MeCP2 degradation in the brain and found that genes with high mCA levels are upregulated 24 hours after degradation. We next plan to study the effects of rapid MeCP2 protein degradation on other molecular and cellular changes, including histone modifications and DNA damage. These experiments are providing insight into the primary function of MeCP2, and this approach can be broadly applied to other proteins implicated in neurological disease.

project_title: Biology of AR+ prostate cancer metastases and the role of the microenvironment
project_abstract_text: This project has resulted in the establishment of various human prostate cancer metastasis models, including several models that are AR dependent and others that demonstrate lineage transformations. The basis of the ability to establish such models is the use of PDX models and the application of organoid growth technologies. The models are highly reproducible and allow for the first time, the role of AR in bone metastasis to be addressed. The details of the models have been published. We anticipate unique and important utility to the prostate cancer community.

project_title: Germline-Somatic Interactions and Association with Treatment Response in Cancer
project_abstract_text: Systematic Review: We are completing a systematic review and meta-analysis of published pan-cancer germline-somatic associations (PROSPERO ID: CRD42022326884). Out of 8,614 publications, we identified only 227 that reported both germline and somatic variants and even studied any association to an outcome in more than 10 study participants or tumor samples. This systematic review has finished data extraction and is moving onto consensus and initial data generation. Validation Infrastructure: The first part of this framework is in progress. We are using the NIH Integrated Data Analysis Platform (NIDAP), an enterprise-wide, cloud-based data relation, aggregation, and analysis platform, to test associations between germline and somatic variants and treatment response. We have identified four breast cancer-specific datasets in which both germline and somatic sequencing of any kind was performed and reported, and treatment responses are reported at the participant level. The Pan-Cancer Atlas breast cancer TCGA dataset includes 779 early-stage patients with basic treatment information and progression-free interval. Of note, however, this treatment information was updated in 2018, prior to the approvals of at least 12 medications used in current standard-of-care breast cancer treatment. We described the early-stage FUSCC-BRCA multi-omics cohort analysis above, which includes distant metastasis-free survival.33 The AURORA-US dataset includes 55 patients with primary and subsequent metastatic disease, all of whom underwent DNA whole-exome sequencing and data to calculate progression-free intervals. The Metastatic Breast Cancer (MBC) Project from Dana Farber and the Broad institute includes 240 patients with treatment category information and duration of response (over or under 2 years). We have also selected 144 patients from the Personalized Oncogenomics Program who had advanced metastatic breast cancer with published variant calls, treatments given, and duration of response. We are evaluating the feasibility of our framework by testing the germline-somatic interactions associated with treatment response in our systematic review using linear or logistic regression. The independent variables are the presence or absence of germline genetic variant(s) and somatic variant(s) (binary variables), an interaction term, and basic clinical covariates (age of diagnosis, race, breast cancer subtype, stage). The dependent variable is the continuous time-related outcomes from these datasets, or for MBC, the binary variable of responding to treatment for more than 2 years.

project_title: Discovery of novel protein complexes across human gut bacteria
project_abstract_text: We have begun to generate whole-cell protein-protein interaction maps of the pathogen Salmonella enterica. We are using proteome fractionation that we are subjecting to co-fractionation MS, crosslinking MS and evolutionary contact analysis. This will combine into a deep interactome with residue-level structural resolution. This project is still in the early stages so does not have many results to report. In parallel, we are using metabolically incorporated photo-amino acids containing diazirine groups crosslink to nearby residues when they are activated with UV-light. We are using Metabolic incorporation to stochastically incorporate photoLeucine at leucine sites. The leucine T-RNA synthase will accept this. We have managed to get the incorporation rate up to over 5%. Here we have some preliminary data from the salmonella proteome where we have mapped the photoleucine crosslinks onto some AlphaFold2 models. We are focusing on the interactome of the RNA polymerase which is a target for antibiotics.

project_title: The topology of protein-protein interactions in situ in eukaryotic cells
project_abstract_text: Significant progress is being made on the protein interactome of both the proteasome interactome and the MYC interactome. We have made stable cell lines for both genetically tagged MYC and subunits of the proteasome. We have identified new binders of the proteasome by proteomics and are in the process of validating their function on the proteasome, including structure by cryo-EM. We are also targeting the interaction network of the proto-oncoprotein MYC. MYC's disorder and 'stickiness' have both served to frustrate confident identification of binders and mapping their binding site. Crosslinking MS will discover these protein-protein interactions (PPIs) with residue-level structural information and so suggest potential avenues for their therapeutic disruption.

project_title: Targeting cancer neoantigens in patients with myeloid malignancies
project_abstract_text: The main goal our research project is to develop neoantigen-directed adoptive cell transfer (ACT) for patients suffering with myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and other myeloid/hematologic cancers. To achieve this, two approaches are used: (1) developing a personalized next-generation sequencing-based platform for identification and validation of cancer neoantigens in patients with myeloid cancers, and (2) using peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) from healthy donors with select common class I HLA types in an attempt to isolate T cell receptors (TCRs) that target common mutations in hematologic (and select solid) malignancies restricted to these HLA molecules.

project_title: DNA methylation-based machine classification of cancer
project_abstract_text: Building on preliminary data I have generated from publicly-accessible DNA methylation data and in combination with data generated through the NCI Laboratory of Pathology, I will develop organ-specific methylation bioinformatic pipelines and machine learning-based classifiers, using the previously described methodology. Additionally, I will perform a large-scale combined analysis to assess the feasibility of a Pan-cancer DNA methylation classifier. Using publicly-available data (DNA methylation, copy number, RNA-seq) and ongoing transcriptome sequencing through the LP, I am working to identify pathways through novel integrated bioinformatic techniques. The signal intensities from DNA methylation array data can be used to infer copy number data, chromatin accessibility (Hi-C A/B compartments), and methylation of repetitive sequences such as Alu and LINE-1 elements. I will computationally integrate these independent data types in order to identify new tumor types/subtypes and potentially refine current classification schemes; this approach will likely reveal functionally-relevant subtypes since DNA methylation, gene transcription, and chromatin accessibility are tightly linked. In order to achieve this, I will apply novel integrative techniques such as density-aware spectral clustering, similarity network fusion (SNF), and Bayesian consensus clustering. Additionally, I will employ a recently described unsupervised factor analysis approach (multi-omics factor analysis, MOFA) to identify shared and distinct sources of variability among CNS tumors. This approach will also serve to identify latent factors that drive the variability in the data and reveal potentially targetable pathways.

project_title: Defining Roles for PSMA PET Imaging in Prostate Cancer
project_abstract_text: Clinical trial NCT05588128: Prospective Monitoring of Subjects With Biochemically Recurrent Prostate Cancer Using 18FDCFP has accrued over 100 patients in the first year and is the only study of its kind to evaluate these patients over time without therapeutic intervention. This is critical because the widely held perspective is that these patients are equivalent to what we have traditionally defined as metastatic castration sensitive prostate cancer as defined by CT and Tc99 in clinical trials heretofore. The data from this trial will likely demonstrate that is not the case and patients currently are being over-treated under incorrect presumptions. A trial using PSMA imaging analyzed by an AI platform has been in development for some time. It has been delayed because of resourcing issues at NCI, but I hope to open this trial in the next few months.

project_title: Inductive germ cell specification and self-assembly of sexually dimorphic gonads
project_abstract_text: Dr. Xintao Fan developed hybridization chain reaction protocols to visualize candidate aPSC and early germ cell biomarkers, including nanos and vasa homologs. He initiated a collaboration with Dr. Kedar Narayan and the Center for Molecular Microscopy to generate volumetric ultrastructural reconstructions of the anterior signaling center at the apex of the Mlig testis. Dr. Fan identified conditions critical to, and assisted with the capture of single cell RNA-Seq samples as part of a collaborative atlas-building project to identify cellular constituents of the reproductive system during development. Dr. Fan conducted initial analyses of scRNA-Seq data prior to his departure from the lab in April 2024.

project_title: Embryonic origin of adult pluripotent stem cells and anatomical systems during planarian embryogenesis
project_abstract_text: Our working hypothesis is that cycling piwi-1+ cells in early embryos are the cellular antecedents of adult pluripotent stem cells (aPSCs). We posit that stage-dependent changes in gene expression correlate, and are potentially causative, in effecting the embryonic to adult pluripotency transition. Clare Booth and I collected single cell RNA-Seq whole-embryo atlases for nine developmental stages encompassing this key cell fate transition and construction of the adult anatomy in the planarian Schmidtea polychroa (Spol). Clare created a de novo transcriptome mapping reference for Spol from paired-end, 100 bp Illumina sequencing reads using Trinity. The transcriptome encompasses samples from all Spol life cycle stages, as well as regenerating adult fragments. Clare performed quality control filtering, benchmarking, and annotation of the transcriptome and we are poised to begin analyzing the scRNA-Seq time course data in collaboration with Dr. Francisco Lobo, Staff Scientist in Bioinformatics for the NCI-Frederick Cancer and Developmental Biology Laboratory. We look forward to characterizing the changing lineage repertoire for the piwi-1+ cells during embryogenesis, and to performing trajectory analysis to generate testable hypothesis about lineage specification. In tandem, we have been developing functional assays that will answer key questions about piwi-1+ cell behavior during embryogenesis, including whether cells at different stages are clonogenic and multipotent, and whether pluripotency is an individual or collective property of piwi-1+ cells at different stages. These studies will also shed light on the contribution and regulation of nascent aPSCs to the establishment of livelong whole-body regenerative abilities late in embryogenesis.

project_title: Retroviral genetic modification of PBLs to optimize expansion for cell therapy
project_abstract_text: We are evaluating whether genes can be overexpressed in T cells and improve effector function. We have previously evaluated multiple constructs including overexpression of CD40 which improved CD8 T cell expansion, cytokine production and tumor killing. However this came at the cost of fratricidal killing of CD40L positive CD4 T cells in cultures. We have since narrowed our effort to overexpressing costimulatory molecules such as CD28, CD27, OX40, 41BB and ICOS. We have generated preliminary data showing these constructs can be combined in a pooled screen and tested in vitro. Our ultimate objective is to model a putative clinical trial that would test overexpression of a carefully selected number of endogenous T cell genes to study their effect of T cell persistence.

project_title: Targeting exploitable vulnerabilities in T-cell Lymphoma
project_abstract_text: Continuing progress has been made in my research program over the past year. A major effort has been the continuing development of the Clinical Trial Protocol 'A Phase I Trial of Anti-CC Chemokine Receptor 4 Chimeric Antigen Receptor T cells (CCR4 CAR T cells) for CCR4 expressing T-cell Malignancies including Peripheral T-cell Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (PTCL) and Cutaneous T-cell Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (CTCL)' (CCR4 CAR T-cell trial). The CCR4 CAR T-cell trial is a first-in-human study of autologous T-cells targeting CCR4 using a CAR-T construct with the intracellular 41BB domain providing co-stimulatory signaling, and I have refined the protocol to the point where it is ready for re-submission to the FDA as part of a New-Drug Application with the NCI Office of Sponsor and Regulatory Oversight serving as sponsor. In addition to providing a novel therapeutic means of targeting T-cell lymphomas, this study will provide insight into immunotherapy considerations when targeting malignant T cells from a clinical, translational, and even basic research standpoint particularly with study samples controlled by my lab. The lab continues characterization of potential targetable vulnerabilities in malignant T-cells using agnostic interrogation of our unique AITL cell lines. We have collaborated with Drs. Craig Thomas and Michele Ceribelli in the National Center for Advancing Translation Studies using the MIPE 6.0 platform to identify targeted therapy platforms for AITL using single and multi-drug screens of the AITL cell lines developed in the lab. We are combining this data with whole genome CRISPR screens as an orthogonal approach to interrogate which pathways are viable targets in AITL. CRISPR screens are additionally being performed in combination with drugs known to have activity against the cell lines and in some cases also in clinical trials of AITL to advance this study. From a basic science perspective, the lab continues to pursue an understanding of the basic mechanisms by which RHOA G17V and TET2 loss-of-function (LOF) mutations contribute to AITL pathogenesis. We have established a system to functionally assess the consequences of reversing the sequestration of Rho Guanine Exchange Factors (RhoGEFs) by the RhoA G17V protein, and we are exploring whether RhoA G17V protein causes subcellular relocalization of these binding partners by directly tagging germline RHOA. We are also testing whether there is an interaction between TET2 LOF with AITL cell line sensitivity to elements of the Polycomb Repressor 2 (PRC2) complex. We also have performed ATAC-seq profiling of multiple T-cell lymphoma cell lines and are comparing these to profiles of non-malignant T cells to better understand the epigenetic landscape of malignant T cells. Finally, we have bred multiple generations of mice and will soon launch experiments to test whether the order of TET2 LOF and RHOA G17V mutation has a functional consequence on the kinetics of T-cell lymphomagenesis. Finally, we have now established an infrastructure for regular generation of novel T-cell Lymphoma models. We are creating novel primagrafts from primary patient samples taken at NCI using subrenal capsular implantation and intravenous injection. We also are continuing attempts to generate cell lines from patient-derived xenograft models using culturing strategies which have worked previously.

project_title: Bench to Beside and Back translational immuno-onocology-Cures
project_abstract_text: Four CCR projects are currently supported by this Cancer Moonshot Bench to Beside and Back award: 1) TME informed NK cell therapy for pediatric sarcomas, led by Rosandra Kaplan (CCR) and Timothy Cripe (Nationwide Children's Hospital). The overall goal of this project is to develop natural killer (NK) cell therapy with TGF-beta imprinting that can be augmented through manipulation of the immune suppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) leading to improved NK cell-mediated anti-tumor immunity, and serves as a potential effective therapy for patients with relapsed pediatric sarcoma. Bone and soft tissue sarcomas are one of the most common solid tumors in pediatric, adolescent/young adult (AYA) patients. Despite improved outcomes due to advances in surgical local control and multi-agent chemotherapy, prognosis for patients who develop recurrent, metastatic, or refractory disease remains poor. For these patients, new therapeutic approaches are urgently needed. The team at Nationwide Children's Hospital (NCH) has developed a genetically modified feeder cell line that enables extensive ex vivo propagation of highly-active human NK cells from various sources, and this methodology has been evaluated in early-phase clinical trials for hematologic malignancies and brain tumors. 2) Targeting neuroendocrine tumors with DLK1 directed immunotherapy, led by Nitin Roper (CCR) and John Maris (CHOP). During the first year of the BtB award we have focused on Aim 1 of our proposal: defining the anti-tumor activity of ADCT-701, a novel antibody drug conjugate targeting DLK1, in neuroendocrine neoplams. In particular, the goal of Aim 1 was to assess whether there is activity of ADCT-701 beyond neuroblastoma, which has been the focus of Dr. Maris' laboratory, our extramural collaborator. The results of our experiments in Year 1 demonstrate evidence of ADCT-701 anti-tumor activity in multiple ACC pre-clinical models. Thus, based on these data, ACC is an indication in our upcoming clinical trial: 'A First in Human Phase I Trial with ADCT-701 in Neuroendocrine Neoplasms'. The IND for ADCT-701 has been FDA approved and we expect to enroll patients in this clinical trial later this year. 3) B2B and Back: CD22 and CD19/22 CAR immunotherapies for childhood leukemia, led by Naomi Taylor (CCR) and Crystal Mackall (Stanford). The Taylor and Mackall teams are carrying out clinical trials with identical CD22 and CD19/CD22-bivalent CAR vectors but the two sites are using different manufacturing procedures to generate the CAR-transduced T cells that are being infused into patients. The current proposal is to test the hypothesis that variability in CAR-T cell immunotherapeutic potential is affected by variations in manufacturing platforms and can be predicted through evaluation of antigen-dependent CAR-T cell activity. High throughput analyses of these parameters will be leveraged to optimize CAR manufacturing, evaluate divergent patient outcomes, and enhance durable responses in pediatric leukemia patients. 4) Alternative splicing of CD22 following Inotuzumab, led by Nirali Shah (CCR) and Andrei Thomas-Tikhonenko (CHOP). Recent work from the Thomas-Tikhonenko lab has shown that CD22 protein expression is highly dependent on the inclusion of exon 2, which is where the open reading frame begins (Zheng et al., 2022). When exon 2 inclusion is negatively affected by aberrant splicing, the number of transcripts capable of being translated is significantly decreased, resulting in the emergence of CD22-low variants. To identify suitable experimental models for mechanistic studies, we quantitated total expression and reads spanning different exon 1 junctions in a panel of lymphoid cell lines from the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (Ghandi et al., 2019). We observed that widely used NALM6 and REH cell lines differ in the relative abundance of the exon 2-skipping/non-coding CD22 mRNA variants, which were prominent in the former but not the latter. Using sgRNAs from the well-validated pooled Brunello library (Sanson et al. 2018) in NALM6 and REH cell lines we identified dozens of positive and negative regulators of CD22 expression that passed our stringent false discovery rate (FDR) cut-offs, with the CD22 gene predictably being the most significant regulator of its own protein expression. Further up on the list are known B cell-specific transcription factors PAX5 and EBF1, but also several RNA-binding proteins with potential roles in splicing. We are currently in the process of cross-referencing them with top correlates of CD22 exon 2 inclusion in B-ALL samples from the NCI. However, we are also prioritizing targets based on their known involvement in mRNA splicing as well as potential druggability.

project_title: Elucidating the role of thrombosis and inflammation in breast cancer metastasis
project_abstract_text: Project 1: To induce asymptomatic ischemic thromboembolic strokes, which are common in general population age over 50 with the incidence of 10-20%, microspheres (Fluoresbrite YG Microsphere 20um) are injected into right carotid artery in female Balb/c mice either 2 days before (day-2 group) or 7 days after (day 7 group) intracardiac 4T1-BR5 brain tropic murine TNBC cell injection. PBS injection is used as a control. At the endpoint (12 days after cancer cell injection), brain metastasis area was found to be significantly larger in the microsphere injection group than control group (P<0.05) in the day -2 group but not in the day 7 group. This suggests the importance of ischemic stroke in premetastatic or early metastatic niche. I will validate this phenotype by using a different murine brain tropic TNBC cell line model (E0771-BR5 in C57BL/6 mouse). Additionally, immunofluorescence staining to evaluate the predominant cells in brain (e.g. astrocytes, microglia, endothelial cell) to describe the tumor microenvironment and premetastatic nice (day 2, 3, 7 days after the microsphere injection) are ongoing. Once the second model confirms the phenotype, I will utilize single-cell RNA sequence to describe the microenvironment comprehensively. Project 2: To study the systemic effects of DVT on brain metastasis, in collaboration with Dr. Yogen Kanthi (NHLBI), I have developed a novel 'DVT-brain metastasis mouse model' by combining the well-established Electrolytic Inferior Vena Cava Model (EIM) with intracardiac 4T1-BR5 brain tropic murine TNBC cell injection in Balb/c. EIM DVT surgery was performed either 3 days (day 3 group) or 10 days (day 10 group) after intracardiac cancer cell injection to assess brain metastasis at the early or later colonization phases, respectively. I have found that at the endpoint (12 days after intracardiac cancer cell injection) the group with DVT has significantly larger brain metastasis than that without in the day 3 group but not in the day 10 group. This suggests that the systemic effects induced by DVT is more important at early time point of brain metastasis. I will validate this phenotype by using a different murine brain tropic TNBC cell line model (E0771-BR5 in C57BL/6 mouse). The complete blood count tests at the endpoint demonstrated the trend of increase of neutrophils and eosinophils in the DVT group compared to the sham surgery group and the flow cytometry exhibited the significantly increased proportion of monocytes in CD45+ cells, which suggests the potential role of immune cells in promoting TNBC brain metastasis. Currently, immunofluorescence staining (e.g. astrocytes, microglia, endothelial cell, pericytes, neutrophils) to describe the tumor microenvironment and premetastatic niche (day 2, 3, 7 days after DVT or sham surgery) are ongoing. Once the second model confirms the phenotype, I will utilize single-cell RNA sequence to describe the microenvironment comprehensively.

project_title: Enhancing anti-tumor immunity in head and neck neoplasms
project_abstract_text: Major activities of our program include progress in both HNSCC and RRP. Our recent work on HNSCC has focused on the rationale sequencing of immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) immunotherapy and surgery for patients with newly diagnosed HNSCC. Previous mouse work in our laboratory revealed that ICB resulted in the development of durable, systemic anti-tumor immunity when administered prior to surgical resection of tumors but not when the ICB was administered after surgery. This observation was striking, but the mechanisms underlying this finding were unclear. To study this phenomenon in patients, we designed and completed a phase II study of neoadjuvant ICB in patients with HNSCC and studying pre- and post-treatment tumor biopsies and blood samples. We observed that tumor-specific T cells became activated and expanded in the tumor after treatment. Additionally, we observed that tumors act as a reservoir for tumor-specific T cells through induction of a tissue residency gene expression program. With ICB treatment, a proportion of the tumor-specific T cells were released from the tumor into circulation, leading to enhanced systemic anti-tumor immunity. These data indicate that without neoadjuvant ICB treatment, most of a patient's anti-tumor immune response would be removed with surgical removal of the tumor. Conversely, neoadjuvant ICB induces egress of some T cells from the tumor, enhancing the patient's systemic immunity. These findings are the strongest scientific argument to date supporting the use of neoadjuvant ICB in patients with HNSCC. We next explored the mechanistic drivers of this tissue resident gene expression program in tumor-specific T cells in the laboratory and found TGF-b to be a major driver. In pre-clinical mouse studies, we observe that the addition of TGF-b blockade to ICB further enhanced the degree of systemic antitumor immunity that develops compared to ICB alone. Our ongoing work aims to determine if other pathways are involved in efforts to uncover more possible therapeutic strategies to enhance systemic anti-tumor immunity in patients with newly diagnosed HNSCC. Our recent work on RRP has focused on identifying non-surgical, medical treatment options for this rare, hard to treat disease. The standard-of-care treatment for RRP is repeat surgery to debulk disease and maintain a functional voice and airway. Our team has pioneered approaches to address the underlying cause of RRP, chronic HPV infection, with immunotherapy. Initial trials with immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) resulted in clinical benefit for some patients, but no patients were cured. Our correlative analyses on specimens from these trials revealed that ICB was not unleashing the activity of HPV-specific T cells in papillomas, due at least in part to the paucity of HPV-specific T cells present in these papillomas at baseline. We next worked with an industry partner to develop a therapeutic vaccine designed to generate new or expand existing HPV-specific T cells in patients with RRP. Phase I clinical study with this new vaccine resulted in robust clinical activity and protocol defined complete responses in 50% of patients. Correlative studies from this trial revealed significant, polyclonal expansion of HPV-specific T cells in the periphery after vaccination and the ability of these T cells to traffic and infiltrate into papillomas in responder patients.This work led to FDA Breakthrough Designation. We have now completed the phase II study, which is a statistically positive study with a 50% complete response rate. Plans are in place to apply for FDA accelerated approval and confirmatory clinical trial plans are taking shape. These data indicated that enhancement of peripheral HPV-specific T cell immunity can lead to papilloma destruction and clinical benefit in patients with HPV-driven neoplasms. Yet, therapeutic vaccination does not result in the expansion peripheral HPV-specific T cell immunity in all patients. Other approaches are needed to enhance systemic HPV-specific immunity in these patients. Adoptive transfer of autologous T cells engineered to express a T cell receptor (TCR) specific for HPV has proven efficacy in HPV-associated malignancies and could be a new approach for life-threatening cases of RRP. Treatment with chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells is not possible currently as no cell surface markers specific for HPV infected papilloma cells are known. A TCR-engineered T cell therapy approach necessitates the discovery of one or more TCRs that recognize antigen derived from HPV 6 or 11. Discovery of novel TCRs that target HPV 6 or 11 antigens is a major research effort currently in our laboratory.

project_title: Tumor organoids and cell polarity: models and mechanisms for cancer research
project_abstract_text: In our investigation of the mechanisms of drug resistance, we generated over-expression and knock-out models of RASGAP and investigated the mechanisms by which it regulates drug resistance by analyzing changes in gene expression and signal transduction. We optimized conditions for biotin labeling and identifying the cell surface proteins by mass spec analysis and completed analysis for 5 cell lines. In the process of optimizing an alternate cell surface labeling technique to complement the biotinylation approach. We are also in the process of generating patient-derived organoid models and generating cultures of autologous T cells from the patient's peripheral blood and initiating studies for conducting genetic screens.

project_title: Biochemical mechanisms cyclin-dependent kinases use to control cell division
project_abstract_text: Determine the substrates and mechanisms of mammalian cyclin-Cdk complexes during the first steps in cell cycle Background: The cyclin-dependent kinases Cdk4 and Cdk6 form complexes with D-type cyclins to drive cell proliferation. A well-known target of cyclin D-Cdk4,6 is the retinoblastoma protein Rb, which inhibits cell-cycle progression until its inactivation by phosphorylation. Recently, we have shown that cyclin D-Cdk4,6 docks one side of an alpha-helix in the Rb C terminus, which is not recognized by downstream cell cycle cyclins. This helix-based docking mechanism for cyclin D is shared by the p107 and p130 Rb-family members across metazoans. Mutation of the Rb C-terminal helix prevents its phosphorylation, promotes G1 arrest, and enhances Rb's tumor suppressive function. However, because Rb can be phosphorylated by other cyclin-Cdks and cyclin D-Cdk4,6 may target other substrates involved in cell division, identifying novel targets of cyclin-Cdk complexes will deepen our understanding how Rb and cyclin D-Cdk4/6 regulate cell-cycle progression. Proposed aims: Our specific aims are: 1) Utilize novel analog-sensitive Cdk4,6 to identify cyclin D-Cdk4,6 substrates across the proteome 2) Identify substrates employing helix-based docking. Experimental systems: I have engineered chemically inhibitable versions of Cdk4 and Cdk6 kinases. While creating analog-sensitive versions of many kinases in the Cdk family has been relatively simple, Cdk4,6 versions have proven more challenging and were considered impossible. Using the developed Cdk4,6 analog-sensitive alleles, we will apply quantitative phosphoproteomic analysis to identify peptides with altered phosphorylation states following specific Cdk4,6 inhibition in vivo. As an alternative approach, we will employ improved proximity-labeling based methods coupled with mass spectrometry to validate the hits from bioinformatic analysis or to characterize entirely new ones in a cellular context. The combined proteomics techniques will allow the identification of proteins interacting with G1 cyclin-Cdk complexes potentially uncovering new docking mechanisms and providing a more comprehensive understanding of the role of G1 cyclin-Cdk complexes. Progress: This work has been started by a special volunteer/visiting scientist and a postbaccalaureate in the laboratory. In addition, we have successfully recruited a postdoctoral fellow who, along with the postbaccalaureate (CRTA), will commence work on this project later in 2023. Moreover, all the essential equipment required for this research has been acquired and set up in the laboratory. Preparation of reagents for the quantitative biochemical assays is now complete, enabling us to conduct critical tests on our novel engineered version of Cdk4,6 kinase. Initial in vitro biochemical assays have already been performed, confirming the activity of the novel analog-sensitive Cdk4,6 kinases and their inhibition by bulky ATP analogs. Next, we are creating cell lines with modified Cdk4,6 kinases to first validate and then perform above proposed experiments to find novel targets G1 cyclin-Cdk complexes. To identify targets phosphorylated through the helix-based docking mechanism, we carried out a proteome-wide bioinformatic analysis. Currently, we are in the process of purifying the identified candidate proteins to evaluate their interactions with G1 cyclin-Cdk complexes. This will be achieved using quantitative biochemical assays to determine if these proteins are genuine substrates of the G1 cyclin-Cdk complexes. Determine promoter-specific RNA polymerase II regulation by cell cycle cyclin-Cdk complexes. Background: Cyclin dependent kinases (Cdks) and cyclins are the key regulators of proper cell cycle progression, phosphorylating their specific target proteins depending on the specific cell cycle phase. Recently, my work showed that in yeast, cell cycle G1 cyclin-Cdk complex directly phosphorylates and regulates RNA polymerase II activity at specific promoters, leading to transcriptional changes critical for the G1 to S phase transition. However, our understanding of how cyclin-Cdk complexes directly regulate transcription through modification of RNA polymerase II in cells during different cell cycle phases remains limited. Proposed aims: Our specific aims are: 1) to understand the molecular mechanisms by which cyclin-Cdk complexes regulate transcriptional changes in a promoter-specific manner during cell cycle, 2) to study how these changes in transcription affect cell cycle progression in normal and cancer cells. Alternatively, should the Cdk-dependent transcription not regulate cell cycle progression, we aim to study whether it is needed for other described non-canonical roles of cell cycle Cdks, including, but not limited to aging, cell differentiation, metabolism, and cell growth. Experimental systems: We will employ a combination of in vitro quantitative biochemical assays, state-of-the-art methods to determine protein-DNA and protein-protein interactions, transcriptomic methods, and genetic screens to determine functional interactions in different cells. We will also use advanced imaging techniques to study the cyclin-Cdk-RNA polymerase II interactions and the effects of cyclin-Cdk binding on transcription kinetics in live cells. Progress: Work on this question has been started by pre-doctoral IRTA student doing rotation in the laboratory and by summer student. In addition, we have successfully recruited two postdoctoral fellows who are set to join the laboratory in second part of 2023. They will be employing either the budding yeast or mammalian system as a model to investigate our research questions proposed above. In preparation for their research, all the essential equipment required for this project has been procured and properly set up in our laboratory, ensuring a fully functional workspace. Moreover, we have made substantial progress in preparing the key reagents necessary for conducting quantitative biochemical assays essential for this project. During this, we have set up a workflow to biochemically reconstitute a key complex required to test our hypothesis described above. We have also generated a key tool, phosphor-specific, antibody to critically test our ideas in cells. As part of the initial biochemical proof of principle experiments, we have performed some crucial assays, testing validity of our proposed approach.

project_title: Development of new treatments for rare CNS tumors
project_abstract_text: My investigator-initiated, IND Phase I/II clinical trial using a Pegylated form of SN38 (PLX038) to test efficacy and predictive markers was approved by the IRB and activated in January 2024 (NCT06161519). To date, 3 participants have been enrolled to the Phase I component of the study. My multi-center basket clinical trial (NCT 03173950) has continued enrollment. Cohort 2 interim data was analyzed and the threshold of disease control rate was reached and surpassed, allowing continuation of enrollment. In collaboration with the pathology team, I lead a multi-center study across the BTTC/CONNECT consortium to collect tumor tissue and structured clinical information in deceased and lost to follow-up adults with rare CNS tumors. Clinical data abstraction has now been completed. Molecular testing is currently underway, with approximately 57 tumor samples pending analysis. Starting in 2020, the weekly multidisciplinary NIH Neuro-Oncology Tumor Board was transitioned to a virtual format and expanded to include NCI-CONNECT consortium sites and neighbor institutions in the area NIH geographic area under my leadership. In collaboration with the information technology team, the database to assist with the logistics of the tumor board, serve as an educational repository of cases and allow interrogation of the database for research purposes has now ben finalized. Retrospective data entry of previously presented cases is underway and approximately 40% completed.

project_title: Proteostasis regulators in blood cell development and function
project_abstract_text: It is now well-established and widely appreciated that the maintenance of genome integrity is essential to the development and homeostasis of mammalian cells including hematopoietic cells. However, despite the fact that the proteome constitutes the largest macromolecular 'universe' in cells, how maintenance of proteome integrity ('proteostasis') regulates immune cell fate and function remains poorly understood. The goal of research in my lab is to understand how hematopoietic cells sense and resolve proteostasis perturbations or proteotoxic stress. In addition, we seek to understand how proteome homeostasis signaling pathways are integrated to and shape the differentiation of hematopoietic cells. Lastly, as dynamic engagement of the translational and proteostasis machinery is required for immune cell differentiation and function, we investigate how defects in proteostasis regulators contribute to immune cell dysfunction and blood cancers. We address these questions using state-of-the-art transcriptomics, genomics, and proteomics to dissect how loss and gain of key mediators of the unfolded protein response (UPR) and the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS) impact normal and malignant blood cell development and function in animal models and relevant human samples. To date, our studies have uncovered fundamental novel mechanisms of hematopoiesis and blood cancers. First, given that stringent regulation of protein synthesis is vital to the hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) that generate the blood system, a considerable aspect of our work and finding is that UPR regulators safeguard HSCs and restrict myeloid leukemias in blood cell progenitors. Second, following our discovery of the protein CHMP5 as a regulator of the UPS in developing thymocytes, we have identified CHMP5 as an essential driver of the T cell leukemia gene program, a finding that links defects in UPS-dependent proteostasis with T-cell leukemia induction. Finally, we have uncovered that T cell function in disease requires the UPR such that UPR deficiency precipitates T cell dysfunctional states like T cell exhaustion, which is a problem in chronic viral infections and cancers. Our long-term goal in these studies is to generate fundamental knowledge on the role of proteostasis in immune cell biology and harness our understanding of these proteostasis pathways in the design of novel and potent therapies against blood cell diseases.

project_title: Checkpoint inhibitor treatment for EBV+ lymphoma among HIV+ individuals
project_abstract_text: We have enrolled over 15 patients and we see complete responses in EBV driven tumors. Enrollment continues to determine the durability of responses. We have witnessed complete responses in patients with CNS involvement that have been durable and no sign of relapse suggesting that this approach alters the natural history of the disease. In other EBV-LPDs, we have seen CR that last beyond the prescribed timeframe of 12 months also suggesting that durable remissions are possible. Enrollment has been slow due to the rare nature of these diseases.

project_title: Pb212 VMT alpha NET in treatment and re-treatment of SSTR+ tumors
project_abstract_text: Study is in the process of opening for enrollment but is currently not open yet. The study has been approved by the National Institutes of Health Central Institutional Review Board but is awaiting other site-initiation activities. We expect the study to be open to participant enrolled towards the end of the calendar year 2024. This project is in collaboration with our industry partner Perspective Pharmaceuticals. Once the study opens, we expect to reach full accrual within three to five years approximately.

project_title: Long-Read DNA Sequencing and RNA Sequencing in LFS-Like Families
project_abstract_text: We completed long-read DNA (Nanopore) sequencing and RNA paired-end sequencing (NextSeq 2000 P3 Illumina Total RNA with Ribo Zero Plus) on whole blood 21 patients classified as having LFS-like syndrome, 16 of whom have a history of cancer and 5 of whom are unaffected relatives. All patients have undergone prior validation that they do not have TP53 mutations, with 12 patients having undergone exome testing and 3 total families. We have also completed initial RNA-seq bioinformatic processing with QC assessment and alignment, count data, as well as initial read alignment and variant calling (indels and structural variants) with Clair and Severus. Annotation and filtering are in progress.In our preliminary data, we found in the RNA that the samples did not demonstrate unusual relative expression of TP53 compared to housekeeping genes (vs. 'normal' samples in GTex). In the DNA, we observed the following: 50 variants in 43 genes shared across >=2 samples with any ClinVar-annotated pathogenic/likely pathogenic annotation, 44 variants = at least one modifier annotation; 21 variants = at least one predicted high impact of variant, 80 single-nucleotide variants (unannotated) shared across all samples, 4531 structural variants (unannotated) shared across all samples. This work-in-progress was presented at the 2024 Vanderbilt-Ingraham Cancer Center Research Day conference.

project_title: IDENTIFY Study: Natural History of Maternal Neoplasia
project_abstract_text: This trial was transferred to another institute (NHGRI) as of January 2024 therefore reporting on the full progress over the year will be completed by the new PI of the trial via NHGRI. CCR did support recruitment efforts to this trial between August 2023 and Jan 2024. The trial is still actively recruiting patients on this study. https://classic.clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04049604. Anticipated initial results of clinical NIPT testing and correspondence with lab and imaging for malignancy are expected.

project_title: Regulation of BRD4 Function
project_abstract_text: Bromodomain 4 (BRD4) is a key regulatory factor in multiple cancers and cellular stress responses with pleotropic functions. BRD4 regulates chromatin remodeling and transcription through its histone acetyltransferase (HAT) and kinase activities, respectively. The mechanism responsible for switching BRD4 from a chromatin to transcriptional regulator is currently unknown. Here, we report that in response to a broad range of stimuli, this switch is mediated by the JNK kinase which directly interacts with BRD4. JNK specifically phosphorylates human BRD4 at Ser1117, Thr1186 and Thr1212, triggering transient BRD4 release from chromatin. JNK phosphorylation of BRD4 halts its HAT-mediated chromatin regulation and activates its transcription-enhancing kinase function. BRD4 release from chromatin is necessary to toggle between its enzymatic activities: chromatin-bound BRD4 is kinase inactive and RNA Pol II-bound BRD4 does not acetylate chromatin. BRD4 release from chromatin augments its interaction with and phosphorylation of key transcriptional regulators RNA Pol II, PTEFb and c-MYC. The PP4 phosphatase dephosphorylates JNK phosphorylated BRD4 in the nucleoplasm, which promotes its interaction with RNA Pol II at transcriptionally active sites. Accordingly, JNK-mediated release of BRD4 from chromatin leads to significantly elevated transcription of BRD4-regulated immune and inflammatory response genes through enhanced BRD4-Pol II interaction at the promoters of these genes. JNK phosphorylation of BRD4 occurs during thymocyte activation and is required for epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) in prostate cancer cells. These findings thus characterize a novel mechanism that triggers the transition of BRD4 from a chromatin regulator to transcriptional activator during stress/immune/inflammatory responses and EMT.

project_title: The role of SMARCA1 in Rhabdomyosarcoma and Skeletal Muscle Differentiation
project_abstract_text: Phenotypic studies showed that SMARCA1 knockout FP-RMS cell lines showed a dramatic decrease in cell confluency and viability after trametinib treatment. Interestingly, trametinib increased SMARCA1 protein in FP-RMS cell lines. It was also found that SMARCA1 deletion reduced cell migration and prevented these cells from developing spheres, unlike control cells, which healed the migration gap and formed spheres. Gene clusters in RMS transcriptomic data showed that SMARCA1 co-expresses with RALA, a RAS effector. SMARCA1, in addition, is clustered with HDAC2. As demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation, SMARCA1 and HDAC2 also interacted in RMS cells. According to our findings, SMARCA1 might influence the proliferation of RMS tumors. ATAC-seq and CUT-N-RUN experiments in SMARCA1 KO cells have been completed and the data analysis is proceeding.

project_title: Unlocking mechanisms of resistance to targeted therapy in thyroid cancer
project_abstract_text: Our major goal is to identify new determinants of resistance to targeted therapy and more specifically to BRAF inhibitors in advanced and metastatic thyroid cancer. Our overall hypothesis is that BRAFV600E driven-ATC cells heavily rely on certain genes or key pathways to survive canonical treatments targeting oncogenic BRAF, We have performed a CRISPR knockout (KO) and activation screen using a focused library. This screen has identified a gene exhibiting synthetic lethality in anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) in response to treatment with a BRAF V600E inhibitor. Our findings have been validated both in vivo and in vitro. We are currently collaborating with Genentech to confirm these findings in preclinical models.

project_title: Valemetostat in combination with pembrolizumab in head and neck cancer
project_abstract_text: Alemetostat (DS-3201) is an EZH1/EZH2 inhibitor that is actively being investigated in phase I and II trials for hematologic malignancies (non-Hodgkin's and peripheral T-cell lymphoma, AML and ALL) [NCT04703192, NCT04842877, NCT04102150]. Furthermore, valemetostat is being investigated in a phase Ib study in combination with ipilimumab in metastatic prostate, urothelial and renal cell carcinomas [NCT04388852]. However, valemetostat has not yet been investigated in combination withPD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor. Patients with R/M pembrolizumab-naive HPV-negative HNSCC have a low 6-month progression-free survival (PFS) (28%) with pembrolizumab monotherapy, thus novel interventions are needed to increase the efficacy of pembrolizumab. We hypothesize that treatment with valemetostat will enhance antigen presentation in HNSCC cancer cells and thus potentiate the anti-tumor effect of pembrolizumab in this patient population. Based on the above, we propose a phase Ib dose finding and safety study of valemetostat in combination with pembrolizumab. Once the safety and RP2D of valemetostat are determined, a single-arm phase II study of pembrolizumab in combination with valemetostat with a randomized lead-in phase of valemetostat or pembrolizumab will be conducted to assess the efficacy of valemetostat and pembrolizumab in front line R/M HPV-negative HNSCC patients. While this study opened, it was prematurely terminated due to withdrawal of the drug supply.

project_title: Biology and molecular vulnerabilities in SMARCB1-deficient tumors
project_abstract_text: During FY24, we examined solute transporters that may be important markers of chordoma tumors and/or targets for treatment. These studies may reveal metabolic dependencies that could be exploited for therapy as well. We have used novel reagents derived from retroviral binding domains to visualize the localization of solute carriers in tissue sections of organs (skin, kidney, stomach, and liver) and cancer tissue microarrays. We find distinct expression patterns for the different solute carriers in different cancers. We are using this information to learn more about the unique biology of rare tumors including chordoma. In addition, we worked with chordoma cell lines to optimize growth characteristics for high-throughput screening. Because the lines are very slow growing it has been difficult to maintain stable lines transduced with different markers. We are testing the hypothesis that different growth factors and extracellular matrix proteins may be needed to improve growth rates and are currently testing these factors.

project_title: Studying Immune Recognition of Epithelial Cancers Using Organoids
project_abstract_text: We are compiling reactivity data versus autologous organoids from patients undergoing adoptive T-cell therapy to investigate associations between organoid recognition and clinical response. We are also investigating the basis for recognition of organoids when no defined autologous neoantigen is found-- so called 'orphan' tumor antigens - in order to identify other classes of tumor antigens involved in response to adoptive cell therapy. Organoids will also be used to select among redundant off the shelf TCRs against common shared antigens for clinical use.

project_title: Identifying antitumor T cell receptors for cellular immunotherapy
project_abstract_text: Following my recent appointment as a Stadtman tenure-track Investigator at the National Cancer Institute, Center for Cancer Research I have now acquired key reagents and the necessary equipment and technology for carrying out my research. I have also recruited postdoctoral fellows and postbaccalaureate fellows to initiate these studies. Our efforts utilizing DNA-barcoded HLA-multimers as well as single cell proteomic and transcriptomic sequencing has resulted in the identification of 11 new neoantigen-specific T cell receptors (TCRs) targeting mutated KRAS against one of the most common hotspot mutations across all human cancer. In addition the HLA-haplotypes associated with these TCRs. These TCRs are part of a new invention that is now filed by the National Cancer Institute (T CELL RECEPTORS AGAINST RAS WITH G12D, G12V, G13D OR Q61R MUTATION, EIR ID: E-161-2024-0-US-01. The 11 anti-mutant RAS TCRs include: 1) Five human TCRs targeting mutant RAS G12V position restricted by HLA-A*11:01 one of the most common HLA class I alleles targeted by CD8+ T cells; 2) One human TCR targeting mutant RAS G12D position restricted by HLA-DRA1DRB1*04:05 targeted by CD4+ T cells. 3) 4 human TCRs targeting mutant RAS G13D position restricted by DQA10505-DQB10301 targeted by CD4+ T cells 4)1 human TCR targeting RAS Q61R position restricted by DQA10101-DQB10501 targeted by CD4+ T cells. These TCRs will be further assessed for potential gene therapy as TCR-engineered T cells.

project_title: Factors that influence age-dependent Ras mutant cancer development in mice
project_abstract_text: This proposal aims to understand how the aging tissue environment can influence tumor initiation and tumor development. We hypothesize that both cell-autonomous mechanisms involving the aging cancer initiating cells and cell non-autonomous mechanisms involving the aging immune system play a role in this process. We plan to contrast two Ras-driven mouse cancer models - cutaneous skin cancer driven by Kras activation that arise from keratinocytes (ectoderm origin), and lung adenocarcinomas driven by Kras activation that arise from alveolar type II cells (endoderm origin) - to understand how their developments differ between young and old mice in identical genetic backgrounds. We believe these models are ideal for examining age-induced change in tumor initiating cells and in macrophages to illuminate distinct differences in tumor development in a young vs. old host. Defining age-dependent tumor initiation by the Ras oncogene and down-stream Ras signaling pathway in mouse tumor models. We will compare the rate of tumor initiation and tumor growth in young (8 weeks) and old (12 months) mice for tumor initiation in the lung and in the skin. We will generate short-term in vitro culture of primary skin keratinocytes and lung alveolar type 2 (AT2) cells and activate the Ras oncogenes using adenoviral-Cre. The tumorigenicity of the resulting cells will be assessed by transplanting them into syngeneic young and old recipients orthotopically and then monitoring tumor growth. Using the generated tumors from young and old mice and primary cell culture from young and old mice, we will conduct phospho-proteomic analysis to profile kinome activity using the software recently developed in the Cantley lab that predicts the kinases that are most activated or inhibited based on phospho-peptide changes between tumors from old vs. young mice. In parallel, we will conduct single cell RNA sequencing to profile age-induced changes in the clustering of tumor, stroma, and immune cells. Using these study models described, TAM abundance and localization will be analyzed in tumors from young vs. old mice. We will also carry out single cell RNA sequencing of these TAMs to understand differences in their gene expression profiles. We will transiently deplete macrophage in young vs. old mice and test the impact on lung metastasis of syngeneic Kras mutant cells. We will transplant bone-marrow-derived myeloid cells from young mice to syngeneic old mice, and vice versa, to test whether tumor development will be altered.

project_title: Studying phenotypic states of antitumor human T cells
project_abstract_text: Following my recent appointment as a Stadtman tenure-track Investigator at the National Cancer Institute, Center for Cancer Research I have now acquired key reagents and the necessary equipment and technology for carrying out my research. I have also recruited postdoctoral fellows and postbaccalaureate fellows to initiate these studies. Summary of studies: 1) We have initiated multiple studies understanding the phenotypic states of antitumor T cells in nontumor sources from cancer patients. These include studies understanding phenotypic states of neoantigen-specific T cells in pre-treatment circulating blood, and regional draining lymph nodes in cancer patients. We have completed and published a study defining transcriptomic and cell surface protein signature of CD8+ neoantigen-specific T cells in the peripheral blood of metastatic cancer patients. [Yossef et al, 2023, Cancer Cell. (Co-corresponding author)]. I anticipate completing the phenotypes of draining lymph nodes study by the end of 2024, or early 2025. 2) We have completed a study defining cell surface protein states of CD4+ neoantigen-specific T cells within metastatic tumors [Hitscherich et al, in preparation to submitted soon, Co-corresponding author]. We analyzed the single-cell transcriptomic states of 41 neoantigen-specific T-cell clonotypes from 4 patients to identify cell surface protein markers that best correspond to human T cell exhaustion transcriptional state. We have identified that cell surface protein expression of CD86 and ADGRG1 (CD4+ CD86+ and CD4+ ADGRG1+) had the highest sensitivity and specificity amongst single surface protein markers in enriching for human CD4+ antitumor neoantigen-specific TCRs from metastatic tumor deposits. Prospective isolation of combination markers suggested that CD4+ ADGRG1+ CD86+ T cells enriched and identified antitumor neoantigen-specific TCR that is currently being tested for TCR-engineered cell therapy for cancer patients. 3) We have completed and published a study defining cell surface protein signature of CD8+ neoantigen-specific T cells within metastatic tumors. [Chatani et al, Journal for Immunotherapy of Cancer, 2023 (Co-corresponding author)] We analyzed the single-cell transcriptomic states of 31 neoantigen-specific T-cell clonotypes from 5 patients to identify cell surface protein markers that best correspond to human T cell exhaustion transcriptional state. We identified that CD8+ CD39+ PD1+ TIGIT+ phenotype expressing T cells (TILTP T cells) highly enrich for antitumor neoantigen-specific T cells. However, TILTP T cells are terminally exhausted with limited cell proliferation capability, and antitumor function. Thus, TILTP T cells represent an ideal population to identify T cell clonotypes for TCR-engineered cancer cell therapies even while the populations themselves might be impaired due to profound T cell exhaustion.

project_title: Development of CAR T cells targeting T-cell malignancies
project_abstract_text: We have developed a series of CARs targeting the gamma-delta T-cell receptor (TCR). We have completed in vitro testing and some animal studies with these CARs. We have submitted an abstract on this work to the American Society of Hematology meeting, and we have recently filed a patent application for the invention of these new anti-gamma-delta TCR CARs. We have initiated preparations for a clinical trial testing these CARs to treat gamma-delta TCR-expressing malignancies. These are very rare and very aggressive malignancies that have limited treatment options. We have continued laboratory studies aimed at developing CAR T cells targeting T-cell malignancies that do not express the gamma-delta TCR.

project_title: Adoptive T-cell Therapies Targeting Mutations in Hematologic Malignancies
project_abstract_text: In the past year, we have continued to make substantial progress in preclinical studies of neoepitope-specific TCR-expressing T cells. We have now proving that neoepitope-specific T cells can effectively treat hematologic malignancies in mice. We have completed in vitro studies on 7 neoepitope-specific TCRs. We have written a clinical protocol to test these TCRs in humans, and this protocol is proceeding through the very lengthy regulatory approval process to allow us to open a phase I clinical trial sometime in 2025.

project_title: NCI-Alliance immune-related Adverse Events (irAE) Biorepository-Cures
project_abstract_text: This project will leverage the clinical trials infrastructure of the National Clinical Trials Network (NCTN) to help develop a greater understanding of the mechanisms of immune-related Adverse Events (irAE) through supporting the ongoing development of a novel resource of tissues and gut microbiome samples from patients with irAEs. Analysis of samples will include stool microbiome metagenomics sequencing. Patients experiencing irAEs will have tissue, blood, and potentially stool collections obtained on an event-driven basis.

project_title: Development of small-molecule autophagy modulators
project_abstract_text: Autophagy has been implicated as a potential therapeutic target in numerous human diseases. My laboratory aims to discover novel autophagy modulators to better understand the fundamental roles of this pathway in human health and disease.
